* devices: switch data-usage to daily nlbwmon fan-out, drop intra-day period

The previous data_usage implementation called `nlbw -c json -g mac,interval`
with a single start-date, which doesn't return per-day points the chart needs
and silently produced empty results when archives were missing. Replace it
with a per-day fan-out:

- Fetch `nlbw -c list` once to learn which YYYY-MM-DD archives are retained,
  then run `nlbw -c json -g mac -t <date>` for each day in the requested
  window (8-way `buffer_unordered`). Days not in the archive set are
  zero-filled, so the series is always dense and oldest-first.
- Drop the `Day` period — nlbwmon archives are daily, so intra-day points
  were never real. Periods are now week (7d), month (30d), and 3months (90d).
- Add `ymd_to_days` / `parse_ymd_to_days` / `lookup_mac_bytes` helpers with
  unit tests covering round-trip dates, malformed input, and missing MACs.
- Persist `/etc/nlbwmon/data/` across sysupgrade so history survives updates.

chore: rework manage-release.sh into a top-level, project-parameterized release tool (#3384)

* chore: rework manage-release.sh into a top-level, project-parameterized release tool

Move projects/start-os/scripts/manage-release.sh back out to
scripts/manage-release.sh and generalize it from a start-os-only helper into a
monorepo-wide release driver: `./scripts/manage-release.sh <subcommand> <project>`.

Each project's version is read from its canonical manifest (Cargo.toml, or
package.json for start-sdk) and its git tag / GitHub release is
`<project>_v<version>` (the convention already in the tag history).

Subcommands:
- pre-check          changelog documents the version + version not already tagged/released
- pull-gha           download build artifacts from a GitHub Actions run
- pull               download released assets from their official location (registry/apt/GH release/npm)
- tag                create + push the <project>_v<version> tag
- create-gh-release  create/update the GitHub release with generated notes
- push               upload to the applicable destination (S3 / GH release / apt / npm)
- index              register + index the version in the registry (os only)
- sign / cosign      GPG signing as before, scoped to the project's release
- notes              print release notes
- release            run the full applicable pipeline per project

Per-project behavior is driven by a "kind": os (iso/squashfs -> S3 + registry
index), cli (per-triple binaries -> GH release), deb (start-tunnel/start-registry
-> apt repo + GH release), npm (start-sdk -> npm publish; changelog already ships
in dist via the SDK Makefile). The npm release is pre-check -> tag -> npm-publish.

start-cli has a `cli-deb` build target but CI only shipped the raw per-triple

  mislabeled "Build Debian Package" name.

  notes list the Pi image under "Image Downloads".
- FORCE=1 now also downgrades pre-check's "already released" guards (tag exists,
  OS version in registry, GitHub release exists) from hard failures to warnings,

Follow-up to review: S3 upload + registry indexing now live in the startos-iso

fix: resolve OS root device from its live mount, not the overlay / fstab entry (#3389)

fix: resolve OS root device from its live mount, not the fstab / entry

At runtime StartOS's `/` is an overlayfs the initramfs stacks over the
real OS partition, so the `/etc/fstab` `/` entry never names the backing
block device — its source is the pseudo-fs token `overlay`, which
`OsPartitionInfo::from_fstab` fed to `blkid -t overlay`, erroring
"blkid: -t needs NAME=value pair" and leaving `root` empty. An empty
root is harmful: `disk::util::list` uses `OsPartitionInfo::contains` to
mark the OS partition `internal`, so the OS disk would show up as an
available data/backup disk.

The OS root device also can't be taken from "whatever the system booted
from": during os_install we boot off the installer USB, which is not the
OS root this struct describes. The initramfs bind-mounts the real OS
partition at `/media/startos/root` on every installed-system boot, so
that mount is the source of truth — present only on a running installed
system, and correctly absent (yielding no OS root) in the live installer.

Resolve `root` from that mount via `get_mount_source`, read only the real
`/boot*` block-device mounts from fstab, and guard `resolve_fstab_source`
so a non-TAG=value source never reaches `blkid -t`.

fix: unbreak CI — drop make -t-incompatible dist co-target + repair getServiceInterface call site (#3393)

* fix: revert start-core/SDK dist co-target — it breaks CI's make -t flow

#3391's grouped `dist/package.json dist/node_modules/.package-lock.json &:`
co-target (to force a rebuild when the bundled node_modules is missing) is
incompatible with the ISO build's "Prevent rebuild of compiled artifacts"
step, which runs `make -t compiled-<arch>.tar` to mark the downloaded
artifacts current. `make -t` reaching the group via `dist/package.json`
touches only that target, NOT the grouped sibling stamp — so the stamp stays
missing and `make startos-iso` re-runs `make -C start-core dist`, which
cascades into a web-UI rebuild that reads an empty config.json and fails
(`Unexpected end of file in JSON`). Restore the plain single-target rule,
which `make -t` suppresses cleanly. Keeps the projects/start-sdk ls-files
dead-edge fix.

The deb job recompiled start-cli from scratch instead of consuming the
binary already produced by the Build Binary (compile) job, and both
matrices keyed off a nonexistent `platform` dispatch input, so the
manual arch picker was a no-op that always fell through to ALL.

  prerequisites so `make cli-deb` skips the redundant recompile

  and mismapped the darwin triple

fix(container-runtime): build image node_modules with --install-links (#3401)

install-dist-deps.sh produces the node_modules that ships in the container
image. It used `npm ci`, which only recreated the `@start9labs/*` file: deps as
symlinks and installed none of their transitive runtime deps. Those deps (e.g.
zod-deep-partial) were then resolved at build time from a hoisted parent
node_modules that never ships in the image.

This only happened to work on clean checkouts, where zod-deep-partial sat nested
in start-core/node_modules and got carried in through the symlink + rsync
--copy-unsafe-links. On incremental builds npm dedupes it up to the shared root
node_modules, so the snapshot — and the image — lose it, and services fail to
start with a missing zod-deep-partial.

Switch to `npm install --install-links`, which packs the file: deps and installs
their full transitive tree as real files, making dist/node_modules self-contained
regardless of hoisting state. The dist/package-lock.json seed is dropped since
`npm install` regenerates a correct one.

feat(tunnel): IPv6 support — prefix delegation + PCP pinholes (WIP) (#3388)

* feat(tunnel): IPv6 address delegation foundation

Add an operator-configured routed IPv6 prefix to the tunnel and carve
per-client global addresses out of it, adapting to the prefix size: a /64
per client when the prefix is shorter than /64 (real prefix delegation),
a single /128 per client for a shared /64 (the common budget-VPS case),
or an indexed /128 for a longer-than-/64 prefix (e.g. DigitalOcean /124).

- wg6: address-allocation module (server_addr + client_v6), unit-tested.
- WgServer.ipv6 prefix field + server/peer/client WireGuard config
  generation carrying v6 addresses, gateway/DNS, and AllowedIPs (v6 is
  full-tunnel so replies from the delegated GUA return through the tunnel).
- set-ipv6 API + CLI to configure/clear the prefix (+ i18n, bindings).
- forward chain: accept client-originated IPv6.

Foundation for the tunnel IPv6 work; runtime dataplane (proxy-NDP, AAAA
DNS), UI, docs, and PCP v6 pinholes follow.

* feat(tunnel): proxy-NDP for on-link IPv6 client addresses

When the configured prefix is a /64 held on-link by a WAN interface
(Hetzner, Vultr), the VPS gateway resolves each client's global address
via Neighbor Discovery on the WAN link. The tunnel host now answers for
those addresses (net.ipv6.conf.all.proxy_ndp + `ip -6 neigh … proxy`) and
forwards to the client over WireGuard. Routed prefixes and per-client /64s
are delivered without ND, so they get no proxy entry.

Reconciled on every network sync and at startup; installed entries are
tracked so stale ones (client removed, prefix cleared) are withdrawn.

* docs(tunnel): IPv6 page, CLI reference, changelog, version bump

Document the new IPv6 delegation: a docs/src/ipv6.md page (linked in
SUMMARY), the `set-ipv6` command in the CLI reference, its generated
manpage, and a CHANGELOG entry. Bump start-tunnel 1.1.0 -> 1.2.0.

* feat(tunnel): IPv6 prefix settings UI

Add an IPv6 card to the tunnel settings page: shows the current routed
prefix, validates and saves a new one (`set-ipv6`), and can disable it.
Wires `setIpv6` through the api service (live + mock) and seeds the mock
db with `wg.ipv6`. Regenerates the tunnel TS bindings (SetIpv6Params,
WgServer.ipv6). Also syncs Cargo.lock for the 1.2.0 bump.

* fix(tunnel): address self-review findings on IPv6 PR1

- resync_v6: guard with a dedicated v6_lock, mirroring egress_lock, so
  concurrent config changes can't leave the tracked proxy-NDP map out of
  sync with the kernel neighbor table (major).
- client config: stop advertising an IPv6 DNS server (<prefix>::1) — the
  DNS proxy binds IPv4 only, and AAAA resolves fine over it; a dead v6 DNS
  entry caused latency/failures for v6-preferring stub resolvers (major).
- set-ipv6: also reject link-local prefixes (fe80::/10); a fat-fingered
  fe80::/64 would otherwise persist and break all client IPv6.
- UI validator: require an explicit /prefix in [0,128] (IpNet.parse does
  not enforce it, so a bare address slipped through to a backend error).
- docs: correct the CLI clearing syntax (omit --prefix, not "--prefix
  null"); note inbound IPv6 hosting is not yet supported; drop the v6 DNS
  claim; move the changelog entry under a [1.2.0] heading.

* fix(net): IPv6 policy-routing parity with leak prevention, and wg peer-PSK persistence

StartOS applied policy routing only to IPv4, so NetworkManager's forced
full-tunnel `::/0` captured the host's entire IPv6 default route into any
imported WireGuard gateway. A tunnel that carried an IPv6 address (e.g. a
StartTunnel with a delegated prefix) but couldn't route IPv6 blackholed
all of the box's IPv6, and a v4-only commercial VPN selected as the
default outbound leaked IPv6 straight out the ISP link.

Mirror the IPv4 policy-routing layer for IPv6 (NAT/reply-routing omitted —
IPv6 has no NAT here):
- wifi.rs: `ip -6 rule` pref 1000/1100 (main/default) above NM's per-tunnel
  `::/0` rules, plus a pref-1200 terminal blackhole so v6 with no usable
  route is dropped instead of falling through to NM's capture.
- apply_policy_routing_v6: populate each managed interface's v6 table
  (`1000 + ifindex`) with main's non-default routes plus a default — a real
  route when the interface can carry v6, else `blackhole default` so a
  non-v6 gateway selected as the default outbound drops v6 (leak guard).
- apply_default_outbound: install the v6 priority-74/75 rules (the desired
  set is family-agnostic, reconciled per family via new snapshot/reconcile
  helpers).
- gc_policy_routing: flush the v6 table for removed interfaces.
A gateway carries the box's IPv6 only when selected as the outbound
gateway, exactly like IPv4 — no hijack, no leak.

Also fix the in-place WireGuard update path (`Update2` + `Reapply`), which
persisted the interface private-key but silently dropped each peer's
preshared-key, so a re-issued PSK-using tunnel failed its handshake and
went dead (taking tunnel-routed DNS with it). Flag the peer PSK
system-owned (`preshared-key-flags = 0`) so Update2 persists it, matching
AddAndActivateConnection on the add path.

* feat(tunnel): validate IPv6 egress before delegating a prefix

A device with an IPv6 assignment routes all its IPv6 full-tunnel
(`AllowedIPs = ::/0`), so a prefix delegated on a server that can't
actually route IPv6 just blackholes the device's IPv6. `set-ipv6` now
hard-errors (leaving the config unchanged) when the server has no IPv6
default route, and logs an actionable warning when the prefix is neither
on-link on a WAN interface nor otherwise verifiable — catching a
misconfigured VPS at set-time instead of on the device. Adds a
`has_ipv6_default_route` helper.

* feat(tunnel): mark IPv4-specific columns in device and subnet tables

Rename LAN IP/WAN IP -> LAN IPv4/WAN IPv4 and IP Range -> IPv4 Range so the tables read unambiguously once per-subnet IPv6 columns are added.

* refactor(tunnel)!: per-subnet IPv6 instead of a global prefix

Drop the single global `WgServer.ipv6` in favor of an optional per-subnet
`WgSubnetConfig.ipv6`, so a server with multiple disjoint IPv6 allocations
can point different subnets at different prefixes. Allocation simplifies to
one `/128` per host with the tunnel IPv4 embedded (`prefix-network | v4`) —
uniform for the server and every client, stable, allocation-free, and
UI-computable. No per-device /64 delegation (StartOS containers use NAT6).

Backend:
- wg6: replace the 3-case client_v6/server_addr/ClientV6 with one host_v6.
- wg/db: remove WgServer.ipv6; add WgSubnetConfig.ipv6 (serde default, no
  migration). Server/peer/client configs source v6 per subnet.
- api: replace the top-level `set-ipv6` with `subnet <net> set-ipv6`,
  carrying the egress + deliverability validation keyed on that subnet's
  prefix. show_config derives the client /128 from its subnet.
- context: resync_v6 iterates per subnet (drops the global running index).
- i18n: about.set-tunnel-ipv6 -> about.set-subnet-ipv6.

Frontend:
- Remove the Settings IPv6 card; add the prefix to the subnet Add/Edit
  dialog + a subnets-table column; setSubnetIpv6 in the api services.
- Devices tables gain an IPv6 column computed in the UI from the subnet's
  prefix + the device's v4 (mirrors host_v6).

Docs/bindings/manpage regenerated for the per-subnet surface.

* fix: correct IPv6 rendering in the shared IP util + bound subnet prefixes

Adversarial review of the per-subnet IPv6 diff surfaced three real issues:

- **Library bug (root cause).** `IpAddress` rendered IPv6 by joining raw
  decimal octets (e.g. "32:1:13:184:…" instead of "2001:db8::…"), and
  `fromOctets`'s 16-octet path spun forever on a no-op `unshift()` when the
  9th octet was 0 — so `zero()`/`fromOctets`/`.address` on any computed v6
  hung the browser or produced garbage. Replace both the `.address` getter
  and `fromOctets` v6 paths with one correct `renderIpv6` (eight hex groups,
  longest zero-run collapsed to `::`). The tunnel devices IPv6 column now
  uses the library directly. Verified across all web projects (npm run
  check) — no consumer regressed.
- **Out-of-prefix addresses.** `host_v6` OR's the 32-bit IPv4 into the low
  bits, which only stays in-prefix for prefixes /96 or shorter; a /124 (or
  any >/96) escaped the delegated block silently. `set_subnet_ipv6` now
  rejects prefixes longer than /96, and the web validator mirrors the bound.
  Added a wg6 boundary test.
- **Stale comments.** Drop the "/64 delegation" / "per-client /64" asides
  left over from the old model in wg.rs and context.rs.

* fix(tunnel): support small IPv6 prefixes; use example addresses in tests

- Clamp the tunnel IPv4 to the prefix's host space in `host_v6` instead of
  rejecting prefixes longer than /96. A /64 keeps the whole IPv4; a smaller
  block (e.g. a /124) keeps only its low host bits, so the address stays
  in-prefix. Drop the >/96 rejection in `set_subnet_ipv6` and the matching
  cap in the web validator; mirror the clamp in the UI's device-IPv6
  computation. A /124 now validates and works.
- Replace the real host/prefix that had crept into tests and docs with
  documentation-range values (RFC 3849 `2001:db8::`, RFC 2606 example.com).

Verified: cargo test (22 tunnel tests, incl. a /124 case and every prefix
length staying in-prefix), UI computation matches host_v6 at runtime,
check:tunnel, build:tunnel, prettier.

* feat(tunnel): reject IPv6 address collisions between devices

Every host on a subnet gets a /128 out of the subnet's prefix with its
tunnel IPv4 clamped to the host space; on a block smaller than the IPv4
that can leave two devices sharing an address. Two devices must never
share one, so enforce uniqueness:

- wg6: `v6_conflict` / `first_v6_collision` helpers (+ unit test).
- add_device: auto-assign skips any IP whose IPv6 collides with the
  server (.1) or an existing device; an explicit colliding IP is rejected
  with a message naming the conflict. All inside the mutate, so atomic.
- set_subnet_ipv6: reject a prefix that can't give every existing host a
  distinct address, checked inside the mutate so a concurrent add can't
  slip a colliding device in between check and write.
- UI getIp: the suggested IP is IPv6-aware, so it never proposes a
  colliding address; a hand-typed one surfaces the backend error.
- docs: note the uniqueness requirement.

A /64 never collides (full IPv4 fits); this only bites on small blocks.

* fix(net): IPv6 CONNMARK reply-routing parity with IPv4

Mark inbound v6 connections by ingress interface (nft mangle in table ip6 startos), restore the mark on replies, and route via a priority-50 fwmark rule — so a reply to an inbound IPv6 connection that arrived over a tunnel (terminated on the host or DNAT'd to a service container) routes back out that interface. The v6 reply-routing layer was previously omitted, so those replies had no route back and were blackholed: inbound IPv6 over a tunnel was dead.

Remove the terminal pref-1200 v6 blackhole; the v6 default is chosen by metric like v4, and leak prevention stays per-gateway — a v6-incapable gateway selected as the default outbound gets a blackhole default in its own table, reached via the pref-75 catch-all. gc_policy_routing now cleans the pref-50 rule and per-interface table in both families.

Validated live device<->tunnel: host-terminated and DNAT'd-container inbound replies route back; a marked packet routes to its own table authoritatively over NetworkManager's ::/0 capture.

* chore(start-tunnel): fold unreleased 1.2.0 into 1.1.0

1.1.0 has not shipped, so the per-subnet IPv6 work tagged 1.2.0 belongs in 1.1.0. Collapse the version (Cargo.toml + Cargo.lock) and merge the changelog section. Update the IPv6 entry: device-side inbound hosting over IPv6 now works with StartOS 0.4.0-beta.10.

* feat(net): un-restrict external port 9050 for the tor service's bridge SOCKS binding (#3407)

9050/9051 were reserved for the 0.3.x host tor daemon, which no longer
exists; nothing host-side binds them in 0.4.x. Freeing 9050 lets the tor

no more dependent restarts on tor install/update/uninstall. 9051 stays
restricted (0.4.x tor uses a Unix control socket).

fix(net): derive StartTunnel PCP gateway from the subnet, not NM (#3410)

candidate_gateways sourced its PCP/NAT-PMP targets only from
NetworkManager's reported gateway (lan_ip). A WireGuard StartTunnel is
on-link — routed by AllowedIPs with no next-hop — so NM reports no
gateway and lan_ip is empty. Since a7c70599b removed the subnet-".1"
fallback, the client had no PCP target for the tunnel and sent nothing,
so no ports mapped over StartTunnel (SSL/SNI HOSTNAME and plain v4
forwards alike); the tunnel server's permanent, never-expiring forwards
masked this on boxes that had mapped before the regression.

Restore a fallback in candidate_gateways, scoped to InboundOutbound
(StartTunnel) gateways and applied per family only when NM gave no
gateway for that family, so a real router always wins:
  - v4: the subnet's first host. add_subnet normalizes every subnet so
    the server address IS hosts().next(), so this equals the real server
    for any subnet size.
  - v6: host_v6(client_prefix, server_v4) — the same mapping the server
    uses for itself. For this to be exact on a small block (a /124 packs
    <16 hosts, where a naive v4-bit swap would corrupt the prefix) the
    client needs the real prefix, so the server now renders the client's
    wg v6 Address at the delegated /prefix instead of /128. That declares
    the tunnel's v6 subnet on-link, symmetric with the existing IPv4 /24;
    the host still owns only its /128 and the server routes just that /128.

A legacy /128 client config yields no v6 candidate (skipped) rather than
a wrong one, degrading to the pre-existing behavior until re-provisioned.

fix(net): pass full settings to Reapply so tunnel update keeps the live PSK (#3414)

update_wireguard_config (net tunnel update / the "Update config" UI
action) called Device.Reapply with an empty settings dict. NM rebuilds
the applied connection without the peer preshared-keys in that path, so
the running wg device lost its PSK: the handshake with a PSK-requiring
StartTunnel died and everything riding the tunnel - visibly, forwarded
traffic - hung. The preshared-key-flags fix (48c4b0ccd) only repaired
persistence, which is why a reboot (full re-activation from the on-disk
profile) fixed it while the live device stayed broken.

Pass the same settings dict given to Update2 (peer secrets inline) to
Reapply so the applied connection carries the PSK onto the live device.

fix(net): skip NM link-local v6 gateways on StartTunnel interfaces (#3417)

NM can report a link-local v6 gateway for the wg connection, and
candidate_gateways accepted any LL gateway (the home-router case) — so the
subnet-derived StartTunnel fallback (#3410) never fired for v6 and every GUA
pinhole request went to an fe80:: the tunnel server doesn't own (WireGuard
links carry no link-local), timing out. Scope the LL acceptance to
non-InboundOutbound interfaces so a real router still wins and the tunnel's
host_v6-derived server address fills the v6 slot.

chore(start-wrt): retire the OpenWrt fork — build from pinned upstream + patches/overlay (#3413)

* chore(start-wrt): replace openwrt fork submodule with pinned upstream + patches/overlay

The OpenWrt image now builds from pristine upstream OpenWrt instead of the
Start9Labs/openwrt fork. build/openwrt-setup.sh fetches the release pinned in
build/openwrt-version (tag + integrity commit), hard-resets the gitignored
openwrt/ checkout, git-applies openwrt-patches/ (3 build-infra patches for the
git-cloned vendor kernel + a 6.18 kmod rename), and rsyncs openwrt-overlay/
(the SpacemiT K1 target, opensbi/uboot-spacemit boot packages, generic-6.18
stubs, one mac80211 build patch). The monorepo's last git submodule is
removed; cloning no longer needs --recursive.

Upgrading upstream is now: bump both values in build/openwrt-version, re-run
make startwrt-openwrt-setup, refresh any non-applying patch (see start-wrt
CONTRIBUTING.md "OpenWrt tree") — one ordinary PR, no fork rebase.

Validated: prepared tree is byte-identical to the retired fork tip c495c5abd9
(git tree hash match, incl. via a fresh clone from upstream exercising the
tag fetch + commit-pin verification); rebuilt image has an identical package
manifest and kernel (6.18.19) vs the last fork-era build; sysupgrade OTA +
boot smoke test passed on the BPI-F3.

* chore(start-wrt): fetch OpenWrt as a sha256-pinned tarball; drop the inner git repo

The openwrt/ build workspace no longer contains a git repo at all.
openwrt-setup.sh now downloads the upstream release tag tarball (pinned by
OPENWRT_TARBALL_SHA256 in build/openwrt-version, cached in openwrt/dl/ so it
rides the CI dl cache), extracts a pristine tree, applies openwrt-patches/
with patch(1), and rsyncs openwrt-overlay/ — replacing the git init/fetch/
checkout/apply mechanism from the previous commit. Generated state the tarball
doesn't provide (dl/, build_dir/, staging_dir/, bin/, feeds/, files/, .config,
signing keys, ...) is preserved across rebuilds; tar's stable archive mtimes
(plus re-stamping patched files) keep re-preps from invalidating build_dir.
The orphaned fork object store (.git/modules/projects/start-wrt/openwrt) is
pruned.

Validated: the tag tarball's content is byte-identical to the previously
pinned upstream commit (git tree hash match, modulo upstream's tracked-but-
ignored .vscode/settings.json which the tarball also carries verbatim), and
the rebuilt prepared tree again hashes to the retired fork tip's exact tree;
rebuild is idempotent and cache-preserving (19G build_dir survives).

Two-line pin bump in build/openwrt-version (version + tag-tarball sha256;

* fix(start-core): make the dist build cross-platform (Windows devs + direct make)

Two Windows-compat regressions from the monorepo migration era, fixed
without re-breaking Linux:

- The copy script's 'cp -a node_modules dist/' (which had replaced cpy
  because npm 10's empty optional-dep scope dirs made cpy fail on Linux)

  cross-platform, tolerates the empty scope dirs, preserves .bin

- The Makefile's 'rm -rf dist' is likewise unix-only, but swapping it
  for rimraf would break the direct-make path (build.mk's
  $(MAKE) -C ... dist on CI and Linux runs with a bare shell PATH where
  node_modules/.bin isn't visible). Move the wipe into an npm-script
  fs.rmSync one-liner and have the dist recipe call a single 'npm run
  build' (clean:dist + tsc + copy) — npm/node are the only commands the
  recipe needs, and they exist everywhere make does.

make clean stays plain rm -rf: it deletes node_modules itself, so a
node_modules-hosted tool can't do that job, and clean isn't part of the
Windows dev loop.

Verified: make -C shared-libs/ts-modules/start-core dist from a bare
shell; dist/node_modules diffs clean against node_modules (symlinks
intact, empty @emnapi/@napi-rs/@tybys dirs copied).

* chore(web): drop the rimraf devDep

Its only use was wiping .angular/cache in build:deps; a node fs.rmSync
one-liner (same idiom as start-core's clean:dist) does the job with no
dependency and identical missing-dir tolerance. Nothing else in the
tree referenced rimraf, directly or transitively.

Verified: npm run build:deps from a clean cache — rmSync ran, start-core
dist and the patch-db client both rebuilt.

* docs(start-wrt): drop the version-bump bullet from the changelog

feat(tunnel): honor PCP mapping leases + clear forwards on admin actions (#3416)

* feat(tunnel): honor PCP mapping leases and clear forwards on admin actions

StartTunnel parsed and echoed the PCP lifetime but never enforced it, so an
auto (PCP-created) forward, pinhole, or SNI route lived forever even after the
requesting device went offline, rotated its key, or withdrew the exposure.

Server: thread the granted lease into GatewayBackend::add_forward/add_pinhole
(PCP passes it; UPnP IGD stays permanent). Track auto mappings in an in-memory
lease table on TunnelContext and add a 30s reaper that tears down any auto
mapping whose lease lapses. Auto entries are re-leased on startup so a client
that never returns is reclaimed; manual forwards carry no lease and never
expire. In-memory (not persisted) so renewals never churn the DB.

Client (StartOS): renew each PCP mapping at ~half its gateway-granted lifetime
(crab_nat expiration()/lifetime()) instead of every 180s tick, keeping fast
retry for failed/not-yet-active mappings.

Admin actions now retire a device's exposure immediately rather than waiting a
lease: deleting a device or demoting it to a client clears all its forwards,
SNI routes, and v6 pinholes (fixes a v6-pinhole leak on delete); disabling
automatic port forwarding clears its auto forwards while leaving manual ones.

Docs + changelog for StartTunnel and StartOS updated.

* refactor(tunnel): event-driven lease reaper

Replace the 30s poll with a reaper that sleeps exactly until the soonest
lease expiry (found while it already enumerates them to reap), woken early
by a Notify when a stamp lands a sooner-expiring lease. No fixed-interval
wakeups, and expiry is reaped promptly instead of up to 30s late.

feat(net): block services from sending DNS straight to the gateway (#3418)

Services must resolve through the OS DNS proxy at 10.0.3.1:53, never by
querying a gateway or public resolver directly — the same posture already
applied to UPnP/NAT-PMP/PCP port-mapping.

Add an nftables forward-hook drop for DNS (udp/tcp 53) originating off the
lxcbr0 bridge to the egress guard table. DNS to the OS proxy (10.0.3.1) is a
host-local input-hook destination and is unaffected; only DNS forwarded out to
an external/gateway resolver is dropped. Scoped to the bridge ingress so
inbound DNS to a DNS-server package is never affected.

Generalize the guard table (startos_portmap_guard -> startos_egress_guard)
since it now covers more than port-mapping.

refactor(net): GUA WAN exposure via public flag — remove gua_access tri-state (#3411)

* refactor(net): replace the GUA access tri-state with gua_wan + public

Remove GuaAccess/gua_access from the data model. A GUA's WAN opt-in now lives
in a gua_wan set that update_addresses projects into HostnameInfo.public, so
public is the single source of truth for WAN reachability — services selecting
addresses for P2P see the correct flag, and net_controller's is_wan special
case collapses to .public. Enable/disable flows through the existing
enabled/disabled sets (a public GUA is opt-in via enabled, like public IPv4;
set-gua-wan carries the row's on/off state across the flip and recomputes
available). No db migration: the new field is serde(default) and the old
gua_access key is ignored on load — alpha boxes revert to LAN-only defaults.

* feat(start-os-ui): GUA rows use the standard toggle + Local/Public from the public flag

Every row now has the same on/off toggle (a public GUA routes through the
enabled set server-side); the access column's Local/Public dropdown reads
address.access — i.e. the projected public flag — and writes set-gua-wan. Mock
mirrors the backend: guaWan set, enabled carry, public re-projection.
Regenerated bindings (GuaAccess/BindingSetGuaAccessParams removed).

* docs(start-os): changelog — GUA exposure is a toggle + Local/Public dropdown

* fix lockfiles

* chore(patch-db): drop unused uuid dep from the ts client

The client never imports uuid, and its exact 8.3.2 pin combined with the
root uuid override made npm before/after 11.14 (arborist 9.5.0 started
propagating overrides through file: links) compute different lockfile
trees, so locks regenerated locally failed CI's npm ci with
"Missing: uuid@8.3.2 from lock file".

* fix(net): reject link-local v6 gateways on StartTunnel even when a subnet contains them

#3417 skipped an NM-reported fe80:: gateway on an InboundOutbound interface, but
the GUA pinhole still timed out via fe80::a3b:1. candidate_gateways also admits a
gateway that falls within one of the interface's subnets, and a WireGuard iface
carries its own fe80::/64 (NM assigns it) — every link-local shares that /64, so
`subnets.contains(fe80::a3b:1)` was true and re-admitted the link-local past the
guard. have_v6 then went true and the host_v6-derived server fallback never fired,
so PCP hammered an fe80:: the tunnel server doesn't listen on. #3417's regression
test passed only because its fixture omitted the iface's own fe80::/64 subnet.

- Reject a link-local v6 gateway on InboundOutbound before the subnet-contains
  clause can re-admit it, so the host_v6-derived server fills the v6 slot. A real
  router (gateway_type None) keeps its fe80:: default gateway.
- Never derive the tunnel server v6 from a link-local prefix.
- OutboundOnly gateways yield no candidates: candidate_gateways is the single
  chokepoint every port-map call site funnels through, so PCP is never attempted
  against an OutboundOnly gateway anywhere (drops the now-redundant per-site guard
  in net_controller and its unused import).

Regression tests cover the live-box fixture (fe80 gateway + the iface's own
fe80::/64) and the OutboundOnly-yields-nothing case.

* fix(net): skip link-local v6 gateways uniformly (address review)

Per review: once OutboundOnly returns no candidates, gating the link-local skip
on `== InboundOutbound` is redundant. A link-local address is never a PCP server
we can reach — a StartTunnel peer owns none on the wg link, and we don't pinhole
a router's LL v6 next-hop — so skip it for every gateway type. Collapses the
type-specific guard and the `is_ll ||` push path into one unconditional skip.

Home v4 port mapping is unaffected (the router still keeps its v4 gateway); only
a v6 link-local next-hop is dropped, which was never a reliable PCP target.

* fix(net): drive forwards only from addresses at the forward's port

Two symmetric leaks let an SSL-port exposure open its plaintext sibling:

- gua_forwards DNAT'd every enabled GUA to the container, including the
  assigned_ssl_port entry — the prerouting DNAT beat local delivery, so
  the vhost TLS listener bound on [GUA]:ssl_port never saw the traffic
  and the https:// address served the container's plain upstream.
- fwd_public/fwd_private for the plaintext v4 forward collected gateways
  from every public/private address, so opting only the https GUA (or
  any ssl-port address) into WAN marked the gateway public for the
  plaintext port's DNAT and upstream port-map.

Both now filter to addresses at the forward's own external port; the
docs book is synced to the GUA toggle + Local/Public remodel it missed.

* fix(net): never expose an insecure port to the WAN

An exposure reaches the public internet only when it is itself secure —
TLS on the wire (add_ssl terminates it, or the service does) or a
self-securing protocol (options.secure set). The gateway's `secure` flag
only ever authorizes insecure traffic on a LAN exposure; it is ignored
for the WAN, which is treated as never secure.

- forward.rs: evaluate the secure gate after the public/private split so
  an insecure public forward is blocked even on an operator-secure
  gateway (and its upstream port-map is not requested).
- net_controller gua_pinholes: no upstream pinhole for an insecure GUA.
- net_controller gua_forwards: block insecure GUAs from the WAN; on the
  LAN require a secure gateway, matching the IPv4 forward gate.

The secure-exposure predicate is per-address (a.ssl || options.secure),
so an add_ssl ssl-port GUA stays secure even when the backend is plain.

* fix(net): downgrade insecure public exposures to LAN, don't drop them

Addresses review on the WAN-secure gate: an insecure exposure the
operator tried to make public should still serve the LAN, just not the
internet. Instead of skipping the gateway entirely, treat an insecure
exposure as never-public so it falls through to the normal (source-
restricted) LAN path — both the IPv4 forward and the v6 GUA DNAT.

fix(net): restore WireGuard peer PSKs on the kernel device after Reapply (#3419)

NetworkManager <=1.52 drops WireGuard peer preshared-keys on
Device.Reapply even when they are passed explicitly in the settings
dict, so an in-place gateway config update (Update2 + Reapply) silently
loses the tunnel's shared secret — including for the gateway carrying
the request that triggered the update.

After the reapply, push each peer's PSK straight to the kernel device
with 'wg set <if> peer <pubkey> preshared-key /dev/stdin' (PSK over
stdin, never argv). The full-settings Reapply stays as-is so other peer
fields aren't stripped, and the wg-set becomes a harmless no-op re-set
if NM ever fixes the upstream bug.

feat(scripts): verify gha assets match the tagged commit in manage-release.sh (#3420)

pull-gha now fails before downloading unless the run's headSha matches the
commit the tag will be cut at (COMMIT, default HEAD), and records that sha
in a .gha-commit marker in the release dir. tag re-verifies against the
marker, so the guard also holds when the steps run in separate invocations.
pull clears the marker since it replaces the dir's assets from official
locations.

refactor(net): make gateway type non-nullable, default inbound-outbound (#3422)

NetworkInterfaceInfo.gateway_type was Option<GatewayType> defaulting to
None; collapse it to a non-nullable GatewayType defaulting to
inbound-outbound. The gateways UI already renders any non-outbound-only
value as "Inbound/Outbound", so this just aligns the model with the
behavior users already see.

Pre-release dev DBs persist `type: null` for auto-discovered gateways
(a None with no skip_serializing_if), and pre_init strict-deserializes
the whole db on every boot — so a bare non-Option change would fail to
load those nodes. A null-tolerant deserializer coerces absent/null to
the default; the boot round-trip then re-serializes the concrete value,
healing the persisted null. The tunnel-add CLI param stays Option so it
can still auto-detect the type from the WireGuard config.

fix(start-wrt): point beta registry constants at the live hostname (#3423)

The beta registry is now deployed at startwrt-beta-registry.start9.com
(the DNS record diverged from the beta-startwrt-registry placeholder).

manage-release.sh's STARTWRT_SOURCE_REGISTRY default.

fix(start-wrt): restore OpenWrt host deps in the CI image job (#3424)

The old standalone repo's setup-build action installed the OpenWrt host
build deps (flex, bison, swig, device-tree-compiler, ..., and the riscv64
binutils) in every job. The monorepo migration adopted the shared
setup-build action, which has no such step, and re-added binutils only to

the pre-monorepo openwrt/ location relative to the cwd; resolve it
script-relative so it finds projects/start-wrt/openwrt/staging_dir/ from

fix(tunnel): manual SNI (hostname) forwards no longer show as Automatic (#3426)

* fix(tunnel): store manually-added SNI forwards as manual, not automatic

The manual "add port forward" API and the PCP auto path both went through
the single GatewayBackend::add_sni_forward impl, which hardcoded auto:true
and label "PCP" on every SNI route. A hand-added hostname forward therefore
landed in the UI's Automatic table and, being treated as an automatic
lease-based route, could be reaped by the PCP lease reaper when no device
renewed it. (DNAT and v6-pinhole manual paths were unaffected — only SNI
shares one function between the manual and auto paths.)

Extract an inherent TunnelContext::persist_sni_forward(.., auto, label): the
PCP trait method delegates with (true, None); the manual API passes
(false, user_label). A pure sni_route_fields() helper decides a route's
(label, enabled, auto) — a brand-new route takes the caller's auto/default
label, an existing route preserves its own owner/enabled/label so a PCP
renewal can't hijack a manual route (and vice-versa). Unit-tested.

Also move the non-bindings tests in tunnel/db.rs to the bottom of the file.

* docs(tunnel): roll the manual-SNI-forward fix into the 1.1.0 changelog

* docs(tunnel): drop changelog entry — fix is for unreleased 1.1.0 work

fix(ci): stop master pushes from cancelling dispatched release builds (#3428)

All five product workflows shared one concurrency group per ref, so a
workflow_dispatch release build and any push run on master landed in the
same group and cancel-in-progress killed the dispatch — the start-wrt
beta.4 image build died 21 minutes in when an unrelated PR (touching
shared-libs/crates/, which correctly triggers the workflow) merged to
master. The old standalone repo carried the same stanza but only built on
tags/dispatch, so the collision surfaced with the monorepo's push triggers.

Scope the group by event_name so push/PR cancellation semantics stay
intact but can't touch dispatch runs, and evaluate cancel-in-progress so
a second dispatch queues behind a running one instead of cancelling a
multi-hour release build.

fix(tunnel): rebind device-bound listeners after wg interface reload (#3429)

* fix(tunnel): rebind device-bound listeners after wg interface reload

sync_network() bounces the WireGuard interface with wg-quick down/up on
every subnet/device config change. The PCP, SSDP, and IGD control
listeners are SO_BINDTODEVICE-bound, which pins the ifindex at bind
time, so the recreated interface left them deaf until a daemon restart —
client renewals went unanswered and their auto forwards, SNI routes, and
pinholes lapsed. The serve loops' error-restart never fired because a
stale device binding receives nothing rather than erroring.

Signal the bounce through a Watch in the tunnel context and select on it
in each serve loop, rebinding immediately.

The same bounce also made DnsProxyController::sync fail to rebind with
EADDRINUSE: aborting a proxy task only schedules the abort of hickory's
internal socket tasks, so the old sockets could still be open at rebind.
Shut down via the server's cancellation token and wait instead.

* refactor(tunnel): signal forward rebind with Notify instead of Watch<()>

Watch<()> carries no data — it's a Notify with extra machinery. Switch
the PCP/IGD rebind signal to tokio::sync::Notify: each listener enables a
Notified before binding (so a bounce during setup still triggers a
rebind) and sync_network wakes them all with notify_waiters() after the
wg-quick bounce.

Also drop the changelog entry, since the feature it fixes is unreleased.

feat(tunnel): per-IPv4 HTTP→HTTPS redirect on port 80 (default on)

Run the shared OS HTTP→HTTPS redirect (net::http::handle_http_on_https) on
port 80 of every public IPv4 the tunnel holds, so a plain http:// request to
an exposed service bounces to https:// instead of a connection error.

- On by default: `HttpRedirects.disabled` (a set of opted-out IPv4s) defaults
  empty, so fresh installs and upgrades both get redirects on every public
  IPv4:80 automatically — no migration or one-time seed needed.
- Reactive: a listener per address is reconciled from the db on every revision
  (mirrors the /webserver HTTPS block); a user toggle or a port-forward change
  takes effect with no restart.
- Mutually exclusive with a port forward: the redirect yields to any forward
  occupying port 80 on that IP (PortForwards::occupied), and resumes when the
  forward is removed.
- UI: a checkbox per public IPv4 on the Port Forwards page; CLI:
  `http-redirect list` / `set-enabled <ip> [--enabled]`.

Docs + changelog rolled into the unreleased 1.1.0.

Removes the v4 redirect-map request/withdraw path and its `redirect_maps`

fix(start-cli): stop rugging s9pk init-workspace users with a legacy ~/.startos

A leftover global ~/.startos (flat config + developer key from the pre-workspace
start-cli) tripped the nested-workspace guard, so any prior user couldn't create a
workspace anywhere under $HOME. The nested check now only treats a provisioned
.startos/ (build-key or schema config) as a workspace, so the legacy global dir is
ignored.

When a legacy ~/.startos is present, init-workspace explains the per-workspace model
and offers to copy the signing key -> workspace build-key and flat host/registry ->
default profiles. Migration is non-destructive: ~/.startos is never modified (it still
backs make install/publish auth). The prompt is synchronous (handler future must stay
Send) and skipped on non-interactive runs. An unreadable legacy key warns instead of
silently minting a new signing identity, and a partially-migrated workspace retries on
re-run rather than falling through to default config.

Two wrong locations are now refused with actionable guidance: running inside a package
repo, and initializing directly in $HOME (which would collide with ~/.startos).

Docs (environment-setup.md upgrade section + corrected make-config note), CHANGELOG,
i18n in all 5 locales, and unit tests included.

  never overlap, so only that nearest entry can reach into the new range.

fix(install): put the s9pk download back in the background (#3431)

The mirror-retry rewrite (#3217) made BufferedHttpSource::from_urls await
the entire download inline (download_from + wait_for_complete) before
returning, leaving a no-op task in _download. package.install awaits that
path before writing any install state to the db, so the initial RPC
blocked for the full s9pk download with no UI feedback — through a tunnel
outbound gateway that reads as a multi-minute hang.

Spawn the mirror-retry loop into _download as before #3217. Readers gate

already calls wait_for_buffered where completion matters. Adds a
regression test that reads the head of the archive while the tail is

refactor(start-cli): allow nested workspaces; drop legacy ~/.startos migration

Per review: nested workspaces are the intended model, not an error. init-workspace
no longer looks at or refuses enclosing workspaces — it just creates the workspace.
Building/signing/config already resolve by walking up from the cwd to the nearest
.startos/, so a nested workspace transparently overrides an outer one (conceptually a
deep merge of every .startos/ on the path; no actual merge performed).

Removes the nested-workspace guard, the home-directory guard, and all legacy
~/.startos migration (detection, interactive prompt, key/config copy). The one guard
kept is refusing to initialize inside a package repo — a workspace holds package

Docs, CHANGELOG, and i18n updated to match; unused migration i18n keys removed.

`build_key()` surfaces a context-aware error: inside a package repo it names the parent
(where the workspace belongs) with a copy-pasteable `cd <parent> && start-cli s9pk
init-workspace`; elsewhere it explains the workspace model and points to init-workspace.

Docs + CHANGELOG updated; new i18n keys in all 5 locales; unit test for the error path.

A non-technical person following the guide verbatim now gets a working

fix(install): keep UploadingFileReader wakers registered across polls (#3432)

* fix(install): put the s9pk download back in the background

The mirror-retry rewrite (#3217) made BufferedHttpSource::from_urls await
the entire download inline (download_from + wait_for_complete) before
returning, leaving a no-op task in _download. package.install awaits that
path before writing any install state to the db, so the initial RPC
blocked for the full s9pk download with no UI feedback — through a tunnel
outbound gateway that reads as a multi-minute hang.

Spawn the mirror-retry loop into _download as before #3217. Readers gate
on Progress, which already surfaces download errors, and cli_download
already calls wait_for_buffered where completion matters. Adds a
regression test that reads the head of the archive while the tail is
still streaming.

* fix(install): keep UploadingFileReader wakers registered across polls

UploadingFileReader::poll_ready{,_for} created a fresh watch wait_for
future, polled it once, and dropped it — dropping a watch future
deregisters its waker, so a progress update landing between polls was
lost and the reader hung forever. Latent since the reader was
introduced: production reads gate through UploadingFile::fetch (a real
await), so only fetch_all on a still-downloading file hits the poll
path. #3431's background download exposed it — the buffered-download
tests read via fetch_all mid-download, hanging the test suite.

Store the wait future across polls, keyed by wait target. Also gate
poll_read on "data available at position or transfer finished" instead
of ready_for(position + buf.remaining()), which spuriously errored with
"file size is less than requested" whenever the destination buffer
overshot the file size mid-download.

* fix(install): tolerate mirror-retry truncation in UploadingFileReader reads

A full mirror retry resets the download file (set_len(0)) and can land
between the DataAt gate resolving and the file read, so poll_read saw a
shortened file and returned a false EOF mid-transfer (flaked the two
full-retry tests in CI). Only report EOF when progress shows a clean
complete with no bytes left past our position; otherwise self-wake and
retry the read.

Also: return Ready immediately for zero-capacity read buffers; check the
wait predicate synchronously before allocating a wait future (the
data-already-available case previously boxed a future + cloned the
receiver on every chunk); collapse ready/ready_for/data_at into one
Progress::check + Progress::wait pair so the gate logic exists once.

ci: skip startos-iso image build on non-image PRs (#3438)

* ci: skip startos-iso image build on non-image PRs

The startos-iso image matrix (ISO/squashfs/img across 9 platforms, ~2h
wall-clock once the emulated riscv builds are counted) ran on every PR
that touched the start-os tree, including pure Rust/web changes. But the
image job only repackages the already-compiled binary, so a change that
compiles and passes tests cannot affect image assembly.

Add a PR-only `changes` gate that inspects the PR's changed files and
runs the image matrix only when the change touches image-assembly inputs
(packaging, image recipe, systemd units, apt/**, shared build/**) — what
the image target pulls in beyond the binary. Pure code/web/docs PRs now
stop at compile + Automated Tests (~33m) and get full image coverage on
the push to master; packaging PRs still build images pre-merge.
push/dispatch/release always build images (the guard is bypassed there).

start-wrt already gates its slow OpenWrt image to workflow_dispatch, so
only startos-iso needed this. Documented the new image-gate ↔ build.mk
coupling in AGENTS.md.

fix(backup): stop enumerating legacy backup folder size on target list (#3439)

* fix(backup): stop enumerating legacy backup folder size on target list

Listing backup targets walked the entire pre-v2 `StartOSBackups` folder
(`dir_size`) to report its size, which is too expensive to do on every
list. `legacy_backup_info` now checks only the folder's presence and
reads the target's free space; `LegacyBackupInfo` drops `size` and keeps
`available`.

The create-backup warning shows the target's free space so the user can
confirm their selected services will fit, and lets them proceed. Removes
the size-based "won't fit" refusal branch, reworks the modal copy and the
five locale dictionaries, and refreshes the docs + changelog.

* feat(backup): show free space for every target, not just legacy ones

Free space is now a per-target field — `available` on `PartitionInfo` and
`CifsBackupTarget`, read via a cheap `df` when the target is mounted — and
surfaced as a "Free" column in both the physical-drives and network-folders
lists. The user can gauge whether a backup will fit before selecting a
target, whether or not a legacy V1 backup is present.

With free space owned by the target, `LegacyBackupInfo` carried no data, so
`legacy_backup` collapses to a plain `bool` and the type is removed. The
legacy-backup modal now reads free space from the target entry.

* fix(backup): scope legacy-backup detection and deletion to the current server

The V1 `StartOSBackups` folder is keyed by server ID (`StartOSBackups/<server_id>`),
exactly like `StartOSBackupsV2`, so a target shared by several servers can hold
more than one server's legacy backup. Detection (`has_legacy_backup`) checked
for the whole folder and deletion (`delete_legacy`) removed all of it, which
would flag — and destroy — another server's backup.

Both now operate on `StartOSBackups/<current_server_id>` only. `has_legacy_backup`
takes the server ID; `disk::util::list` threads it through `part_info` (as
`None` for the install/setup/disk-management callers, which have no server yet);
the backup-target list, cifs add/update/list, and the post-backup notification
pass the current server's ID; and `delete_legacy` removes only this server's
subfolder, leaving other servers' backups and `StartOSBackupsV2` untouched.

* feat(backup): always offer legacy cleanup, with an extra confirm when no current backup

The "Delete old backup" button was gated on the target already having a
current (V2) backup, so a target holding only a V1 backup — the case where
cleanup matters most — never showed it. It now appears whenever this server
has a V1 backup on the target, regardless of whether a V2 backup exists.

Because deleting the V1 backup when there is no V2 backup would leave this
server with no backup on that target, the delete flow adds a second,
explicit confirmation in that case. "Current backup" is judged per-server
(this server's `StartOSBackupsV2/<server-id>`), matching the per-server
scoping of detection and deletion.

* fix(backup): show "backing up" instead of "0%" for indeterminate phase progress

A backup phase whose progress is `false` (running but not reporting a
fraction) rendered as "0%", implying nothing had happened yet. Show the
"backing up" label alongside the loader in that case instead.

fix(sdk): don't destroy a daemon's subcontainer on a dependency pause (#3446)

* fix(sdk): don't destroy a daemon's subcontainer on a dependency pause

Since 2.0.0's hold/release refactor, Daemon.term() unconditionally destroyed the daemon's SubContainer, and HealthDaemon calls term() every time a dependency goes not-ready. When the dependency recovered, start()'s hold() on the already-destroyed subcontainer threw "already destroyed"; because that start() was un-awaited it surfaced as an unhandled rejection and the daemon wedged permanently (e.g. c-lightning / BTCPay web UIs), curable only by a full package restart.

Split teardown into a non-destroying stop() (abort the loop, terminate the process, release the hold, but keep the SubContainer) and term() (stop() + destroy). HealthDaemon now pauses a dependency-gated daemon with stop() instead of term(), and awaits+catches start() so a start failure becomes a health failure rather than an unhandled-rejection wedge.

Also serialize HealthDaemon pause/resume transitions on an in-order promise chain: updateStatus() runs fire-and-forget from dependency watchers, so a fast readiness flap could otherwise run a resume's start() against a still-draining stop(), no-op against the not-yet-cleared run loop, and strand the daemon stopped-but-believed-running.

Adds lib/test/DaemonLifecycle.test.ts and bumps @start9labs/start-sdk to 2.0.3.

* style(core): collapse stray double blank line flagged by rustfmt

Pre-existing drift in start-core/src/system/mod.rs (present on master): two blank lines between the `use` block and `pub fn experimental`, which rustfmt's `blank_lines_upper_bound = 1` collapses to one. Surfaced because `make format-check` runs rustfmt over the whole tree on PRs; unblocks this PR's Formatting check.

fix(tunnel): survive fd exhaustion in the SNI demux (#3449)

* fix(tunnel): survive fd exhaustion in the SNI demux

A client that vanished without closing its connection left the demux's
userspace splice blocked forever, pinning an fd pair (client leg in
FIN-WAIT-2 + backend leg). Enough of them exhausted the process fd
limit, and the accept loop treated EMFILE as fatal: the listener task
exited permanently and the forwarded port refused connections until
restart (observed on prod, 2026-07-09, port 443).

- set TCP keepalive on accepted demux connections so vanished peers
  error out of copy_bidirectional within ~2 minutes (same mechanism
  vhost already relies on)
- retry accept on transient errors (EMFILE, ECONNABORTED) with backoff
  instead of tearing down the listener
- retry bind with backoff instead of permanently poisoning the port
- LimitNOFILE=65536 in start-tunneld.service (matching startd.service)

* fix(core): prevent spurious SNI divert-setup warning on concurrent listener startup

Each SNI listener ran ensure_divert_infra() directly, so listeners
starting simultaneously raced its check-then-add commands: losers hit
EEXIST from `ip rule add` and logged "source preservation may be
degraded" even though the divert infra was installed correctly
(observed twice on prod at a daemon startup that spawned three
listeners at once).

Route the demux through ensure_divert_infra_once(), which serializes
initialization behind a OnceCell and caches success, and make it return
the Result so genuine failures still warn at the call site.

* fix(core): periodically re-assert SNI divert infra to heal external flushes

The reply-path divert (ip rule + table-1344 route + nft sni-divert) is
installed once and never re-checked, but external actors can strip it
mid-run: systemd-networkd removes foreign policy rules on restart
(ManageForeignRoutingPolicyRules defaults to yes, and
unattended-upgrades restarts networkd), and an nft flush drops the mark
rule. Losing it silently hangs all demuxed traffic - replies stop
diverting into the transparent sockets and nothing logs.

Re-run the idempotent ensure_divert_infra() on the demux's 30s prune
tick while any listener is active. It now reports whether a missing
piece was re-added (warn - it healed an external flush) and failures
log once per outage instead of every tick. A mutex serializes the
check-then-add sequences so the periodic tick cannot race a listener
startup into the EEXIST warning fixed previously.

fix(ci): retry add-mirror on dropped connections

registry package add-mirror downloads the entire s9pk and hashes every
file body to verify the mirror serves an intact package. For a large
package that is a multi-hundred-MB single-shot stream, and GitHub's
release-asset CDN occasionally closes it early:

  add-mirror: client error (SendRequest): connection closed before
  message completed

The step had no retry, so one dropped connection failed the whole
release job after the package had already been published. Retry up to
three times with linear backoff.

The verify download cannot simply be skipped: the registry's own
add_mirror handler reads only the archive header, so a truncated upload
would pass server-side validation and be registered as a mirror.

Also document why range requests are disabled in HttpSource, since the
`&& false` reads as dead code and invites removal.

fix(startos): keep lxc-net + mounts up through the graceful teardown on host reboot/poweroff (#3442)

* fix(startos): order graceful-teardown hooks after lxc.service/lxc-monitord

On a host reboot/poweroff, systemd stopped lxc.service (whose ExecStop is Debian's
`lxc-containers stop`) and lxc-monitord concurrently with the graceful-teardown
hooks, so each container was killed before startd's Exit RPC could reach it —
`lxc-stop ... is not running` / `Connection refused (os error 111)` and a stalled
reboot. Order startos-{restart,shutdown}.service After=lxc.service lxc-monitord.service
so the LXC container-stop infrastructure stays up until the teardown has finished.

Validated on a beta.10 VM with a real service: clean teardown, no 111, hook <1s.

* fix(startos): exit startd promptly when systemd is driving the shutdown

When the teardown runs inside a systemd shutdown transaction (the hooks' ExecStop),
startd must not re-issue its own reboot/poweroff — that force-reboots mid-transaction.
It now detects `systemctl is-system-running == stopping` and exits at the top of
Shutdown::execute, before the `systemctl stop systemd-journald` and volume-group export
that block mid-transaction (which otherwise hung startd until its ~90s stop timeout);
systemd finishes the unmounts and power action. Raspberry Pi poweroff still self-drives
its standby reboot, since systemd can't power the board off.

scope, and still flags real modifications.

and ctrl/build.rs fallback, and s9pk packaging's GitHash (start-cli/SDK

target's existing backup used a different password" and prompt for the original.

fix: stop sending password hashes and backup key material to the frontend

Now that the browser no longer verifies passwords, the two hashes we shipped it
are pure attack surface.

`serverInfo.passwordHash` was a copy of the master password's argon2 hash living
in the *public* database, so it replicated to every authenticated client. It
existed solely for the client-side verify. Drop the field; the real hash stays in
the private database. No migration needed -- `Current::pre_init` round-trips the
db through the typed `Database` model on every boot (both the Equal and Less
branches), and with no `deny_unknown_fields` that drops the removed key from
existing databases on the next start.

Worse, `StartOsRecoveryInfo` -- returned by `getBackupTargets`, `setup.cifs.verify`
and the disk listing -- carried each backup's `passwordHash` *and* its
`wrappedKey`: the backup's encryption key sealed under that password. A client
holding both can crack the hash offline and then unwrap the actual backup key.
It couldn't simply skip_serializing them: the same struct is written back to the
backup drive as unencrypted-metadata.json, so that would blank the hash and
wrapped key on disk and make the backup undecryptable. Split it -- on-disk
`BackupUnencryptedMetadata` keeps the key material and never leaves the server;
the ts-exported `StartOsRecoveryInfo` is now just hostname/version/timestamp, and
`recovery_info` maps between them.

Also drop the dead `passwordHash` write from the v0_3_6_alpha_0 migration, so the
hash never lands in the public db even transiently.

fix(start-sdk): make Daemons.dynamic compose with setupMain

`main` is always `sdk.setupMain(...)`; what varies is the `DaemonBuildable`
returned from it — a static `Daemons.of(...)` chain, or the reconciler for a
runtime-varying daemon set. The ABI already said so: `ExpectedExports.main`
returns a `DaemonBuildable`, and both `Daemons` and `DaemonsReconciler`
implement it.

Two signatures made that composition unwritable:

- `setupMain` demanded a `Daemons` instead of the ABI's `DaemonBuildable`, so
  it could not accept a reconciler.
- `Daemons.dynamic(fn)` returned a `main` export, burying the
  `DaemonsReconciler` it constructs inside a closure.

So the only shape that compiled was the wrong one — replace `main` with
`Daemons.dynamic(...)`, then nest `Daemons.of()` inside its builder. Packages
adopting dynamic daemons were funnelled straight into it, and the recipe docs
taught it ("`main` IS the reconciler — no `setupMain` wrapper").

- Breaking: `Daemons.dynamic(effects, fn)` now returns `DaemonsReconciler`.
- `setupMain`'s callback widened to `T.DaemonBuildable`.
- Fix the pattern in main.md, recipe-dynamic-daemons.md, and ARCHITECTURE.md.
- Add tests locking the composition. Nothing exercised it before, which is how
  the broken shape shipped and spread to three packages.

Reconcile semantics are unchanged: inside the builder `constRetry` reruns and
reconciles rather than firing `effects.restart()`, so a watched-state change
touches only the daemons whose `configHash` moved and the service stays
`running`.

Closes #3470

fix(net): reconcile public-domain exposure on sibling bindings and ranges (#3464)

* fix(net): keep port ranges disabled when a public domain is added

A public domain targets a single binding: add_public_domain enables it on that binding and disables it on every OTHER single-port binding on the host. Port ranges were skipped, so — because a range's synthesized domain address is enabled-by-default (opt-out, like any domain) — a domain added to a sibling binding silently forwarded the entire range while the range's WAN toggle read "disabled".

Extend the sibling-binding cleanup to binding ranges: the domain is now disabled on every range too. A range is WAN-exposed only when the operator enables the range's own public address (set-range-address-enabled), giving ranges parity with single-port bindings — both stay disabled by default.

* fix(net): honor an already-enabled WAN IP when isolating a domain on siblings

add_public_domain now reconciles the domain on sibling bindings and ranges instead of blindly disabling it: for a non-SSL sibling whose co-located WAN IPv4 is already enabled, the domain is enabled to match (no SNI — same packets); otherwise, and always for SSL rows, it stays isolated. This keeps a domain and its bare WAN IP in lockstep even across domain re-adds or additional domains on the host, and shares one helper (reconcile_domain_on_sibling) between sibling bindings and ranges for true parity.

* fix(net): honor a public GUA, make domain re-add idempotent, check the SSL port

- reconcile_domain_on_sibling now honors an enabled WAN IPv6 GUA the same as an enabled IPv4 WAN address (no SNI over v6 either), so the domain and IP stay in sync on both protocols.

- add_public_domain only force-enables + reconciles for a NEW domain; re-adding an existing one is a no-op for exposure, so it can no longer re-isolate a binding whose WAN IP the operator has since enabled, or clobber any other per-address choice. (Enabling a domain on a specific binding is done via set-address-enabled, not by re-adding.)

- the post-add reachability check now prefers the SSL (vhost) external port over the plaintext one, so it validates the TLS forward the operator actually cares about.

* feat(net): link WAN IPv4 and IPv6 GUA through the dual-stack domain

On a non-SSL port a public domain is dual-stack, so it ties the bare WAN IPv4 and the WAN IPv6 GUA together: enabling one must publish the other, disabling one unpublishes it. Without a domain the two protocols stay independent.

Add set_nonssl_wan_group / has_nonssl_domain and route the enable/disable cascade through them — set_address_enabled_on (IPv4 and PublicDomain branches), set_gua_wan (reverse direction), and reconcile_domain_on_sibling now all move the whole {domain, IPv4, GUA} group as one when a domain links them.

* fix(net): only cascade the GUA link when the GUA ends up enabled

set_gua_wan's group move force-enabled the GUA regardless of the on gate, contradicting it for a public-but-off GUA. Per the mirror model (public GUA ~ WAN IPv4, local ~ LAN IPv4), flipping an *enabled* GUA to public cascades to enable the domain + v4; a public-but-off GUA mirrors a disabled WAN IPv4 and cascades nothing. Gate the enable cascade on on; flip-to-local still mirrors the WAN IPv4 going LAN and takes the group down.

* fix(net): isolate a newly-added binding/range from existing public domains

Domain isolation ran only inside add_public_domain, so a binding or range added AFTER a domain already existed inherited the domain enabled-by-default and leaked onto it. bind()/bind_range() now reconcile a *newly* bound binding/range against the host's existing public domains (skipping re-binds, which would clobber a domain's target binding), then re-derive addresses so the port forwards reflect the isolation.

* refactor(net): name the public-domain reconcile helpers explicitly

Per review: the reconcile logic is specifically about PUBLIC domains (private domains are similarly tied to LAN addresses, handled elsewhere). Rename domain_gateways -> public_domain_gateways, reconcile_domain_on_sibling -> reconcile_public_domain_on_sibling, reconcile_domains_on_new_binding/range -> reconcile_public_domains_on_new_binding/range, and has_nonssl_domain -> has_nonssl_public_domain.

* feat(net): mirror the dual-stack link for private domains / LAN addresses

Extend the non-SSL linking to the LAN side: a private domain ties the bare LAN IPv4 and the IPv6 GUA-as-local together, mirroring public domain / WAN IPv4 / GUA-as-public. The GUA is shared and public wins (a public GUA is reachable on LAN too); resolve_nonssl_gua recomputes it from the two levels (public > local > off) after any change.

- Add set_nonssl_lan_group / has_nonssl_private_domain (LAN mirror of the WAN helpers); set_nonssl_wan_group now defers the GUA to the resolver. set_address_enabled_on and set_gua_wan drive the LAN level for private domains and the bare LAN IPv4.

- reconcile_private_domain_on_sibling: private domains stay ON by default (LAN is trusted, not isolated), but a binding whose bare LAN IPv4 is disabled takes the private domain down too. add_private_domain runs it across the host (is_new-gated).

* fix(net): treat the GUA's WAN opt-in as a stored preference, not derived

Per review: resolve_nonssl_gua recomputed the GUA's public/local state and REWROTE gua_wan, so any LAN-level change (e.g. adding a private domain) demoted an operator's standalone WAN-published GUA back to local. gua_wan — projected to the HostnameInfo.public field — IS the operator's stored WAN opt-in.

Now resolve only READS gua_wan to derive reachability and never clobbers it; only the WAN cascade (set_nonssl_wan_group, gated on a public domain) and set_gua_wan write it. set_gua_wan's standalone branch routes through resolve instead of a stale disabled-key 'on' check. Removes the now-unused nonssl_wan_on.

fix(cli): config precedence + .local (mDNS) resolution — start-cli 1.0.3 (#3471)

* feat(cli): unify host/registry config into one namespace model — start-cli 1.0.3

Give every config source — the workspace `.startos/config.yaml`, `~/.startos`,
`/etc/startos`, and `-c` files — named `host`/`registry` profiles, resolved through one
model instead of the previous flat-config-vs-workspace split.

- One `ClientConfig`: the workspace config folds into it (a `schema` key marks a real
  workspace for the walk-up); `WorkspaceConfig` is gone.
- `host`/`registry` are each an `Option<Profiles>` namespace with a single config key.
  A bare URL is shorthand for the `default` profile; a value may name another profile.
- `-H`/`-r` parse (via `Profiles`' FromStr/ValueParserFactory) straight into
  `{ default: <value> }`, the top of the precedence stack — no separate selector.
- Sources layer highest-first (`-H`/`-r`, `-c`, workspace, `~/.startos`, `/etc/startos`)
  and combine per-alias: distinct names union, a shared name takes the higher tier. The
  walk-up workspace contributes only its host/registry, not TLS/proxy/key settings.
- `resolve_target` follows `default`, chasing profile references to a URL (cycle-guarded),
  parsing the final value lazily so a stale ambient config can't fail an unrelated command.

Fixes the precedence bug where an ambient `~/.startos` config silently shadowed the
workspace's `default`. Ships as start-cli 1.0.3.

Co-authored-by: Matt Hill <9935159+MattDHill@users.noreply.github.com>

* fix(cli): resolve .local (mDNS) hosts via the system resolver

start-cli ships as a static musl binary, and musl's getaddrinfo implements no NSS: it
ignores /etc/nsswitch.conf, so mdns4_minimal is never consulted and a `.local` name is
unresolvable in-process — the lookup falls through to unicast DNS and dies on musl's
hard-coded 5s timeout, which is why curl resolves a name start-cli cannot.

Pin a `.local` host to an address at context build via `getent` — a separate,
dynamically linked binary that goes through the host's real NSS stack, the same path
curl takes — so everything downstream (the HTTP client and the log/progress websockets)
is handed an address; the server's cert carries IP SANs, so TLS still verifies. Applies
to the registry URL too. Linux only; darwin resolves `.local` via mDNSResponder natively.

Originally PR #3474, mistakenly merged into the config branch rather than master.

Closes #3469

docs: keep the root CONTRIBUTING.md; state why rules must be inline in AGENTS.md

The fold is right for sub-scopes and wrong for the root. AGENTS.md is plain
Markdown with no import syntax (unlike CLAUDE.md's @file, which expands into
context at launch), so a pointer from AGENTS.md is only a suggestion the agent
spend a tool call — which is how the SDK release step got skipped in the first
place. Rules go inline; links are for reference material that can be skipped.

GitHub surfaces CONTRIBUTING.md only at the repo root (the contributing prompt
on new issues/PRs, the community profile), so the root file stays as the human

follows a link and an agent doesn't. Sub-scope copies earn nothing and still

docs: release from a merged master; out-of-band publishing is a debt

manage-release.sh doesn't check that HEAD is on master, and shouldn't — an
out-of-band publish is occasionally the right call. But it isn't free: the
commit you publish from is squashed or orphaned when the branch merges, leaving
the tag nowhere honest to point. Say so, and say what it obliges — merge, then
tag and release at the resulting master commit, having checked the shipped
subtree still matches the artifact. start-sdk 2.0.5 is the worked example.

fix(service): restore volumes before reloading old service on update rollback (#3478)

* fix(service): restore volumes before reloading old service on update rollback

When a package update is cancelled or fails partway, Service::load's
Updating/Undo arm reloaded the old s9pk before restoring the pre-update
volume snapshot. The old service's init then ran against on-disk data the
update had already migrated forward, so its VersionGraph.init attempted an
impossible new->old migration and threw "cannot migrate from <new> to
<old>", leaving the service in an error state (restore only ran afterward
in the Err fallback).

Restore the pre-update volume snapshot before reloading the old service so
its init sees old-version data and the migration is a no-op. Guarded to the
Undo disposition so the forward Retry resume path (and its live volume
mounts) is untouched; the existing Err-arm restore remains as the failed-
Retry fallback and is an idempotent no-op for Undo.

* refactor(service): move rollback restore before old-service reload

Consolidate the update-rollback volume restore into a single call placed
just before handle_installed in the shared fall-through, instead of a
guarded pre-load restore plus the Err-arm restore. restore now runs once
for both the cancel/Undo path and the boot-time failed-Retry fall-through;
the Err arm only logs. Same behavior, clearer control flow (per review).

fix(install): stop re-polling sideload progress oneshot after it resolves (#3486)

On a successful sideload the spawned install task drops `err_send`
without ever sending, so the progress-websocket's `err = (&mut err_recv)`
select arm resolves once with `Err(RecvError)`. The `if let Ok(e)` body
doesn't match that case, the arm falls through, and the loop re-polls the
already-completed `oneshot::Receiver` on the next iteration — which
panics with "called after complete" (tokio-1.52.1 src/sync/oneshot.rs:1289;
the receiver sets `inner = None` after its first `Ready`).

The panic unwinds the websocket task and resets the TCP connection with
no close handshake, so the client sees a phantom
"WebSocket protocol error: Connection reset without closing handshake"
and exits non-zero even though the install completed. This also makes
`make install` (s9pk.mk) report failure (exit 9) on successful deploys.
It's reliable in practice because the progress stream only ticks every
200ms while `err_send` drops the instant the install task finishes, so
the receiver almost always resolves inside a tick window and the re-poll
wins the race.

Fuse the receiver (`err_recv.fuse()`) so that once it resolves it yields
`Pending` forever instead of panicking on re-poll; the error arm then
simply stops firing. On the success (`Err(RecvError)`) path we keep
draining the progress stream rather than returning, so the final
`is_complete` frame still reaches the client. The real-error path
(`Ok(e)`) is unchanged.

fix(net): stable, predictable IPv6 address (EUI-64) across reboots (#3489)

* feat(net): set NetworkManager IPv6 addr-gen-mode=eui64, disable ip6-privacy

Add a [connection] defaults section to the base NetworkManager.conf so every
interface uses a stable EUI-64 IPv6 address with RFC 4941 privacy extensions
disabled. This keeps the server on one predictable global-unicast address for
the GUA-based clearnet/domain features to advertise and pinhole.

* fix(net): persist /var/lib/NetworkManager so IPv6 address survives reboot

The root overlay's writable upper is a tmpfs, so /var/lib/NetworkManager —
which holds NM's stable-privacy address seed (secret_key) and its DHCPv6 DUID —
was wiped on every boot. That made the server draw a new IPv6 global-unicast
address each reboot regardless of addr-gen-mode: the default stable-privacy
seed regenerated on a SLAAC network, and the DUID regenerated on a DHCPv6 one.

Bind-mount it from the data partition alongside the existing system-connections
bind (before NetworkManager is restarted), the same way StartOS already
persists /var/log/journal, so the address stays stable across reboots.

* fix(net): apply eui64/no-privacy to existing connections, not just as a default

NetworkManager.conf connection defaults only fill in properties a connection
leaves unset, so a wired/wifi profile created before the [connection] default
was added keeps its old stable-privacy addressing — whose IID is a hash of a
per-boot secret_key on the tmpfs overlay upper, giving a new IPv6 every reboot.

Force ipv6.addr-gen-mode=eui64 + ipv6.ip6-privacy=0 directly onto every physical
connection in synchronize_network_manager (runs from the image every boot); the
existing NetworkManager restart re-activates them with a deterministic,
MAC-derived address. The postinst [connection] default still covers newly
created connections.

Drops the /var/lib/NetworkManager persistence bind from the previous commit:
with real eui64 the address is MAC-derived, so the stable-privacy seed is
irrelevant.

fix(net): bind vhost listeners with IP_FREEBIND, retry on failure (#3490)

An addSsl binding's IPv6 GUA listener could be permanently absent: the
kernel refuses to bind an address still tentative from IPv6 DAD, and
update_vhost_listeners aborted the whole reconcile on the first bind error
(via `?`). Because poll_accept marks the ip_info/bind_reqs watches seen
before that error propagates, the failed bind was never retried until the
next unrelated network change — so check-port-v6 reported the GUA
internally unreachable until a server restart re-ran the reconcile. The v4
listeners sort first and bound before the failing GUA, so v4 stayed up
while v6 silently didn't.

- Set IP_FREEBIND/IPV6_FREEBIND on listener sockets in build_listen_socket
  so a not-yet-assignable address (e.g. a tentative GUA) binds immediately.
  Linux-only, cfg-gated so the darwin (start-cli) build still compiles.
- Reconcile the listener set as a desired-set diff, binding best-effort: a
  failed bind is logged and left unbound rather than aborting the pass, and
  a backoff timer re-runs the reconcile so any remaining transient failure
  (e.g. a port briefly held by a torn-down listener) self-heals.
