refactor(exver): remove the unpublished wasm surface

The crate's wasm build was never used. `@start9labs/exver` has never been
published -- npm 404s with no unpublish tombstone -- nothing in or out of the
monorepo consumes it, no CI workflow references it, and start-core takes
`exver` with `features = ["serde"]` only. dr-bonez confirms: we don't use the
wasm build, and the TypeScript ExVer in start-core is a reimplementation, not a
binding to it.

It could not have worked in any case. `publish.sh` passed
`--features=wasm-bindgen`, the implicit feature of the optional `wasm-bindgen`
dependency rather than the `wasm` feature that `src/lib.rs` gated `src/wasm.rs`
behind, so it built a package with no exported functions. That this went
unnoticed is the point: nobody ever ran it successfully.

Keeping it was not free. `getrandom` was a non-optional dependency with zero
source references, present only so `wasm = [..., "getrandom/js"]` could enable
its js feature. `crate-type = ["cdylib", "rlib"]` built a cdylib on every
`cargo build -p exver` that nothing linked. `exver.d.ts` was a hand-maintained
type sidecar for a package that did not exist, free to drift with nothing to
catch it.

So remove `publish.sh`, `src/wasm.rs`, `exver.d.ts`, the `wasm`/`js-sys`/
`wasm-bindgen` features and deps, `getrandom`, the wasm-pack metadata, the
cdylib crate-type, and the `/pkg` + `/node_modules` ignores that only wasm-pack
and npm produced. The crate is Rust only, and its .gitignore now matches its
Rust-only siblings.

The docs claimed the npm package existed, which sent TypeScript callers to a
404 rather than to `@start9labs/start-sdk`. They now say the crate is Rust only
and record what replaces the deleted section: the TypeScript implementation
shares this spec but none of its code, and nothing enforces that they agree, so
a format or ordering change must land in both.

`cargo test -p exver --all-features` passes (22 tests). crates.io is untouched
-- that is `cargo publish`; this removes only the npm/wasm path.

fix(tunnel): rebind device-bound listeners on wg ifindex change, not an edge notify (#3494)

* fix(tunnel): rebind device-bound listeners on wg ifindex change, not an edge notify

The PCP/IGD/SSDP listeners are SO_BINDTODEVICE-bound to wg-start-tunnel,
which pins the ifindex at bind time, so the `wg-quick down/up` on every
subnet/device change leaves them deaf on the recreated interface. #3429
signalled the bounce with a tokio::sync::Notify + notify_waiters(), but
that is edge-triggered: a bounce that fires while no serve loop is parked
on its notified() future — the window in run() between an Ok return and
the next re-subscribe, or the 5s error-retry sleep — is lost (notify_waiters
stores no permit), and a concurrent sync_network's down phase can then bind
a socket to a soon-dead ifindex.

Publish the interface's actual ifindex through a watch::Sender<u32>. Each
serve loop captures it before binding and rebinds when it changes. The
watch is level-triggered (retains the value), so a listener re-subscribing
after a bounce still observes the new index; comparing the value also skips
a needless rebind when wg-quick reuses the same ifindex (the existing
SO_BINDTODEVICE binding is still valid).

fix(sdk): don't require a git index that a fresh repo doesn't have (#3497)

s9pk.mk listed $(GIT_DIR)/index as an unconditional prerequisite of the
s9pk targets, but `git init` creates no index until the first `git add`.
Make aborted with "No rule to make target '.git/index'" before the pack
step ever ran.

This broke every freshly scaffolded package: `s9pk init-package` runs
`git init` and stages nothing, the generated TODO.md sends the packager
straight to `make` as their first build, and workflow.md tells them to
iterate with a dirty tree and commit once at the end. So the documented
path hit the failure every time.

The existing $(if $(GIT_DIR),...) guard asked only whether a repo exists,
not whether these files do. Filter GIT_DEPS through $(wildcard) so a
missing HEAD or index drops out of the prerequisite list.

Nothing else needed changing: s9pk pack already handles a commit-less
repo, reporting "No git commit found in ." and packing a null gitHash.
These entries are rebuild triggers, not build requirements.

fix(core): unmount tmp mounts only while the slot has no live guard (#3498)

* fix(core): unmount tmp mounts only while the slot has no live guard

A temporary mount's teardown unmounted by path, so a stale detached
unmount (from Drop, after the last Arc already dropped) could tear a
drive down after its shared TMP_MOUNTS slot had been reused by a fresh
mount at the same hashed path. A concurrent operation loading
mount.backup-fs off that drive then hit ENOENT ("could not load
backup"), intermittently failing backups to physical exFAT/BTRFS
targets — the periodic backup-target listing kept churning the slot.

MountGuard now carries its slot; teardown takes the per-mountpoint slot
lock and unmounts only when the slot's Weak has no strong holders, so it
can't unmount a mount another operation just established. Per-entry lock
only (no global lock, no epoch): strong_count == 0 means the path is
unowned and safe to unmount; > 0 means a live guard owns it and will
tear it down itself.

* minor cleanup

* chore(core): drop the slot lock explicitly at the end of unmount_slot

fix: auto-forward public IPv4 on addSsl interfaces + tunnel SNI fallback (#3501)

* feat(tunnel): treat a hostname-less forward as the SNI fallback on a shared port

A StartTunnel external port was strictly either an nftables DNAT or an
SNI-demultiplexed set of hostname routes — "mutually exclusive for a given
external address". So a hostname MAP arriving on a DNAT'd port (or vice versa)
was rejected (718 / HOSTNAME_TAKEN), and a bare public IP could not share a port
with named domains. The SNI demuxer already had a `fallback` slot (select() does
exact -> wildcard -> fallback) but nothing ever populated it.

Wire it up: `PortForward::Sni` gains `fallback: Option<SniRoute>` (serde default,
so no DB migration). A hostname-less MAP on an SNI port now sets the fallback,
and a hostname MAP on a lone same-owner DNAT promotes that DNAT to the fallback
(tearing down the kernel rule, registering the demux listener, carrying the
lease to a new SniFallback lease key). Traffic whose TLS SNI matches a named
route reaches that route's device; a bare-IP client or unmatched/absent SNI
reaches the fallback device.

The DNAT->SNI promotion is owner-scoped (`plan_dnat_conversion`): a DNAT is an
exclusive whole-port claim, so only the DNAT's own client (target IP forced to
its tunnel IP) may fold it into the fallback — another client's hostname is
rejected, as before.

Threaded through the data-plane demux, the PCP/UPnP backend (lease stamping
centralized into apply_peer_forward_range), lease seed/reap, startup + WAN-IP
reconcile, peer teardown (clear_for_peer / gc_forwards), and the manual API.
The tunnel UI lists the fallback as a hostname-less row.

* fix(net): auto-forward a public IPv4 enabled on an addSsl interface

Only a public domain on an SSL-terminated port triggered automatic upstream port
mapping (PCP/NAT-PMP/UPnP); enabling the bare public IPv4 on the same binding
left the port closed until it was forwarded by hand. The bare-IP WAN address got
a `*` reverse-proxy listener but no pinhole request: the IPv4 auto-map path
(`forwards` -> InterfaceForwardEntry -> pmap.ensure) is only built in the
non-SSL block, public domains take the hostname-map path, and IPv6 GUAs take the
gua_pinholes path — the bare public IPv4 on an SSL port fell through all three.

Request the pinhole for the SSL port directly, mirroring the IPv6 gua_pinholes
mechanism: for each enabled bare public IPv4 at the ssl port, ask the gateway to
forward that port to the box's own LAN IPv4 (the host TLS `*` vhost is the
listener, so this is a pure pinhole with no local DNAT). Tracked in a new
`HostBinds.ssl_ip_pinholes` set and withdrawn on the same reconcile as the GUA
pinholes. Covers the StartOS admin UI too (add_ssl without secure.ssl).

A co-located public domain still requests its own SNI-keyed mapping; on a
StartTunnel gateway the two now share the port, the bare-IP forward acting as
the SNI fallback (see the preceding tunnel commit).

* refactor(net): each controller owns its ports' port maps; gate WAN accept per address

net_controller no longer requests any upstream port map itself. Every port map is
owned by the controller that owns the underlying exposure:

- The vhost controller derives and reconciles every port map made on behalf of a
  vhost — IPv4 (a PCP HOSTNAME mapping for a public domain, a plain pinhole for a
  bare public IPv4 `*` vhost), IPv6 GUA firewall pinholes, and the v6 80->443
  redirect — from the ProxyTargets it holds, in one IpAddr-keyed map whose
  per-owner diff handles withdrawal. `sync_hostname_mappings` / the `hostname_maps`
  net_controller built for it are gone.
- The interface forward controller owns each forward's DNAT *and* its upstream
  pinhole together — already true for IPv4 (`InterfaceForwardEntry::update`), now
  also for IPv6 via `forward6`/`unforward6` methods that do the nft DNAT and, for a
  WAN forward, the pinhole. net_controller hands it the v6 DNAT'd bare GUAs (a
  `secure`-without-`add_ssl` binding that no vhost owns) and computes nothing else.
  (The 80->443 redirect is a smart-listener behavior, so it stays a vhost concern —
  remapping HTTP-port traffic into a raw-DNAT'd TLS service would break it.)

Doing this required the controller to know, per address, whether it is WAN-public —
which it needed anyway for its accept decision. `ProxyTarget.public` splits into
`public_v4: BTreeSet<GatewayId>` and `public_v6: BTreeSet<Ipv6Addr>`, and
`ProxyTarget::filter` gates WAN acceptance by the arrival address: IPv4 by gateway
(NAT hides the WAN IP), IPv6 by the exact GUA. v6 is per-IP because one gateway can
carry several GUAs (SLAAC / multiple prefixes) that are independently Local vs
Public. This also fixes a latent over-acceptance: a gateway whose GUA is public but
whose bare IPv4 is not used to accept IPv4 WAN via family-blind `public.contains(&gw.id)`.

The IPv4 pinhole falls out of `public_v4`, so accept and forward agree. Bind stays
broad (IPv4-public gateways' IPs + each public GUA + private IPs); `filter` gates
per address at accept time. New unit tests cover the per-address accept matrix.

* refactor(net): the port-map hostname set is a BTreeSet, not a Vec

Per review: the hostnames on a `(box IP, port)` port-map entry can't repeat and
don't care about order, so a BTreeSet says that outright and drops the hand-rolled
`contains()` dedup. The gateway candidates stay an ordered Vec — the port-mapper
tries them in preference order and keeps the first that binds.

* fix(tunnel): give the tunnel web mocks the new SNI `fallback` field

`PortForward::Sni` gained a required `fallback`, so the two tunnel-web sites that
construct an SNI forward (the mock API and the mock patch-db fixture) no longer
type-check against the regenerated binding. Add `fallback` to both — `null` in the
API mock, and a demonstrative hostname-less fallback in the fixture so the
published-ports UI shows the coexistence. (Missed locally: the tunnel web build
needs the full Angular workspace, which wasn't installed in the slot.)

make IPv6 published ports track SLAAC-owned device addresses (#3504)

* fix(wrt): stop claiming IPv6 addresses can be reserved

Devices choose their own IPv6 addresses via SLAAC; a router cannot
reserve one. The IPv6 "Reserve" toggle wrote a DHCPv6 hostid that no
mainstream client ever requests (our RAs never set the managed flag,
Android has no DHCPv6 client at all — and odhcpd would misparse the
colon-separated suffix anyway), so the option was pure fiction.

- Device page: IPv6 is now read-only with a note explaining the device
  owns its address; the Reserve toggle remains for IPv4 only.
- Publish-port dialog: no longer claims the IPv6 address "will be
  reserved"; instead states the rule follows the device's current
  address.
- Device tables: lock icon only on reserved IPv4 chips.
- LAN IPv6 page: the SLAAC toggle now locks while enabled published-port
  rules use IPv6 (the real constraint), not when "reserved" devices
  exist.
- devices.update RPC: ipv6_static/ipv6 fields removed; the host
  section's hostid is untouched by device edits. It remains as backend
  bookkeeping pinned by published-ports for the prefix-rotation
  reconcile fallback.
- Help, user guide, and API contract updated; strings updated across
  all five locales.

* feat(wrt): track device IPv6 changes and retarget published-port rules

IPv6 published-port rules pinned the device's observed GUA at save time
and were only re-resolved on a wan6 prefix event. SLAAC devices own
their addresses: RFC 4941 temporaries rotate ~daily and RFC 7217
stable-privacy IIDs are re-derived per prefix, so device-side changes
broke rules silently — and the address pinned in the first place was
whichever GUA the neighbor table listed first, often a temporary.

New ipv6_tracker module (self-contained: MAC in, elected stable GUA
out, so the future PCP/UPnP feature lands beside it untouched):

- Follows `ip -6 monitor neigh` for the daemon's lifetime (respawn
  with backoff), seeds from a neigh dump at start, and prods ff02::1
  every 10 min so quiet devices survive kernel neighbor GC. Runs on
  its own single-threaded runtime (reconcile's uciedit futures are
  !Send).
- Persists per-(MAC, GUA) first/last-seen history to
  /etc/startwrt/ipv6_neighbors.json (device_names.rs pattern; added
  to keep.d).
- Elects each device's stable address: EUI-64-of-MAC beats
  48h-persistent (outlives any RFC 4941 temporary) beats oldest-seen.
- On an elected-address change for a forwarded MAC, debounces 20 s and
  re-runs published-ports reconcile.

reconcile/set now prefer the elected address over raw neighbor-table
order (via resolve_device_info_for_macs), and reconcile's offline
fallback is history-informed: an EUI-64 elected address supplies the
suffix; recent non-EUI-64 history suppresses a legacy stored hostid
(recombining a prefix-dependent suffix would target an address the
device will never own). set() no longer writes hostids at all — the
value lives in odhcpd's namespace in a form odhcpd misparses, and the
tracker's history supersedes it; existing entries remain as a
last-resort fallback.

* fix(wrt): stop the admin outbound from silently disabling LAN IPv6

The admin LAN is itself a profile (interface 'lan'), so both profile-sync
paths re-gated dhcp.lan.ra/dhcpv6 on whether the admin outbound VPN
carries IPv6:

- lan::ipv6_set's dhcp sync loop overwrote the RA state it had just
  written from the request, so enabling LAN IPv6 with a v4-only WireGuard
  admin outbound reported success but reverted to disabled in the same
  transaction (confirmed on hardware: ra='disabled' + ip6assign set, the
  asymmetry from the network loop skipping LAN while the dhcp loop
  didn't).
- profiles::rewrite_dhcp did the same on every admin profile edit, so
  pointing the admin at a v4-only VPN silently disabled LAN IPv6 — and
  kept it off after switching back, because is_ipv6_enabled reads that
  very option.

The LAN IPv6 page now solely owns the admin LAN's RA/DHCPv6 state, per
the existing design note in rewrite_interface: a VPN-routed admin fails
v6 closed via the kill-switch route, so devices get LAN addresses while
internet-bound v6 cannot leak around the tunnel. Non-admin profiles keep
the outbound gating.

Also truths up lan.md's disable-lock note (published-port rules, not the
removed IPv6 reservations) and documents the v4-only-VPN behavior in
both affected pages.

* fix(wrt): show the elected stable GUA as the published-port endpoint

`published_ports::list` reported `device_ipv6` straight from
`devices::list` -> `Device::ipv6`, i.e. `pick_ipv6`'s neighbor-table-order
choice, while `reconcile` writes the tracker-elected stable GUA into the
`pp_*_v6` rule. When a device holds more than one GUA the two diverge, so
the Endpoints column (and the stale-prefix status) could name a different
address than the open firewall pinhole — e.g. a rotating RFC 4941 privacy
address the rule never targets.

Resolve `device_ipv6` via `ipv6_tracker::elected_live` (same precedence
reconcile uses), falling back to the direct pick when the tracker has no
live history. compute_status now reasons about that same address too, so
the displayed endpoint and status match the rule.

* fix(wrt): scope published-port election to the current delegated prefix

The IPv6 tracker's elect() ranks a device's addresses purely by
stability/age (EUI-64 > 48h-persistent > oldest-first-seen) and is
deliberately prefix-blind. After an ISP prefix rotation, while the device
still holds its old-prefix address, that address is older/persistent and so
outranks the fresh new-prefix one. reconcile then wrote it into the rule's
dest_ip verbatim — pinning the forward to an address in a prefix that is no
longer routed — until the old address aged out of the live window (~30 min,
longer if the device kept it warm). set() and the endpoint display had the
same blind spot.

Add elected_live_in_prefix (a thin wrapper that filters candidates to the
current /64, then defers to the unchanged, still-prefix-agnostic elect())
and use it wherever an address becomes a rule target or the displayed
endpoint: reconcile, set()'s initial dest_ip, and list. A device with no
live address in the current prefix drops out and is handled by reconcile's
existing prefix ++ suffix recombination. resolve_device_info_for_macs's
ipv6 field (and its ULA/link-local validation semantics) is left untouched.

Prefix-match helper added as system::addr_in_prefix; unit test covers the
straddling-rotation case.

* fix(wrt): give published ports a stable sort order

The list is assembled from HashMaps in extract_ports (randomized
iteration order), and neither list(), the frontend service, nor
tuiTableSort's default stabilized it — so every 5s FormService poll
returned the rows in a different order and the table visibly reshuffled.

Sort the returned list by label (case-insensitive), tie-broken by id, in
list() so both the web table's default order and the CLI list output get
one deterministic order. Kept out of extract_ports so its position-based
unit tests stay valid.

* fix(wrt): harden IPv6 published-port targeting across bridges and SLAAC churn

Close the correctness holes the ipv6-reserve-honesty audit found in how
IPv6 published-port rules pick and maintain their target address, and
drop the last of the "reserve IPv6" fiction.

Multi-prefix awareness:
- Replace read_lan_gua_prefix (admin LAN only) with
  read_gua_prefix_assignments, returning every LAN-side interface's GUA
  /64 (admin LAN *and* profile bridges). A guest-profile device holds
  its address in that profile's /64, so election scoping now accepts an
  address in any currently-assigned prefix, and the offline
  prefix ++ suffix fallback recombines with the /64 of the device's own
  bridge (tracked via last_seen_iface), never the admin LAN's. A device
  whose bridge is unknown on a multi-prefix router is left untouched
  rather than rewritten into a /64 it never owns.

Neighbor-table liveness:
- Only REACHABLE/PERMANENT/NOARP sightings refresh an address's
  liveness; STALE entries linger below the kernel GC threshold and would
  otherwise keep a dropped address electable forever. Unicast-ping every
  rule-relevant address each rescan so a present-but-idle device's GUAs
  stay verified, and surface age-outs (invisible to a single record())
  via a live-set sweep.

reconcile correctness:
- Forward reconcile to the daemon (with_call_remote): the wan6 hotplug
  runs it as a one-shot CLI with no access to the tracker's live
  in-memory history. Widen the reconcile trigger from "elected address
  changed" to any live-set change of a rule-relevant MAC, gated by a
  V6_RULE_MACS relevance filter so guest churn stays cheap to ignore.

Stop reserving IPv6:
- Compute extract_ipv6_hostid's IID from parsed segments, not text
  slicing — zero-compression can span the prefix/IID boundary and yield
  an unparseable suffix.
- Drop the ipv6_static field and the DHCP hostid pinning it reflected
  (devices choose their own IPv6 addresses; odhcpd misparses colon
  hostids); reconcile keeps rules current instead. Remove the lock icon
  from the device IPv6 summary.
- Add the PublishedPortsUseIpv6 error and reject disabling LAN SLAAC
  while any enabled pp_*_v6 rule exists — the authoritative backend
  mirror of the UI's toggle lock.

* fix(os-install): refuse preserve selections that would erase the data drive

Choosing "Preserve" for a data drive whose StartOS pool lives on a
partition of that drive (the 0.3.x single-drive layout) while installing

through to setup_data_drive() — silently reformatting the very drive the

  guidance instead of the mid-install "Cannot protect the entire disk"

fix(net/dns): eliminate forwarder catalog write-starvation livelock (#3473) (#3507)

The DNS forwarder kept its upstream hickory `Catalog` behind a
`tokio::sync::RwLock`. Every forwarded query held `catalog.read()` across
the entire upstream forward (up to 30s) while the rebuild task waited only
10s for `catalog.write()`, timed out, slept 1s, and retried at the back of
the fair-lock queue. Under sustained query load with slow or dead upstreams
(exactly the conditions after a WAN/tunnel/DHCP event) the writer starved
indefinitely, and because tokio's RwLock is write-preferring, every new
forward blocked behind it too — a box-wide container DNS outage, while the
one action that would repair the upstream list was the thing being starved.

Snapshot the catalog instead of guarding it: store `Arc<SyncRwLock<Arc<Catalog>>>`
(the same pattern `ResolveMap` already uses in this file). Readers clone the
inner `Arc` under a sub-microsecond synchronous lock and forward on the owned
snapshot, so no lock is ever held across the await. The rebuild task builds a
fresh catalog and swaps it in atomically — no write timeout, no retry, no
starvation; a pending upstream change always applies immediately.

Also:
- Lower the per-attempt forward timeout from 30s to 5s. Container stub
  resolvers give up around 5s, so a longer server-side forward serves nobody.
- Answer names in the private `.startos`/`.embassy` zones that no running
  service claims with an authoritative NXDOMAIN instead of forwarding them
  upstream. This closes a standing internal-hostname leak and removes the
  episode amplification from restarting-service lookups piling onto the
  forwarder. Names a service does claim (including empty answers for the
  queried family, i.e. NODATA) are unchanged; only previously-forwarded
  unclaimed names in those zones change.

Remove the now-dead `net.dns.timeout-updating-catalog` i18n key.

* fix(backup): reclaim legacy-backup space in the background

Deleting a V1 backup was a synchronous remove_dir_all over an
unlink-per-encrypted-file tree — 10-15 minutes for 200 GB on SSD, hours

feat(net): per-gateway port-map capability tracking, per-interface sharding, retry backoff

Automatic port mapping (PCP/NAT-PMP/UPnP) previously ran every interface's
attempts through one serial actor with a flat 15s retry floor, and the 180s
refresh re-applied every failed mapping unconditionally. A gateway that
refuses PCP and has no UPnP (measured on a live box: ~4s per key per
attempt, six public forwards) could saturate the actor and delay unrelated
gateways' mappings by minutes.

- GatewayPortMapCapabilities on NetworkInterfaceInfo (synced to the db):
  per-gateway PCP / NAT-PMP / UPnP / PCP-HOSTNAME verdicts with timestamps,
  fed by periodic watcher probes (new port_map::probe module; the UPnP WAN
  probe's SSDP discovery doubles as the UPnP verdict) and by the outcome of
  every mapping attempt. A yes is trusted for an hour, a no re-probed after
  five minutes.
- PortMapController is sharded per local IP (one task per interface), so a
  slow or absent gateway never head-of-line-blocks another interface's
  mappings or the check-port query.
- Protocols a gateway is fresh-known not to speak are skipped before any
  I/O; attempt outcomes (including crab_nat failure classification:
  refused/timeout = unsupported, protocol answers = supported) feed back as
  verdicts.
- Per-key exponential backoff (15s doubling to a 16-minute cap) replaces
  the flat retry floor; the refresh tick now honors it instead of
  re-applying every failed key every 180s. A spec change resets backoff so
  operator changes retry promptly.

fix(install): pace writeback + preallocate instead of O_DIRECT for s9pk transfers (#3517)

* fix(install): pace writeback + preallocate instead of O_DIRECT for s9pk transfers

Downloading and unpacking a large s9pk streamed through the page cache with no
writeback pacing, so on fragmented copy-on-write btrfs the temporary and
installed archives scattered across thousands of extents and their accumulated
dirty pages flushed in one enormous final fdatasync — a seconds-to-minutes
lock-up whose victim varied by package size and each box's on-disk layout.

Replace the download/sideload O_DIRECT writer (which also blocked mirror-resume,
since O_DIRECT can't seek/truncate) with a buffered tokio::fs::File fronted by a
WritebackPacer: sync_file_range kicks async writeback every 16 MiB and caps
un-synced data at a 64 MiB window, so dirty RAM stays bounded and the final
fsync is cheap. Reserve space up front with fallocate and mark the temp dir and
installed s9pk nodatacow (chattr +C) so large writes stay contiguous on btrfs.
Linux-only mechanics; no-ops elsewhere (start-cli on macOS).

* refactor(install): tighten s9pk writeback cleanup

Review follow-ups on the writeback-pacing change:

- Set chattr +C on the install download file BEFORE fallocate, not after.
  btrfs's NOCOW flag only takes effect on an empty file, so preallocating
  first left the extents copy-on-write and defeated the anti-fragmentation
  goal on the sideload/install path.
- Make set_no_cow linux-only with a no-op stub elsewhere (matching
  preallocate and pace), and log the expected off-btrfs miss at debug instead
  of error, so start-cli on macOS and non-btrfs hosts stop logging on every
  TmpDir creation.
- cfg-gate KICK_EVERY/DIRTY_WINDOW to linux to avoid dead_code warnings on the
  darwin build.
- Fold the two duplicated "set expected size + preallocate" blocks in the
  download loop into one helper, and note why the 206 resume path needs no
  seek or pacer reset.

* feat(install): show a "Reserving Space" phase during preallocate

fallocate reserves real extents on btrfs, looping over free space, so on a
fragmented / near-full box a multi-gigabyte reservation can stall for seconds —
long enough to look frozen. Give the install/unpack reserve its own
indeterminate phase so the UI spins instead of pinning "Unpacking" at 0%, and
run the download/sideload reserve before their phase's set_total so those show a
spinner during the reserve rather than a frozen 0%.

* feat(install): make Unpacking indeterminate during preallocate

Drop the standalone "Reserving Space" phase; instead let the Unpacking phase
itself spin during its reserve (start before preallocate, set the byte total
after) — matching the download path, which already shows indeterminate until
its preallocate completes.

fix(migration): write start-os/admin into tor's onion-migration handoff (#3527)

The 0.3.5.1 -> 0.4.0 OS migration handed the tor package its onion-import
file with the server UI's entries keyed by the legacy STARTOS sentinel
(packageId STARTOS, hostId STARTOS or startos-ui). Those are not valid Ids
in the 0.4.0 service model, so tor's init died on
getHostInfo({packageId: "STARTOS"}) with
'Invalid params: Deserialization Error: Invalid ID: STARTOS' and the bundled
tor package never installed during v0_4_0_alpha_20's post_up — before
v0_4_0_beta_10's migrate_tor_service_identity could rewrite the file.

Emit the real service identity (start-os/admin) when collecting the 0.3.5.1
tor keys in v0_3_6_alpha_0 and in v0_4_0_alpha_20's fallback path, and
normalize the legacy sentinels when consuming a private.torMigration that a
pre-fix dev build already persisted.

fix(install): pace the install serialize path and harden s9pk resume (#3528)

Follow-up to #3517:

- The install/restore serialize path now paces writeback too
  (PacedWriter wraps the output file; WritebackPacer gains a poll-based
  driver), so the bounded-dirty/cheap-final-fsync guarantee covers the
  whole transfer, not just the download half.
- preallocate() reserved the pre-filter s9pk size, permanently
  over-reserving disk for multi-arch packages (KEEP_SIZE extents beyond
  EOF survive the rename into installed/). release_beyond() punches the
  unused tail after serialize.
- Scope chattr +C out of TmpDir::new() (which hit overlayfs upperdirs,
  os_install targets, rpc tmp dirs, ...) to just the s9pk transfer files.
- 206 resume now seeks to bytes_written: a short write committed before
  a transient error used to resume k bytes shifted and, since the byte
  count still added up, be accepted as complete.
- A size change between attempts (Content-Length / Content-Range) now
  fails the download instead of splicing two generations of the file —
  concurrent read-while-write readers have already consumed the old
  prefix and have no way to recover, so there is nothing safe to resume.
- Full restarts clear a stale expected_size left over from the previous
  attempt.

Adds a regression test for the changed-mid-download case.

fix(core): tolerate transient failures querying clock-sync status (#3520)

* fix(core): tolerate transient failures querying clock-sync status

check_time_is_synchronized() shells out to `timedatectl`, which reaches
systemd-timedated over D-Bus and can transiently fail (e.g. an
activation timeout under boot load). Both call sites treated that as
fatal:

- the init sync-clock loop propagated the error out of init(), dropping
  the server into Diagnostic Mode over a momentary hiccup
- the background recovery poller unwrap()ed it, silently killing the
  task, so the "Clock sync failure" warning stuck for the rest of the
  boot even after time synchronized

Treat a failed query as "not synchronized yet" instead: log it and
retry on the existing cadence (1s during init, 30s in the poller).

feat(net): automatic .local DNS injection over WireGuard gateways (#3523)

* docs(tunnel): add FAQ entry for Android .local resolution with the tunnel up

Android excludes VPN connections from mDNS (.local) resolution, so once a
WireGuard config carries the DNS = line (all configs generated since
0.4.0-beta.10), .local lookups go to the tunnel's resolver — which has no
record for them — instead of the local network. This breaks .local even on
the home LAN, while the LAN IP keeps working (only name resolution moves;
routing is untouched). The existing docs only cover ".local doesn't work
over VPN", not this at-home case.

The new FAQ entry explains the mechanism and the fix: a manual A record
mapping the .local hostname to the device's LAN IP (restoring the exact
pre-DNS behavior), or a private domain, which is injected automatically
and works from anywhere.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(net): auto-inject <hostname>.local over WireGuard gateways

StartOS now injects a DNS record for its own <hostname>.local name into
every live WireGuard-type gateway (e.g. StartTunnel) via RFC 2136 — and
only those gateways. Clients on the tunnel can't resolve .local by mDNS
(Android and others exclude VPN connections from mDNS), so without this a
.local lookup hits the tunnel's resolver and NXDOMAINs; now the tunnel
answers it and the name resolves from anywhere the tunnel reaches.

.local is server-global (local_domain_name = <hostname>.local), so the
injection is driven at the server level by a new always-on task
(spawn_server_mdns_injection) rather than per-host, which would flap the
shared record. Plain LAN gateways are left untouched — mDNS already works
there — and the tunnel's own per-device DNS-injection policy still gates
the record, so a gateway with injection off falls back to a manual record.

The tunnel side needs no change: it already serves injected names
authoritatively and authorizes updates per device. Docs (StartTunnel FAQ +
DNS Records; StartOS FAQ + mDNS page) now lead with the automatic behavior
and keep the manual DNS-record workaround as the fallback for when
injection is disabled. Also corrects the StartTunnel FAQ's "DNS =" version
reference (1.1.0, not the StartOS 0.4.0-beta.10).

* feat(net): list .local on WireGuard gateways once DNS injection is confirmed

The RFC 2136 client now feeds each UPDATE outcome back as a
dns_update CapabilityVerdict on the gateway's NetworkInterfaceInfo —
the same evidence pattern the port-map probes use, trust windows and
all. A WireGuard gateway whose resolver accepted the record lists the
server's <hostname>.local among its addresses (LAN gateways list it
unconditionally, served by mDNS); one that refuses — e.g. the tunnel
device's DNS-injection toggle is off — does not.

Outcomes are aggregated per gateway per reconcile round (supported if
any of its resolvers accepted): a gateway carries one resolver per
address family, and a per-target report flapping the verdict rewrote
the interface watch on every pass, retriggering a full reconcile in a
tight loop. A gateway whose last round failed is skipped while the
negative verdict is fresh and retried once it goes stale — the same
dead-gateway cadence as the port-map client — instead of being
hammered every refresh tick.

* feat(tunnel): serve and authorize DNS over the tunnel's IPv6

Each subnet's DNS proxy now also binds the server's IPv6 address out
of the subnet's delegated prefix (best-effort alongside IPv4), and a
device allowed to inject records is authorized at its tunnel IPv6 —
derived from its IPv4 via the same host_v6 rule the addressing already
uses — with the same per-device TSIG key. A StartOS server can then
publish and refresh its automatic records, including the AAAA record
for its .local name, over either family.

Client configs still advertise only the IPv4 resolver: AAAA resolution
works fine over it, so a second advertised address buys nothing.

feat(auth): replace cookie auth with signature auth for the web UI (#3526)

* feat(start-core)!: replace session-cookie auth with enrolled signing keys

The web UI and CLI now authenticate with per-request Ed25519 signatures
instead of a session cookie. `auth.login` verifies the password and
enrolls the caller's public key; enrolled keys carry the metadata sessions
used to (enrolled-at, last-active, user agent), are reaped after 30 days
idle, and are listed/revoked through the existing `auth session`
commands and System > Active Sessions.

- Request signatures commit to a protocol tag, timestamp, nonce, body
  size, and blake3(body), plus the server identity (hostname/IP/domain)
  in the signed bytes, using pure Ed25519. The Ed25519ph+context scheme
  remains for package/registry protocol signatures and is still accepted
  for request auth so deployed CLI and tunnel-device clients keep working.
- The signature context now includes the server's own IPs, so signature
  auth works when the server is addressed by IP instead of hostname.
- The session middleware, session token store, and cookie issuance are
  removed (start-os and start-tunnel); local on-box auth via the `local`
  cookie is unchanged. Replay-protection nonces are now actually recorded.
- s9pk static-asset routes authorize by signature instead of session
  cookie; the unused `/proxy` relay is removed.
- start-cli login generates (if needed) and enrolls the developer key.

* feat(web): add request signing and device-key storage to shared TS libs

`@start9labs/start-core` gains the client side of request signing
(pure Ed25519 over tag || commitment || server identity, PEM header
encoding matching the Rust verifier; interop locked by a test vector
embedded in start-core's signature tests). `@start9labs/shared` gains an
AuthKeyService holding the browser's enrolled key in localStorage.

* feat(start-os): enroll a device key at web UI login

The login page generates an Ed25519 key, enrolls it via auth.login, and
every RPC and authorized static-asset request is signed with it. Login
state is the presence of the enrolled key; an RPC 34 discards it and
returns to the login page, which surfaces an explicit error when a
just-enrolled key is immediately rejected. Resolves #3511.

* feat(start-tunnel): enroll a device key at web UI login

Same authentication move as start-os: the tunnel web UI generates and
enrolls an Ed25519 key at login and signs every RPC. Device keys added
via `auth key add` keep their names; UI-enrolled keys carry the
enrolling user agent. v1.2.0.

* fix(auth): address review findings on signature auth

- signature.rs: clamp request-body pre-allocation to MAX_BODY_PREALLOC so a
  forged self-signed commitment can't drive an unbounded allocation before the
  enrollment check (unauthenticated pre-auth memory DoS).
- tunnel/db.rs: rename the stale get_session/__Auth_session to
  get_signer/__Auth_signer so the db.subscribe continuation is bound to the
  signer key and torn down on logout/revocation (matches the OS side).
- signature.rs/auth.rs: re-inject __Auth_userAgent on login via a get_user_agent
  metadata flag, so enrolled keys record their user agent again.
- auth.rs: enforce that the enrolled pubkey equals the key the login request was
  signed with (get_signer on login + __Auth_signer), so enrollment actually
  proves possession of the enrolled key.
- static_server.rs: authorize /s9pk asset requests against ephemeral_auth_keys
  too, matching check_pubkey, so kiosk/ephemeral sessions can load package assets.
- start-tunnel CHANGELOG: fold the unreleased 1.1.3 fix into 1.2.0 instead of
  orphaning it under a heading that will never be tagged.

* refactor(auth): review cleanups for signature auth

Follow-up cleanups from the code review; no behavior change beyond the
noted robustness fixes.

Rust:
- add AnyVerifyingKey::interned_pem() and use it for the ~7 duplicated
  InternedString::intern(key.to_string()) AuthKeys lookups
- CheckPubkeyRes now carries the interned key, so post_auth_hook no longer
  re-encodes the pubkey to PEM on every authenticated request
- factor the shared check_pubkey skeleton into check_enrolled()
- rekey the replay-nonce cache: HashSet for O(1) membership plus a
  BTreeSet<(Instant, nonce)> for eviction, so two nonces recorded at the
  same Instant can't collide and evict each other
- use i64::abs_diff for the timestamp-skew check so an i64::MIN timestamp
  can't overflow (which panics in debug/CI builds)
- factor the duplicated 30-day session reaper (startup + daily cron) into
  reap_idle_sessions(), iterating as_entries() instead of keys()+as_idx
- rename the __Auth_signer param fields from `session` to `signer`
  (metrics-follow, sideload, attach, db-subscribe, tunnel db-subscribe)
- drop the dead rest-pattern in ListParams { signer, .. }

TypeScript:
- signature.ts: use @noble/hashes/utils hexToBytes/concatBytes instead of
  hand-rolled copies; export bytesToBase64/base64ToBytes
- auth-key.service.ts: simplify get(); reuse the shared base64 helpers
- add AuthKeyService.signRpcHeaders() and use it in both web clients so the
  "signed bytes must match the RPC body" contract lives in one place

* refactor(auth): make key unenrollment a SignatureAuthContext operation

Redraw the auth trait line: SignatureAuthContext owns the signer set —
the enrolled-key stores, the continuations signers leave open, and now
unenrollment itself. A provided `unenroll` kills a revoked key's open
continuations and removes it from the ephemeral and persisted stores
via a per-context `remove_enrolled_keys` hook; HasUnenrolledKeys (né
HasLoggedOutKeys) is the proof token plus the in-transaction core.
LoginContext (né AuthKeyContext) is only the password login surface:
check_password, access_auth_keys, post_login_hook.

Every revocation path now goes through unenroll, closing the ones that
dropped keys without killing what they had open: tunnel `auth key
remove`, the 30-day idle-session reaper (its cron now holds a Weak
seed so it can reach the continuations map), and registry
`admin signer remove` / `admin signer edit --remove-key`.

The tunnel db's enrolled-key store is renamed authPubkeys →
sessionPubkeys to match the StartOS private db, with serde(default) so
a 1.1.x db upgrades with no migration — previously the field had no
default, so a released-db upgrade would have failed deserialization.

fix(backup): hold per-package progress open through image write; weight rsync phase (#3541)

* fix(backup): hold per-package progress open through image write; weight rsync phase

Two backup-progress fixes.

Hold-open: a package's per-package phase was marked complete as soon as the
container's data procedure returned, while the .s9pk image was still streaming
to the target — so it read as "done" with a visible gap before the next
package. Completion now happens in Service::backup after the s9pk write (rather
than in the actor transition), and the SDK's createBackup no longer self-
completes its progress tracker. The OS backup harness owns completion and holds
the phase open until the whole package, image included, is done.

Weighting: rsync package backups sat at 33% for the entire transfer because
createBackup's pre/rsync/post phases carried equal weight — the instant pre-
backup hook owned a third of the bar and the rounded overall couldn't move
within the rsync's narrow band. Each rsync sync now weighs 80, each pre/post
hook 10, and a pre/post phase is added only when its hook is set. All weights
are overridable via new optional arguments. Restore gets the same treatment.

* refactor(backup): pass hooks a handle to their own phase, not the tracker

Pre/post backup and restore hooks now receive a PhaseHandle for their own
progress phase (tracker.addPhase) instead of a child FullProgressTracker
(addNestedPhase). Also syncs package-lock.json to the 2.0.7 bump.

* fix(backup): weight overall progress so it tracks per-package progress

Each package phase now contributes 100 to the server-level backup progress
(was 1) and the OS-data phase 10, so the overall bar advances as each package
copies — floor(ratio * 100) gives ~1% granularity — instead of stepping one
whole package at a time. The reclaim-space phase keeps its weight of 1.
fix(ui): keep protocol column from wrapping TCP/UDP in interface address tables

fix(ui): make the snake playfield edge match the collision boundary

The game's #111 background sat on a full-width container with the canvas
centered inside it, while wall collisions used the canvas dimensions. On
most window shapes the height cap makes the canvas narrower than the
container, leaving same-colored out-of-bounds strips left and right — so
the snake died at an invisible wall seemingly mid-field. Shrink-wrap the
container to the canvas so the visible box edge is the wall, and measure
the host for grid sizing since the container's width now derives from
the canvas.

fix(ui): stop snake input queue from building lag on held or mashed keys

Every keypress while playing was queued (including auto-repeat, which
fires faster than the ~50ms tick) and consumed one per tick, with an
inapplicable move still burning the tick's slot — so holding a key grew
the queue without bound and a subsequent turn executed seconds late.
Queue only arrow keys, dedupe against the last queued move, cap the
buffer at 3, and drain until an applicable move so stale presses never
delay a real turn. The two-press corner buffer still works.

fix(backup): validate password up front, background the encrypted mount (#3542)

The create-backup RPC opened the target's encrypted store (BackupMountGuard::
mount) on the request thread before returning. Opening replays the whole
backup-fs segment log, which on a large backup or a slow target reads for a
minute or more — so the initial call blocked that long and, with no timeout on
the path, surfaced to the user as a request timeout rather than a running backup.

Keep only the cheap, must-be-synchronous work on the request: mount the target
block device and validate the backup password against unencrypted-metadata.json
(new BackupMountGuard::validate_password), so a wrong password is still returned
inline as BackupPasswordMismatch. Move the encrypted mount, change-password, and
legacy check into the existing background task; any failure there now clears the
progress and posts a backup-failed notification via the status guard instead of
hanging the request.

fix(tunnel): route each device ipv6 /128 over the wg interface (#3545)

When a provider configures the delegated block directly on the WAN
interface at its exact size (DigitalOcean assigns its /124 this way),
the kernel holds two equally-specific on-link routes for the block - WAN
and wg - and the WAN wins. Traffic toward device addresses, including
replies to connections devices opened, exited the WAN and blackholed, so
devices had IPv6 addresses but no connectivity. wg-quick installs no
per-peer routes because its Address-derived interface route covers them.

resync_v6 now installs an explicit /128 route over the wg interface for
every device address, which outranks any tie. Installed unconditionally
(fresh `replace` each resync, no tracking): every resync_v6 call follows
a wg-quick down/up that wiped the interface's routes, so the desired set
is a complete reconcile.

fix(net): dedupe url-plugin exported addresses by address identity (#3544)

export_url inserts into a binding's `available` BTreeSet, whose Ord spans
the full HostnameInfo including the Plugin row-action fields
(remove_action / overflow_actions). clear_urls, however, retains entries
via matches_hostname_info, which compares address fields only and ignores
those actions. So re-exporting the same URL with changed row-actions
inserts a second, Ord-distinct entry that clear_urls also keeps —
accumulating duplicate addresses on the binding.

Dedupe on insert using the same match predicate clear_urls uses, so a
re-export updates the existing entry instead of adding a duplicate.

fix: stub missing instructions.md when migrating v1 packages (#3547)

The v1->v2 conversion (from_v1) never wrote instructions.md, so migrating
a 0.3.5.1 package to 0.4.0 produced an archive without it and validation
failed with "file instructions.md missing from archive", aborting the
upgrade. Carry over the package's instructions when present and fall back
to a placeholder when absent, so a missing file can never break migration.

fix(backup): don't start backup until the service has stopped (#3548)

Service::backup awaited the shared backup future directly, driving it
itself concurrently with the actor's stop transition. Because a Shared
runs on first poll from any clone, and the actor only reaches the backup
transition once the service is stopped, Service::backup's poll (as soon
as s9pk serialization finished) could start CreateBackup while the
service was still shutting down — reading a live data volume with no
quiesce. It also returned as soon as the backup work completed, before
the service left the BackingUp state.

Replace the .shared() with .remote_handle(): the actor holds the driver
half (stored for it to run once the service has stopped) and the caller
holds the handle. Awaiting the handle only reads the result, never
drives the work, so a backup can't start before the actor runs it. Move
the leave-BackingUp mutation into the driven future so the handle also
doesn't resolve until the service has left the backing-up state.

Co-authored-by: Aiden McClelland <me@drbonez.dev>

fix: preserve asset file permissions when migrating v1 packages (#3550)

The v1->v2 conversion (from_v1) unpacked the package's assets tar with
tokio_tar's default settings, which do not preserve file modes, then
re-packed the directory with mksquashfs. Files were recreated at the
process umask default (e.g. 0644), so any executable asset lost its +x
bit and the migrated package broke whenever the service ran that asset
directly. Build the archive with set_preserve_permissions(true) so the
tar header modes carry through to the squashfs.

feat(backup): show an "Initializing" progress phase during target mount (#3552)

* feat(backup): show an "Initializing" progress phase during target mount

Create-backup progress showed a bare 0% with no phases from when the request was
accepted until perform_backup added the per-package phases — the whole window
that mounts the target and opens (and, on a large/slow target, replays) its
encrypted store.

Create the progress tracker up front in backup_all with an "Initializing"
phase, seed the db and start the progress->db stream before the mount, and
thread the tracker into perform_backup, which completes the Initializing phase
and adds the reclaim/per-package/OS phases once the store is open. The mutate
that claims the backing-up slot seeds a plain FullProgress snapshot, since it
runs under catch_unwind and can't hold the tracker's watch channels.

* fix(backup): complete Initializing phase after the other phases are added

Move init_phase.complete() below the reclaim/per-package/OS add_phase calls so
the phase list is already populated when Initializing flips to complete, avoiding
a moment where it is the only (completed) phase.

fix(version): report the start-cli version, not the OS version, from startbox (#3553)

On StartOS, /usr/bin/start-cli is a symlink to the startbox multi-call
binary, which seeds a single PRODUCT_VERSION (the start-os crate version)
that every applet reports as --version. So `start-cli --version` on the
server printed the OS version (0.4.0-beta.10) instead of the
independently-versioned start-cli crate version.

The start-cli applet lives in start-core, so bake the start-cli crate
version in via a start-core build.rs (reading projects/start-cli/Cargo.toml,
the single source of truth) and have the applet report bins::cli_version()
instead of product_version(). This fixes both the runtime --version and the
generated man page — rendered by the export_manpage_start_cli test in
start-core, where no wrapper main() runs, so it likewise showed the OS
version. The standalone start-cli is unchanged; other products keep
product_version().

fix(backup-fs): persist a sealed index checkpoint to skip log replay on mount (#3551)

* fix(backup-fs): persist a sealed index checkpoint to skip log replay on mount

Mounting an encrypted backup rebuilt the whole in-RAM index by reading and
decrypting every segment-log frame. On a large backup or a slow target that took
long enough that a restore — whose mount cannot be backgrounded like create —
appeared to time out.

Persist the built index as a sealed checkpoint (index.cache) on the target at
unmount, after compaction + syncfs. On the next mount, if the checkpoint opens
with the store key and its per-segment (id, size) fingerprint exactly matches the
on-disk segments, reconstruct the index from it and skip the replay; on any
mismatch, corruption, wrong key, or absence, fall back to the existing full
replay. It is a pure rebuildable cache, so correctness never depends on it, and
an existing backup becomes fast once backed up to again from this version.

The checkpoint is written atomically (tmp + rename) but not fsynced — being a
rebuildable cache, a torn/lost checkpoint just triggers a replay, so it isn't
worth an fsync on every unmount (costly on a slow target).

Tests: the harness serialized fusermount3 for mount but not unmount; the extra
teardown work exposed the documented self-race on umount_and_join, so hold the
same mount_lock across unmount too.

* chore(backup-fs): log checkpoint hit/replay and split mount timings

Instrumentation to see where a mount's time actually goes and whether the index
checkpoint is written and reused:
- "superblock opened in {}" / "segment log opened in {}" split Controller::new
  into the PBKDF2 superblock open (unaffected by the checkpoint) vs the seglog
  open the checkpoint short-circuits.
- "loaded index from checkpoint (N segments)" vs "replayed N segments, M bytes,
  in {}" vs "index checkpoint present but stale — replaying" distinguish a hit,
  a full replay, and a written-but-mismatched checkpoint.
- "wrote index checkpoint (N segments)" confirms save_checkpoint (at unmount)
  actually ran.

* fix(backup-fs): write the index checkpoint through a held fd (survives lazy unmount)

save_checkpoint runs from Filesystem::destroy, which fires AFTER start-core's
lazy `umount -l` has detached the backing store from the mount namespace. It was
doing fresh path lookups (File::create + rename + read_dir), which then resolve
to the now-empty mountpoint and fail with ENOENT — so the checkpoint was silently
never written and every mount kept full-replaying (which is why restore stayed
slow even after a backup).

Match how the unmount syncfs and the segment appends already work on that
post-detach path: hold an fd on the index-cache file (opened at mount, before the
detach) and write through it, and take the segment fingerprint from the in-RAM
seg_meta (whose total tracks each segment's on-disk size) instead of re-reading
the directory. Drop the tmp+rename — a torn cache is ignored on load anyway.

fix(os-install): preserve data pool selected by partition path (pre-installed Pi) (#3556)

fix(os-install): preserve data pool selected by partition path

A pre-installed device (Raspberry Pi) offers its data partition (e.g.
/dev/mmcblk0p5) as its own data-drive selection. The setup wizard's
drive list enumerates disks with the real OsPartitionInfo (from_fstab),
which promotes that partition to a top-level DiskInfo keyed by the
partition path, so the UI offers Preserve. But install_os_inner
enumerates with an empty OsPartitionInfo, so the partition stays nested
under its disk and plan_data_drive's lookup by logicalname finds no
top-level disk for the exact path the frontend sent -- refusing a
preservable pool with "no StartOS data was found on <part>".

Resolve the pool on the exact selected partition path directly when the
target is not a top-level disk. Only ever returns Attach (import of an
existing VG), never Create, so it cannot reformat. Existing whole-disk
flows are unaffected (disk is Some, branch skipped).

fix(scripts): 0.4.0 release tooling follow-ups (#3555)

* docs(start-os): pin install docs to the start-os/v0.4.0 release tag

* feat(scripts): support redeploying a live migration payload with --replace

Redeploying an already-published version now requires --replace, which
remounts the new payload over the live one, prunes superseded payload
files for that platform, and updates the existing os_version row's
headline/notes in place.

* fix(scripts): repair start-os pre-check developer-key and docs-link checks

- accept ~/.startos/id.key.pem (start-cli's current key path, which
  auto-migrates a legacy developer.key.pem) in the promote pre-check
- keep zero grep matches in the docs-link count from tripping
  errexit/pipefail so the check reports instead of aborting

* fix(scripts): derive release-notes URLs from the registry, ship a gzipped Pi image

The OS release notes rebuilt their S3 links from locally pulled filenames, but
`registry os asset get` names its output startos-<ver>_<platform>.<ext> while the
published basename carries the build's commit hash
(startos-0.4.0-514af0c_x86_64.iso). Nothing local reproduces that hash, so every
generated link 403'd; 0.4.0's had to be hand-patched after the fact, which is how
its checksum block kept the wrong names.

Links now come from the registry index (the only authority on where an asset is
published), and `pull` lands each asset under its published basename so
checksums, signatures, and the notes all name the object you actually download.
`pull` also warns about leftovers in the release dir that are not published
assets, since release_files() would otherwise hash and sign them under names
that are on no URL we publish. StartWRT's notes get the same treatment — they
were only accidentally correct, relying on pull's rename.

The Raspberry Pi image ships gzipped for download: the registry keeps indexing
the bare .img (an installer streams it, and the signed commitment is over the
raw bytes), while the notes link a .gz put beside it on S3 by the new `push-gz`
step. Both the bare image and the .gz are hashed and signed.

Regenerating an existing release's notes now preserves anything hand-written
above "## What's Changed". release_notes() cannot reproduce that block, and
`gh release edit --notes` replaces the whole body — so a repair run against
0.4.0 would have deleted its "Before You Update" warning and highlights.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(scripts): add --publish-only alongside --replace for migration payloads

--skip-publish already stopped a deploy before the os_version insert, but there
was no way to resume one: rerunning it re-uploaded and re-mounted every payload
just to reach the go-live switch. --publish-only skips exactly the staging steps
(free-space check, upload, sha256 verify, loop-mount) and goes straight to the
insert, so the squashfs files need not still be on local disk — only their names
are read, for the version and platform.

It is orthogonal to --replace, which governs the DB row rather than staging, so
the two compose: --publish-only --replace goes live over an existing os_version
row against payloads an earlier run staged. --skip-publish and --publish-only
are rejected as contradictory — one skips the go-live switch, the other skips
everything but it.

The rsyncd module and the external pull verification still run either way, so
--publish-only re-proves the staging is actually live before flipping the
switch rather than trusting the earlier run on faith.

feat(start-sdk): add sdk.host.getBridgeAddress

Every package that dials a dependency carried its own copy of a helper
resolving `bindings[<internalPort>].net.assignedPort` and prefixing
`getOsIp` — 44 of them, near-identical, and the packaging guide shipped
the same code as a block to paste.

The pattern was also wrong. Only one of `assignedPort` /
`assignedSslPort` is ever populated, and which one is a property of how
the *dependency* bound the port: a binding with addSsl and secure.ssl
frees `assignedPort` entirely, a passthrough binding is the reverse. So
every caller implicitly asserted how its dependency terminates TLS and
resolved null the day that changed, which is what happened to LND's
dependents when LND moved REST behind the OS proxy.

Resolve the binding's own derived address instead, which is correct under
either arrangement. `GetBridgeAddress` extends Watchable, so callers get
the same const/once/watch/onChange/waitFor strategies as sdk.host.get
rather than the two the copied helper exposed. Keying off the binding
rather than an exported interface also resolves bridge-only ports such as
tor's SOCKS proxy, which an interface-level addressInfo cannot reach.

`ssl` narrows a binding that publishes both a plaintext and a TLS address
(protocol 'http'/'ws', or secure: null with addSsl); `fallbackPort` keeps
the value non-null while the dependency is absent, for a flag that must
be passed unconditionally against an allocator-guaranteed port.

The guide now calls the helper instead of shipping a copy, and notes that
packages predating 2.0.8 should delete their local one.

fix(start-sdk): type getBridgeAddress non-null when fallbackPort is given

`fallbackPort` exists precisely so the value is never null — it resolves
to `<osIp>:<fallbackPort>` while the dependency is absent — but 2.0.8
typed every call `string | null` regardless. So the one case the option
exists for still made callers handle a null that cannot occur, and
assigning it straight to a non-nullable config field (Bitcoin's `proxy`,
LND's `tor.socks`, CLN's `proxy`) failed to compile.

Overload on the presence of `fallbackPort`, which is what the per-package
helper this replaced already did. Verified by npm-linking the build into
lnd, cln, bitcoin-core, btcpayserver, monerod, robosats and am-i-exposed
— each of which failed to compile against 2.0.8 and now type-checks.

docs(start-sdk): correct what make bundle verifies, and require a consumer typecheck before publishing

The build table claimed `make bundle` runs `test` + `check-fmt`. It does
not — the Makefile deliberately keeps verification off the build path so
consumers like the OS build don't re-run jest every time. Believing the
table is how a CHANGELOG edit reached master unformatted: `check-fmt` is
`.ts`-only anyway, while the CI gate is repo-root `prettier --check .`
over every file type.

Add the release gotcha that goes with it: the SDK's own `tsc` cannot
exercise its public API, because nothing inside the SDK calls it. 2.0.8
shipped `getBridgeAddress` without its `fallbackPort` overload for that
reason — clean locally, and then twelve service packages could not
compile against it. The `make link` + `npm link` flow this repo already
documents catches it in one step.

docs(start-sdk): require npm overrides for the SDK in packages with service dependencies

A packaging repo that depends on another packaging repo pulls in that repo's
own @start9labs/start-sdk pin. When the two differ by even a patch, npm nests
a second copy and ncc bundles both — one fleet package shipped nine copies and
a bundle roughly twice the size it needed to be.

Pin the SDK through npm overrides so the whole tree resolves to the root's
version. The $ form tracks that pin with no further edits, and because
tsconfig.json includes node_modules/**/startos, a dependency that genuinely
needs a newer SDK now fails the build by name instead of silently duplicating
it. Where there is nothing to collapse the lockfile and bundle are unchanged,
so the template carries it unconditionally.

Also replaces the file:../synapse-wrapper pin in the dependencies and tasks
notes: every package in both registries uses a branch-pinned git dependency.

fix(start-os): unquote the migration grub.cfg paths so PureBoot can parse them (#3572)

The Server Pure (Librem Mini v2) runs PureBoot, which never executes GRUB: it
parses /boot/grub/grub.cfg with its own shell parser and kexecs the result.
That parser does no quote removal, so `linux "/vmlinuz-..."` yields a kernel
token whose first character is `"`. fix_path() tests `[ "${path:0:1}" != "/" ]`,
reclassifies the absolute path as relative, prefixes it with the config's
directory, and check_path() then stats /boot/grub/"/vmlinuz-..." — unreadable,
so echo_entry() drops the entry silently.

The migration payload writes exactly one menuentry, so the box ends up with
zero boot options: basic-autoboot.sh finds an empty options file and never
calls kexec-boot, and the box parks on the PureBoot menu with no serial console
to reach it by. Real GRUB strips the quotes, which is why every other x86 box
boots this file, and why 0.3.5.1 booted fine — its grub.cfg came from
grub-mkconfig, which emits paths bare.

Verified by running PureBoot's own kexec-parse-boot over the generated config:
quoted yields 0 entries, unquoted yields 1 with the correct kernel, initrd and
append. grub-script-check still passes.

appeared in the same usage line. No invocation worked: one subnet failed

subnet". `add`, `remove` and `set-dns` already used the inherited form.

The RPC params are unchanged — the CLI flattened parent and leaf params into

Reported in #3565.

fix(start-sdk): drop check-init's stale key-file guard (#3569)

* fix(start-sdk): drop check-init's stale key-file guard

`check-init` ran `start-cli init-key` only when
`~/.startos/developer.key.pem` was absent. start-cli 1.1.0 renamed that
file to `id.key.pem`, so the guard stopped matching anything and
`init-key` ran on every `make install`, announcing "Initializing StartOS
developer environment..." before start-cli reported the key already
exists. Cosmetic only — `init-key` is idempotent and `check-init` gates
`install` alone, not the s9pk build targets.

Remove the condition rather than repoint it at `id.key.pem`. `init-key`
already performs that existence check itself and says so, so the guard
only duplicated it while giving the filename a second place to go stale
the next time a path moves.

Cuts 2.0.10, since 2.0.9 is tagged. The package template's pin stays at
2.0.9 deliberately: `s9pk init-package` scaffolds from the checkout's
template, so pinning an unpublished version would break `npm install`
for anyone scaffolding before 2.0.10 reaches npm. `pre-check` enforces
the match at release time, where `make sync-template` belongs.

* docs(start-sdk): sync the template pin with the release, not the bump

The release runbook folded `make sync-template` into step 1 alongside
the version bump. That is right only when the release follows the bump
immediately; it is wrong for a version that accumulates on `master`
first, because `s9pk init-package` scaffolds from the checkout's
template rather than from npm — a pin ahead of what npm has breaks
`npm install` for anyone scaffolding a package in the meantime.

Split it into its own step, with the reason attached so the next person
doesn't collapse it back. `pre-check` already fails a release whose
template pin doesn't match the version being cut, so the invariant holds
either way; this only moves when it is satisfied.

Root AGENTS.md already says to bump the pin "with the release", so no
change is needed there.

fix(ci): unbreak package builds on fork PRs (#3568)

`build.yml` writes the identity key one of two ways: from the `DEV_KEY`
secret, or — when there is no secret — by generating one with `start-cli
init-key`. Fork PRs get no secrets, so they take the second path. Since

working only because start-cli renames a legacy key file when it loads

and provision the workspace key as `.startos/build.key.pem` — the name
`s9pk init-workspace` creates and `s9pk pack` looks for.

Other call sites (`release.yml`, `start-wrt.yaml`, `startos-iso.yaml`,
`s9pk.mk`) still use the pre-1.1.0 names. They work today via that same
legacy-rename shim and are deliberately left alone; they belong with
whoever removes the shim.

feat(net)!: assignedSslPort carries every TLS external port (#3558)

* feat(net)!: assignedSslPort carries every TLS external port

A binding whose container serves its own TLS certificate (`secure.ssl`
with no `addSsl`) put its external port in `assignedPort` — the
plaintext field — because that port is DNAT'd straight through rather
than fronted by one of our listeners. Which of the two fields holds the
port now says whether the port speaks TLS, not who terminates it.

`BindOptions` grows the three predicates that decide this, so the
allocator, the address synthesis and the forward wiring stop restating
it in slightly different terms. The self-TLS domain address was `else`
-chained on `assignedSslPort` being absent, so it is un-chained and
re-keyed; the direct-forward block now covers every port with no
listener of ours in front, which is what it always meant.

`update` releases both ports before reallocating so a binding that
changes how its port is served keeps the same number, carrying it
between the fields — the external port is in the user's address book and
keys their per-address overrides.

0.4.0.1 migrates the persisted port, preserving its number. The mdns SSL
address is gated on there being an mdns gateway, matching the plaintext
leg — without it a self-TLS binding would gain an mdns address it never
had.

`sdk.host.getBridgeAddress` resolves the binding's derived address, so it
is correct either way; its docstrings described the old mapping.

* feat(net): front self-tls ports with sni passthrough instead of dnat

Container-terminated SSL now behaves identically to proxy-terminated
SSL, with `passthrough: true` the only difference:

- Every assignedSslPort is one of our TLS listeners: the `*` vhost
  terminates for addSsl and pipes the raw TLS stream through for
  self-TLS (client source IP preserved via transparent connect). The
  nft DNAT now covers only the plaintext port, so a self-TLS port
  accepts TLS connections only and no longer relays UDP.

- AvailablePorts flags every ssl allocation as one of ours, so a
  binding that loses its preferred port to a self-TLS holder can still
  advertise its domain there and SNI-route through it.

- Domains take the addSsl treatment: one advertised address riding the
  preferred port whenever a listener of ours answers there
  (preferred_ssl_port() drives the rewrite), and a single domain-vhost
  loop builds both modes with the same gateway merging — so a public
  domain accepts WAN even where the bare IP is disabled. ACME is
  skipped on passthrough, since the backend is the ACME client.

- The 0.4.0.1 migration flips the persisted availablePorts flags for
  migrated self-TLS ports (and back on down).

* fix(core): accept localhost as a signature auth identity

`sig_context` derived the accepted identities from the server host's
enabled addresses, which never include `localhost`. `CliContext` falls
back to `http://localhost` when no host is configured and binds its
signature to that name, so a signed request over the default URL was
rejected.

* chore(container-runtime): sync the sdk version in the lockfile

The lockfile's entry for the linked `../../start-sdk/dist` still pinned
2.0.6; the SDK is now 2.0.10.

* fix(net): let the os ui claim its privileged ports

`AvailablePorts::try_alloc` refuses any port <= 1024, so 443 was never
allocatable. It didn't have to be: `BindInfo::update` short-circuited on
the port a binding already held, so the 443 written into the seed survived
every boot untouched. Now that `update` frees both ports and reallocates,
the allocator is asked for 443 on every boot of `os_bindings` — and
refuses, dropping the admin UI onto a random ephemeral port. The server's
own UI, its domains included, left 443.

StartOS runs as root, so its bindings — the admin UI's, the only ones
there are — may claim the privileged range. `try_alloc`/`try_alloc_range`
take a `privileged` flag, set from `pkg_id.is_start_os()` where a binding
is made; a package's container is unprivileged as before. RESTRICTED_PORTS
stay off limits to both, since a host daemon holds those whoever asks.

`Database::init` no longer pre-marks 80 and 443 allocated. That reservation
was redundant against the privileged-range check, and it now actively locks
the OS out of ports it owns — the admin UI claims both through the
allocator instead, which is also what records 443 as one of our TLS
listeners' ports so a package's domain can be advertised there and SNI
routed. 443 was already the UI's HTTPS port; 80 replaces the random port
its plaintext address had, and is the same port startd's WildcardListener
already serves.

This does not repair a database that has already drifted onto an ephemeral
port: `update` prefers the port a binding holds over its preferred one, so
that a binding which once lost a race doesn't later migrate off an address
the user has bookmarked. Only builds off this branch can be in that state.

* fix(net): don't use transparent egress for a client on the box

The SNI passthrough opens the internal leg from the client's own address
so the container sees the real peer. A client on the box itself is its own
peer, and neither half of that works: binding its `(ip, port)` collides
with the socket it already holds there, so the bind fails EADDRINUSE and
the connection is dropped mid-handshake; and had it succeeded from a
loopback source, the container's reply would go to its own loopback and
hang. Every on-box client of a self-TLS service — 127.0.0.1, the bridge IP
and the LAN IP alike — got `unexpected eof` where the kernel DNAT this
replaced had worked.

Connect plainly when the client is one of the box's own addresses. The
container then sees the bridge IP, which is what the DNAT presented too,
and StartOS's own accept filter has already run on the real peer address
by this point, so nothing is gated on the substitution.

Fall back to a plain connect if transparent egress fails anyway — a
missing capability, a flushed divert table, a local address the target
doesn't list. Losing source-IP fidelity beats dropping a working
connection, and the warning says which one happened.

Not in the tunnel demux, which only logs: a backend admits its LAN-only
addresses on the source being private, and this server's own wireguard
address is private, so falling back there would present every WAN client
as LAN-local.

* feat(net): preserve the client source address for IPv6 too

`transparent_connect` was v4-only, so only a v4 client of a self-TLS
service reached the container as its real peer; a v6 client was proxied
plainly and arrived as the bridge address. It now takes `SocketAddr` and
picks `IP_TRANSPARENT` or `IPV6_TRANSPARENT` per family, refusing a
mismatched pair — the source is bound on the socket that dials the
backend, so both legs are necessarily one family. The reply-path divert
is mirrored: `ip -6 rule`/`route` alongside the v4 pair, and `sni-divert`
in `ip6 startos mangle_prerouting` as well as `ip`. v4 and v6 keep
separate rule and route tables, so DIVERT_TABLE and DIVERT_MARK serve
both.

That needs a v6 backend to dial, so `ProxyTarget` carries the container's
bridge v6 (`addr_v6`) beside its v4. Only the source-preserving leg reads
it; the plain connect stays on `addr`, leaving every terminating target
exactly as it was.

The guard for who gets a preserved source is now `gateways_client`, and
it also excludes a client on lxcbr0. Source preservation needs the
backend's reply to transit this host to be diverted back, and a client
sharing the container bridge is answered directly over that link — so the
connection hung. That was already true of a v4 container client; without
this, v6 would have inherited it, having previously worked by virtue of
being proxied plainly.

* fix(net): don't warn when a backend has no listener on the client's family

Verifying IPv6 source preservation turned up that every self-TLS service
on a test box binds `0.0.0.0`, so its container refuses the v6 leg and we
fall back to the plain connect. That is the ordinary case for a service
that never asked for v6, not a misconfiguration, and it logged a warning
on every such connection. Log a refused connect at debug and keep the
warning for the failures that mean something — a missing capability, a
flushed divert table.

The guide taught plain termination and the addSsl rewrap but never the

fix(update): create and heal current.rootfs across migration, boot, and prune (#3595)

The 0.4.0 initramfs's migration created current.rootfs with 'ln -rsf', but
the initramfs's ln is busybox, which has no -r — so every over-the-air
0.3.5.1 -> 0.4.0 migration booted without the pointer (via the newest-image
fallback) and every later OTA update failed its first step, prune-images
('No current.rootfs, not safe to prune').

- migration writes the relative symlink target explicitly (busybox-safe)
- the boot fallback recreates the pointer when missing or dangling
- prune-images rebuilds a missing/dangling pointer from the newest installed
  image instead of failing; still refuses when no image exists at all

Deliberately carries no version bump: a build from this branch produces a
0.4.0.1-labeled migration payload that replaces the live 0.3.5.1 -> 0.4.0.1
OTA image 1:1. The changelog entry and version bump ride the next release.
Already-affected servers are handled via support (they cannot reach this
fix OTA: the failing prune-images runs from the installed 0.4.0 rootfs
before any downloaded code executes).

fix(ci): read release notes from en_US, not the never-matching en-US

The reusable package release workflow builds the GitHub-release body from
`.releaseNotes | .["en-US"] // first(.[])`. StartOS locale keys are
underscore-separated — `LocaleString::localize_for` splits on `_`, and every
package, the SDK's i18n scaffold, and the package template all key on `en_US` —
so the `en-US` lookup never matches and the expression always falls through to
`first(.[])`: whichever locale the packager happened to write first in
`releaseNotes`.

That is the first key in serialization order, not a language choice. The
manifest's map is insertion-ordered, so it works by convention today (packages
write `en_US` first, following the template) and silently ships the wrong
language the moment one doesn't:

    $ echo '{"releaseNotes":{"de_DE":"GERMAN","en_US":"ENGLISH"}}' \
      | jq -r '.releaseNotes | (.["en-US"] // first(.[]))'
    GERMAN

`first(.[])` stays as the fallback for a package with no `en_US` at all, and the
`type == "object"` guard still passes a legacy plain-string `releaseNotes`
through untouched.

feat(sdk): add sdk.getRootCa for this server's root CA

A service that dials an address the *user* supplies — a monitor target, a
notification endpoint, a webhook — cannot resolve a bridge address for it, and
users cannot see bridge addresses anyway, so what they paste is whatever
StartOS showed them: on the LAN, always HTTPS with a certificate chaining to
this server's root CA. No container trusts that root, so the dial fails
verification.

The only way to obtain that root was to mint a certificate you didn't want and
take the last link of the chain, and packages doing it by hand have taken the
wrong link. hermes-agent and openclaw slice the tail correctly; dev-env takes
`certs[0]` — the leaf — and installs it as a trust anchor, so it trusts nothing
while looking correct and no error is ever raised. That is one in three on a
call whose failure is invisible.

Implemented over `getSslCertificate` rather than as a new OS effect, so it
works on shipping StartOS instead of gating callers on the next release. The
pretext hostname is the OS bridge IP: the sole hostname admitted by the
allowlist's compiled-in `HOST_IP` subnet check rather than by whatever the
gateway table currently holds, which is what admits `127.0.0.1`. If the OS
later exposes the root directly, only `GetRootCa.fetch` changes — the SDK
surface is already right.

Returned as a Watchable for consistency with the other readers, not to fix
anything: the root is minted once at setup with a ten-year life and there is
no rotation flow, so in practice it never changes.
