fix(start-registry): make os asset remove reachable from the CLI (#3698)

`registry os asset remove`'s three handlers were registered `.no_cli()`, and
unlike `add`, `sign`, and `get` — which each pair their RPC handlers with a CLI
counterpart — nothing was registered in their place. `remove_api` has no root
handler, so it became a node that demands a subcommand while offering none:

    $ start-cli registry os asset remove iso 0.4.0 x86_64
    error: unexpected argument 'iso' found

It also mounted without `.with_about()`, so it listed with a blank description.
Both date to 5c473eb9c, where `remove_api` was copied from `add_api` directly
above it. `.no_cli()` is right there — `add` does local blake3 hashing and
signing in a hand-written `cli_add_asset` — but `remove` does no local work at
all, so the sibling was never written and nothing replaced it. The RPC route
was always fine; only the CLI was unreachable, on both `start-cli registry` and
the standalone `start-registry` binary.

The three subcommands now take `<VERSION> <PLATFORM>` and call the registry
directly, mirroring `registry os asset get` at the same depth. This follows
`registry package remove`, which is already `get_signer` + `with_call_remote`
and whose params struct is a field-for-field template — `RemoveAssetParams`
gains `Parser`, and `signer` becomes `Option` because `#[arg(skip)]` requires
`Default`, which `AnyVerifyingKey` does not implement. A missing signer now
fails as `InvalidRequest` rather than a serde error.

Removing a platform a version holds no asset for warned nothing and reported
success, because `Model::remove` returns `Ok(None)` for an absent key. The
handlers return whether anything was removed and warn when nothing was, again
as `registry package remove` does; the call stays idempotent, so CI's
`|| echo "::notice::"` idiom is unaffected.

Per-platform removal is the primitive both deploy jobs wanted: they drop the
whole version entry to re-index one, and 7695ab1ff notes that a dispatch naming
a single platform "deliberately skips it rather than silently wiping the other
eight."

The parent `asset` about key is renamed rather than edited in place so the key
id keeps describing its contents.

fix(core): create granted device nodes with the host's permissions (#3706)

`LxcContainer::mknod` shelled out to coreutils `mknod` with no `-m`, so a
granted `/dev` node landed at `0666 & ~umask(startd)` = 0644 root-owned. A
service running as a non-root user then gets EACCES opening it read-write.

It went unnoticed because the guest repairs it by accident: the
container-runtime rootfs ships systemd's `static-nodes-permissions.conf`
(`z /dev/net/tun 0666`, `z /dev/fuse 0666`), and `systemd-tmpfiles-setup-dev`
chmods the bind-mounted inode back to 0666 — if it runs *after* the bind lands.
`handle_devices` runs after `lxc-start -d` returns, concurrently with the
guest's boot, so the two race; tmpfiles `z` only adjusts paths that already
exist, so on the losing side the node keeps 0644 for the life of the container.
Measured on 0.4.0: created 0644, tmpfiles-setup-dev finished ~30ms later, node
0666. Forcing the losing side reproduces gitea-runner-startos#13 verbatim —
`pasta failed with exit code 1: Failed to open() /dev/net/tun: Permission
denied` — and slirp4netns fails identically, since both open the same node.

`handle_devices` already stats the host node; pass its mode through to
`mknod -m`, which sets the mode explicitly rather than through the umask. Both
opt-in devices come out 0666 as the host has them (and as the packaging recipe
already documents), and `/dev/dri`/`/dev/kfd` keep the host's 0660 instead of
being widened.

Only the two CI-runner packages combine a device grant with a non-root
consumer, which is why the GPU packages never saw this.

fix(start-os): unbreak the NVIDIA image on GB10 — drop unusable GSP firmware, stage MOK enrollment (#3693)

* fix(image-recipe): drop nouveau GSP firmware from the NVIDIA images

The -nvidia images blacklist nouveau and drive the GPU with NVIDIA's
proprietary driver, but live-build's --firmware-chroot still installs
firmware-nvidia-graphics and firmware-nvidia-tesla-535-gsp, and
initramfs-tools copies the firmware every included module declares
regardless of the blacklist. nouveau.ko is included under MODULES=most,
so its GSP blobs are pulled in too.

Measured in the published startos-0.4.0.1-fdb27c7_aarch64-nvidia.iso:
usr/lib/firmware/nvidia/ is 159,225,325 B across 381 entries — 57% of
the 266 MB uncompressed initramfs, every directory a nouveau chip
codename. None of it is the proprietary driver's own firmware, which the
.run installs under a version-named directory that never enters the
initramfs, since no nvidia*.ko does either.

That is why -nvidia asked the bootloader to read a 163.5 MB initrd where
the plain aarch64 image reads 45 MB — and on an NVIDIA GB10 (DGX Spark)
it left the machine stopped on the bootloader's last line with no kernel
output. Confirmed on hardware: 0.4.0.1 hangs, this build boots. Note
0.4.0 booted a payload of essentially the same size under kernel 7.0.13,
so the fault is an interaction with 7.1.3 rather than a fixed size
limit; this buys margin (101 MB against a ~209 MB failure point) but
does not remove the class.

Neither package is depended on by anything in the image —
firmware-misc-nonfree only Recommends the first, which apt does not act
on at removal.

* fix(start-os): retry the container-runtime base image download

The riscv64 build failed on a truncated transfer from
images.linuxcontainers.org — `curl: (18) transfer closed with 79061983
bytes remaining to read` — after the Rust compile had already succeeded.
The download had no retry and runs under `set -e`, so one blip on that
CDN fails the whole job.

The rootfs download also moves from a shell redirect to -o, which is
load-bearing: curl rewinds an output file it owns before each retry
attempt but cannot rewind stdout, so `> file` with --retry concatenates
every partial attempt into one corrupt file. Measured against a local
server that always truncates: `> file` with --retry 2 yields 1200 bytes
from three 400-byte attempts, `-o file` yields 400.

Verified by running the script for real: 105,336,832 B fetched,
`debian.x86_64.squashfs: OK`, exit 0.

* docs(start-os): name the second firmware package correctly

firmware-nvidia-tesla-535-gsp is NVIDIA's proprietary GSP firmware for
the 535 driver series — /usr/lib/firmware/nvidia/535.274.02/gsp_ga10x.bin
and gsp_tu10x.bin — not nouveau's. Only firmware-nvidia-graphics carries
nouveau's chip-named GSP blobs, and only those reach the initramfs.

Both are still correct to purge: the .run installs the driver's own
firmware under nvidia/580.173.02, which neither package owns. Verified
at the ELF level — nvidia.ko's only firmware references are
nvidia/580.173.02/gsp_{ga10x,tu10x}.bin, and both survive the purge in
the built image at the .run's exact byte sizes.

* fix(start-os): stage MOK enrollment when the password is set

Closes #3702.

enroll_mok refuses to stage the import unless the start9 user already
has a password hash, and on a fresh Secure Boot install neither caller
could satisfy that:

- os_install/mod.rs resolved mok_pub inside the target overlay but read
  the hardcoded host /etc/shadow — the installer's, not the target's.
  The target has no password at install either way.
- init.rs runs once per boot, and setup_init calls init() at setup.rs:185
  but write_shadow() at setup.rs:226, so the attempt always preceded the
  password it depends on, in the same function.

The import was therefore first staged on the boot after setup, and
MokManager only prompts on the boot after that — two restarts, with every
skip logged at info and the install-time caller logging only on Err. On a
server, which is rarely restarted, the modules stay unloadable
indefinitely: Secure Boot lockdown refuses the unsigned NVIDIA driver,
nvidia-smi reports it cannot talk to the driver, and a GPU service fails
with no CUDA device and nothing pointing at signing.

Stage it in write_shadow instead, which is the single point every path
that sets a password goes through (setup, restore, password change), so
the prompt appears on the next restart. enroll_mok now takes the root
holding both the certificate and etc/shadow, which also corrects the
install-time read; that call stays for the case where the target already
carries a password.

* docs(start-os): note what the preserve path must not delete

A preserve-reinstall keeps config/overlay wholesale, deleting only named
paths, which is what makes Secure Boot survive it: the MOK key at
overlay/var/lib/dkms is reused, so modules re-signed during install still
match the certificate already enrolled in firmware, and no re-enrollment
is needed. Nothing said so, and adding one more delete_dir would break it
silently — the modules would simply stop loading.

* fix(start-os): back up the config before repartitioning on a preserve install

Closes #3704.

install_os_to called partition(), which rewrites the OS partitions, and
only then tried to read the previous install's config off part_info.root.
By then that filesystem is gone, so the mount failed, the backup was
skipped with no log at all (`if let Ok(guard) = ...`), /tmp/config.bak
never existed, and the restore fell to create_dir_all — an empty config.

Confirmed on a DGX Spark: config/overlay/var/lib/dkms was lost, the
install generated a new Secure Boot MOK key while the firmware still
trusted the old certificate, and Secure Boot then refused every module
signed with the new one. The GPU disappeared with nothing naming signing
as the cause.

Take the backup before partition() instead, locating the previous root by
content — the first partition carrying a `config` directory — rather than
by label, so an install predating any labelling scheme is still found.

Three things this ordering makes possible or necessary:

- Failure now aborts. partition() has not touched a byte at that point
  (gpt::partition runs quiesce_disk first, which does not write), so
  failing costs a retry, while continuing lets mkfs destroy the only copy
  of a config the user asked to keep.
- The previous root is mounted read-only and the prune list is applied to
  the copy, so an install that aborts leaves the old system intact.
- The copy is staged at /tmp/config.bak.staged and renamed only once the
  prunes succeed. `cp -r` writes a partial tree and still fails, and the
  restore accepts whatever sits at the final path, so a half-copied tree
  must never occupy it — an unpruned one would layer the previous image's
  overlay/lib and overlay/usr/lib over the new squashfs.

An install that preserves nothing now clears any backup an earlier
attempt in the same boot left behind, since the restore is unconditional
and would otherwise copy it onto a drive the user asked to wipe.

* fix(start-os): restore initcall_blacklist=tegra234_cbb_init on aarch64-nvidia

Reverts the drop in the previous revision of this branch. The hardware
evidence that retired it was misread: adding the parameter by hand to
0.4.0.1 and still hanging showed only that it was not SUFFICIENT, not
that it was unnecessary. 0.4.0.1 carried both faults — the 163 MB
initramfs and this driver — so fixing either one alone still hung.

The full 2x2 on a DGX Spark now reads:

  163 MB initrd, no blacklist  -> hang   (0.4.0.1)
  163 MB initrd, blacklist     -> hang   (added by hand)
   54 MB initrd, blacklist     -> boots  (f8d0c0a7)
   54 MB initrd, no blacklist  -> hang   (91d631b0)

The last two differ only by this commit; nothing else between them
touches boot. Both faults are independent and both must be fixed.

Applied to aarch64-nvidia only, gated on PLATFORM.txt, in both boot
paths since they run the same kernel: the installed system via
debian/postinst and the live installer via --bootappend-live.

* fix(image-recipe): build the open NVIDIA kernel modules for aarch64-nvidia

Confirmed on a DGX Spark: with 580.173.02's proprietary modules the GPU is
found but never initializes —

  NVRM: GPU at PCI:000f:01:00: GPU-0f059bf0-...
  NVRM: Xid (PCI:000f:01:00): 169, fd8cd000 94000000
  NVRM: GPU 000f:01:00.0: RmInitAdapter failed! (0x62:0x1a:2631)

repeating every ~60s, with nvidia-smi hanging and then reporting no
devices. Installing the same driver version's open modules on the machine
makes the GPU work, so the flavour is the variable, not the version.

That matches NVIDIA's README for this driver — "Blackwell and later are
only supported by the open kernel modules" — and GB10 is Blackwell. It
also explains why 0.4.0 was fine on proprietary: it shipped 580.159.03,
before that restriction applied. NVIDIA's own DGX OS ships
nvidia-driver-580-open on this hardware.

Scoped to aarch64-nvidia. x86_64-nvidia keeps the proprietary flavour,
where open would drop Maxwell, Pascal and Volta; aarch64 has no
pre-Turing NVIDIA hardware to lose.

* fix(image-recipe): actually pass the chosen NVIDIA module flavour

fa848190 added NVIDIA_MODULE_TYPE and never read it — the installer line
still hardcoded proprietary, so the commit was a no-op and aarch64-nvidia
would have shipped the flavour that cannot initialize a GB10.

Interpolated unescaped on purpose: the hook heredoc at :260 is unquoted,
so this expands at generation time like ${QEMU_ARCH} does, unlike the
escaped \${KVER} on the next line. Verified by generating the hook for
both platforms: aarch64-nvidia yields kernel-module-type=open,
x86_64-nvidia yields proprietary.

Also corrects the rationale in fa848190's message. That claimed 580.159.03
predated the Blackwell-is-open-only restriction; it does not. Between
.159.03 and .173.02, README/kernel_open.html is byte-identical, the
"Blackwell and later are only supported by the open kernel modules"
sentence appears verbatim in both, supported-gpus.json is byte-identical,
and GB10 lacks proprietary support in both. So GB10 was never officially
supported on the proprietary modules; .159.03 drove one anyway and we do
not know why. The flavour flip stands on the measured A/B — same driver
version, open works, proprietary does not — not on a policy change that
did not happen.

* feat(image-recipe): build the open NVIDIA kernel modules on every platform

Blackwell is open-only, so the proprietary modules leave a GB10, an RTX
50-series or an RTX PRO 6000 found but unusable — x86_64-nvidia has the
same defect the DGX Spark hit, not just aarch64. Dropping the
per-platform split in favour of open everywhere is a deliberate call by
dr-bonez: current hardware works, and Maxwell, Pascal and Volta are given
up, since the open modules need the GSP first shipped in Turing.

Verified by generating the hook for both platforms — each yields
kernel-module-type=open.

The lost cards are named in the changelog under Changed rather than
buried, since a GTX 1080 or Tesla P40 owner updating to this loses GPU
compute with no other signal. The docs' download list also gains the
NVIDIA variant, which it never described at all, now that choosing it
carries a hardware floor.

* fix(image-recipe): let UVM register a GPU the kernel cannot offer ATS to

Debian builds no CONFIG_IOMMU_SVA, so UVM pins every VA space to
ATS_UNSUPPORTED while an integrated part like GB10 still advertises ATS.
uvm_va_space_register_gpu then refuses the GPU with NV_ERR_INVALID_DEVICE,
which UVM never logs, and libcuda reports only CUDA_ERROR_NOT_INITIALIZED:
nvidia-smi works while every CUDA program fails at startup.

Extract the installer, drop that guard, and build from the patched source.
Measured on a DGX Spark: cuInit 0, 122552 MiB visible, and vLLM serving a
122B model at 74% GPU utilisation.

Dropping the guard forfeits mixing coherent and non-coherent GPUs in one
process, which these images do not support. The hook aborts if a future
driver moves the guard, so the patch cannot silently stop applying.

* fix(start-os): restore only a preserved config that belongs to the disk being installed

The restore after mkfs was gated on /tmp/config.bak existing at all, and /tmp
outlives a failed install attempt within one live boot. Two shapes that opened:

- A failed preserve attempt on disk A left its backup behind; a retry on a
  different disk whose pool was preserved but which had no OS root kept the
  stale backup and restored disk A's config — shadow and MOK key included —
  onto disk B.
- A same-disk retry after a late failure found the new root's fresh default
  config and staged it over the good backup the earlier attempt had taken.

preserve_config now writes a marker naming the disk a backup came from and
clears any leftover backup that does not match the disk being installed, and
previous_os_root only recognizes a config that completed setup (has a
disk.guid), so a failed attempt's default config is no longer staged over a
good backup. A same-disk retry after an early failure still restores the
leftover backup, which is then the only surviving copy of the real config.

fix(core/net): close the client leg when the upstream leg closes (#3733)

* fix(core/net): close the client leg when the upstream leg closes

The HTTP-aware vhost proxy pins one client connection to one upstream
connection. `try_join` short-circuits only on `Err`, so a backend closing
its idle keep-alive leg — a clean FIN, which hyper reports as `Ok(())` —
left the client's half being driven for up to `header_read_timeout`. The
client kept a connection it had every reason to believe was healthy, and
the next request on it hit `send_request` against a dead connection; the
service error tears the connection down without writing a response, which
a client reports as a bare remote close.

Apache's default `KeepAliveTimeout` is 5s and Nextcloud Desktop polls
`status.php` every 30s, so that window was hit on essentially every idle
cycle — Connected/"Network error" flapping with no user-visible cause.
The raw-splice path (`copy_bidirectional`) has never had this: it
propagates the FIN, and client pools recover from it invisibly. This
makes the HTTP-aware path behave the same way.

Replace the bare `try_join` with a select loop that calls
`graceful_shutdown` on the client connection once the upstream one has
resolved, on both the h1 and h2 paths. Two things the obvious version
gets wrong:

- On a 101 the upstream connection also resolves `Ok(())` — that is how
  hyper hands the upgraded IO off — and it resolves *before* the client
  one. Shutting down in that window makes hyper's `enforce_version`
  replace the relayed `Connection: Upgrade` with `Connection: close`,
  which conformant WebSocket clients reject even though the tunnel still
  carries bytes. Hence the latch, set before `send_request`. h2 needs no
  equivalent: `Dispatched::Upgrade` is `unreachable!()` there.
- Re-polling a resolved hyper connection is a contract violation, and the
  client's `UpgradeableConnection::poll` unwraps an `Option` its upgrade
  path takes, so it panics outright. Hence the disarmed select arm.

Both are covered by the new tests: reverting to `try_join` fails the
first, dropping the latch fails the second.

Fixes #3731

* fix(core/net): fuse the upstream connection instead of a manual disarm

`.fuse()` is what that guard was reimplementing: it drops the inner
future on completion and returns Pending forever after, so the select
arm can stay unconditional.

* test(core/net): pin the upgrade response ordering

The proxy relays the backend's 101; it never answers an upgrade on the
backend's behalf. Nothing enforced that.

* fix(core/net): relay the final response unedited when the backend closes

`disable_keep_alive` only closes the connection outright when it is idle
(`proto/h1/conn.rs`); called while a response is in flight it sets
`KA::Disabled`, and `enforce_version` then `insert`s `Connection: close`
into the head on the way out. So a backend that answered and closed in the
same breath had a header added to its reply that it never sent:

    http/1.1 200 ok / content-length: 2 / connection: close / date: ...

The proxy should carry the close by closing, not by editing the reply.

Defer the shutdown until the relayed response has actually been written,
tracked by a guard the response body holds — so it drops once hyper is
done with that head and body, at which point the connection is idle and
`disable_keep_alive` takes its clean-close branch.

This subsumes the upgrade latch: a 101 is just the case where the head is
written before the guard drops, and `UpgradeableConnection::graceful_shutdown`
is documented as a no-op once the connection has upgraded. The service_fn
loses the flag entirely. Both are covered — making the shutdown
unconditional again fails `a_relayed_response_is_not_rewritten_when_the_backend_closes`
and `relayed_101_keeps_its_upgrade_header`.

fix(sdk): enforce action input patterns on every path, not just the form (#3735)

A text field's `patterns` reached the browser and nothing else. An action
invoked through `start-cli package action run` or a direct RPC call
arrived at the handler with a value that had never been tested against
them, and the handler wrote it — the field's own declaration was the only
statement that the value was invalid, and it was ignored precisely where
no human was reading the form.

Apply them in the input spec's parser, which `Action.run` already runs
over the submitted input, so the check covers every caller rather than
one client.

Mirror the form exactly, including the two behaviours a hand-rolled check
gets wrong. A pattern is anchored at both ends unless it already is, as
Angular's `Validators.pattern` does for a string regex, so `[a-z]+`
constrains the whole value rather than a substring — testing it
unanchored here would accept values the form rejects, which is worse than
not checking. And an empty value passes every pattern and is left to
`required`, matching `Validators.pattern`'s short-circuit, so an optional
field left blank does not fail a pattern it could never satisfy.

Covers Value.text, Value.textarea, List.text and their dynamic variants —
every builder that declares `patterns`. Colour and datetime are left
alone: they declare none, and the form validates them by other means.

Found auditing navidrome-startos, whose Session Timeout declares
`^([0-9]+(s|m|h))+$`. Over the CLI, `2min` saved cleanly and the daemon,
which reads that setting reactively, restarted straight into
`FATAL: 'SessionTimeout' time: unknown unit`. Verified against a
0.4.0.1 box with the package's own handler check disabled, so the SDK was
the only guard: the action now fails with the pattern's description and
the store is left untouched, while a valid value still saves.

fix(sdk): reject manifest fields the SDK does not define (#3736)

setupManifest infers its parameter type from the argument, and TypeScript
applies its excess-property check only when a fresh object literal meets a
non-generic target — so an unknown field joined the inferred type,
compiled, and was then dropped on the way to the built manifest. It never
reached the registry and nothing ever said so.

That is how `docsUrls` came to sit in twelve packages doing nothing, and
how `alerts` outlived its removal from the SDK in the packages that still
declare it.

Retype the unknown keys so the compiler names them. The replacement is a
string literal rather than `never` only because the resulting error says
what is wrong instead of "not assignable to type 'never'".

docs(packaging): document what maintaining a package takes past the first release (#3749)

* docs(packaging): document what maintaining a package takes past the first release

The guide covers making a change well and says nothing about keeping a
package alive: the branches it accumulates, the upstream it chases, and the
sibling packages it depends on. Every packager using the shipped template
meets all three — `syncNext.yml` creates a `next` branch whether or not
anyone has explained it — but the conventions lived only in maintainers'
private notes, where each reader rediscovered them by getting one wrong.

Adds `maintaining-a-package.md`, covering:

- Base vs. `next`, and why a long-lived head branch takes a merge commit
  where a feature branch takes a squash. The rule is about the head
  branch's lifetime, which is what makes it easy to get backwards.
- Parallel release lines: `next/<base>`, why git forces that slash order,
  and that every operation applies to every line. Illustrated with an
  anonymous multi-major-version package rather than naming ours.
- Chasing upstream: verify the artifact resolves before pinning it,
  prereleases and the unreliable "Latest" badge, scrutiny scaled to the
  jump, and fork parents via the API rather than the manifest's
  `upstreamRepo` (which names the upstream software, not the fork parent).
- Sibling package deps: pin `#next` and let the lockfile do the pinning,
  why `npm update` is a no-op on a git ref, which import shapes actually
  reach the shipped s9pk, and the two-SDK-copies type error.

`workflow.md` gains two disciplines that belong with the per-change rules
rather than the per-package ones: reinstall before believing a type error
(and never bisect against a shared `node_modules`), and finish one package
before starting the next.

Targets live-docs: all of it is true of the shipped SDK and the template's
current workflows. Hunks sit in regions identical on master so
docs-backport.yml applies cleanly — the drift in workflow.md and
agent-context.md is elsewhere in both files. The agent-context diff is one
new table row; the rest is prettier reflowing the table to the new width.



* docs(packaging): stop using construct names for ordinary English

"Task" is a StartOS construct — `sdk.action.createTask`, the prompts a
package raises against the user — and the guide also used it 60-odd times to
mean "a unit of work you are doing," with nothing distinguishing the two.

The two worst were not the navigational ones:

- `main.md` defined one construct with another's name: "Oneshots are tasks
  that run on every startup." A oneshot is a command that runs to
  completion, which is both unambiguous and more accurate.
- `init.md` had "simple sequential tasks (like database migrations)" — two
  overloaded construct names in five words, on the page that teaches init,
  right after two changes separating app-level migrations from
  `migrations.up`.

Three senses, three words, since one replacement reads badly everywhere:
**objective** for what you are trying to accomplish (the recipe index and
the navigation around it), **change** for the unit a discipline applies to
(`workflow.md` already opened with "apply to every change"), and
**step**/**work**/**command** for a stage in a sequence.

Genuine construct uses are untouched — cross-service tasks, critical tasks,
the task sections of the README contract.

Also drops the third sense of "host". `sdk.host` is a construct and "the
host" is the machine; two lines used it for StartOS itself, which is now
what they say.

Checked the other reserved words and left them alone: `action` has no
generic uses; `store` and `interface` collide only with different domains
("system trust store", "web interface"); `dependency` is genuinely
double-loaded but the guide already qualifies the npm sense at every site.



* docs(packaging): two more conventions that only lived in private notes

Both are general — any packager with a `next` branch meets the first, and
anyone who opens a neighbouring package meets the second — and both were
sitting in a maintainer's workspace notes rather than the guide.

A rebased `next` can be carrying a version the base has since released, or
release notes announcing work the base already shipped. Neither announces
itself: publishing the first ships different bytes under a live version,
and the second just quietly lies to the user.

And a stale reference checkout misleads with total confidence — reading a
dependency's credential scheme after upstream dropped it yields an
integration that type-checks, builds, and cannot work.

fix(start-sdk): refresh bundled brace-expansion and js-yaml past their advisories (#3753)

* fix(start-sdk): refresh bundled brace-expansion and js-yaml past their advisories

`bundleDependencies` ships `eslint` and `typescript-eslint` physically inside the
published tarball, so their nested `brace-expansion` and `js-yaml` copies land
under `node_modules/@start9labs/start-sdk/` in every package that installs the
SDK — where neither `overrides` nor `npm audit fix` can reach them. A package
author auditing their own repo saw High-severity findings under a production
dependency with nothing they could do about it.

This refreshes the lock alone, each version within the range its parent already
declares, so no other package in the tree moves and `package.json` is untouched:
`brace-expansion` 1.1.15 → 1.1.18 and 5.0.6 → 5.0.9, `js-yaml` 4.2.0 → 4.3.1,
plus the dev-only 1.1.14 / 2.1.0 / 3.14.2 copies that do not ship.

The advisory ranges moved after the issue was filed: `brace-expansion` 1.1.16 and
5.0.8 and `js-yaml` 4.3.0 — the versions the issue names as fixed — are
themselves covered by GHSA-rgw5-rvv9-x895 and GHSA-5p4m-2wfm-xmqj.

Closes #3592

* docs(start-sdk): list `### Security` among the changelog subsections

The scope doc enumerates `### Added/Changed/Fixed/Removed`, which is what a
contributor reads before writing an entry — but the root changelog rule lists
`### Security` and this release is the first in the SDK's changelog to use it.
Left as-is, the next security entry gets filed under `### Fixed`.

* docs(start-sdk): name every bundleDependencies entry, not just start-core

Both docs said `dist/` bundles `@start9labs/start-core`, when it bundles
`eslint` and `typescript-eslint` too — and those were documented nowhere in the
scope. They are production `dependencies`, so they land in every consuming
package as `inBundle` entries that no downstream `overrides` or `npm audit fix`
can reach, which is exactly the dead end #3592 ran into: a package author sees a
High advisory under a production dep with no way to clear it, and nothing in the
docs explains why or says an SDK release is the only fix.

* fix(start-core): refresh brace-expansion and js-yaml in the sibling lockfile

The SDK lockfile's three dev rows had byte-identical twins next door —
brace-expansion 2.1.0 and 1.1.14, js-yaml 3.14.2 — and CI installs both trees in
the same step, so `npm audit` here kept printing the advisories the SDK's
changelog entry announces as cleared. Same `npm update brace-expansion js-yaml`,
three rows, each inside its declared range.

These are devDependencies of a bundled dep and do not reach the published
tarball — npm packs only start-core's production graph — so this is consistency,
not reach.

docs: route book-only fixes to live-docs, and say which docs that means (#3727)

Two problems with the branch rule for documentation.

It was stated as "Edit the books in master; use live-docs only to fix what
is already live", which reads as master-by-default with live-docs as a
narrow exception. A doc-only correction is in fact the live-docs case, and
opening it against master leaves the published site wrong until that
product is next tagged.

It also never said which files it governs. docs-deploy.yml triggers on
projects/start-docs/** and projects/<product>/docs/** and nothing else, so
the routing applies to the published books alone. Every AGENTS.md,
ARCHITECTURE.md, CONTRIBUTING.md and README.md in the repo is ordinary
content that nothing publishes — live-docs' copy of this very file is
already stale against master with no mechanism to reconcile it — and those
land on master like code.

State the scope, then the test: does the change accompany code? If yes,
master, in the same PR as the code. If it only corrects a book, live-docs,
and it reaches master through the backport.

Also records the split case: a book-only change can partly target text that
exists only on master, and that part needs its own master PR rather than
being folded in.

docs: replace the comment rules that were producing unreadable comments (#3757)

The root CONTRIBUTING.md told everyone "Comments should be shorthand, not
prose", and start-registry's told them "one short line". Both buy brevity by
deleting grammar, which is how a comment that was merely too long becomes one
nobody can read: `// tz-naive dt -> UTC; DST fold => dup hr, keep 1st`.

Rewrite AGENTS.md's Code style section around the two directions a comment goes
wrong — the essay that buries one fact in narration, and the telegram an essay
becomes when someone asks for shorter — and set the bar between them: one idea,
a complete sentence, present tense, the actor named. Shorten by removing ideas,
never by removing grammar.

Also in this change:

- Doc comments on a public surface stay. A `///` on an exported item or a JSDoc
  on an SDK type a package author reads in their editor is documentation, which
  a strict reading of "default to none" put at risk.
- A `// TODO` becomes an issue, matching the Filing issues section and the SDK
  guide, rather than CONTRIBUTING.md's `// TODO(username): reason`.
- Fix bad comments in a file you are already editing, scoped so cleanup cannot
  grow into a comment sweep of its own.
- Drop start-registry's duplicate comment bullet. The hierarchy rule in
  AGENTS.md says a scope must not repeat what a higher scope already states.

CONTRIBUTING.md keeps a human-facing summary and points at AGENTS.md for the
rule itself, per the split AGENTS.md describes.

The wording is distilled from Google's developer documentation style guide at
developers.google.com/style, chiefly its voice and tone, jargon, global
audience, and timeless documentation sections.

fix: ACME domains on non-443 ports get a certificate, and never fall back to the local CA (#3734)

* fix: route the ACME challenge to a domain served on another port

Let's Encrypt validates a name by dialling it on port 443 with the
`acme-tls/1` ALPN, whatever port the name is actually served on. A domain
bound to an interface's own SSL port — Electrum on 50002, TURN on 5349 —
had nothing answering there: only the OS host can claim 443, and each
vhost server answers by name for its own port alone. The order never
completed, so the domain kept serving the local CA chain instead.

Ask the gateway to route the challenge port for such a domain to the port
it does serve, and answer a challenge for a name a server does not route
from the controller-wide cache of orders in flight — which covers a box
whose 443 is forwarded to it directly.

The port-map request needed a per-hostname box-side port: the desired map
carried one internal port for every hostname sharing an external port, so
two ACME domains would have collapsed onto whichever was reconciled
first. The PCP HOSTNAME request already carries internal and external
independently and StartTunnel already targets `(peer, internal_port)`, so
the relay is unchanged.

The derivation is now a free function over the vhost targets, which is
what makes it testable.

Fixes part of #3717

* fix: refuse a connection to an ACME domain with no certificate

When no ACME certificate was available for a name — the order failed, or
we are inside its backoff — the resolution chain fell through to the
local root CA, which mints a leaf for any name asked of it. The client
got a certificate signed by an authority it does not trust, under a name
the UI still labelled Let's Encrypt, and the fallback was invisible from
the server itself, whose own trust store holds that root. The root CA
chain is the same on every address the server exposes, so handing it out
links them to one server.

A handler can now refuse a connection rather than decline it, which stops
the chain, and the ACME handler refuses for a name it holds a provider
for. A name with no provider still declines, so LAN addresses, `.local`,
bare IPs and private domains are unaffected.

Refusing puts far more connections through the reject path, where the
fatal alert was never reaching the wire: the io still buffers writes at
that point, so the client saw a bare close. Stop buffering first.

A renewal that cannot complete no longer takes the domain down either.
`should_use_cert` turns false 30 days before expiry to trigger renewal,
and that cert is still publicly trusted — it is now the answer of last
resort when an order cannot produce a new one, including when the
provider has been removed from the server's settings while a domain
still names it.

Fixes part of #3717

* fix: keep a domain's local side working, and say why the public one is refused

A domain can be reachable two ways at once — split DNS resolves it to a LAN
address inside the network and a public one outside it. Both were one vhost
entry carrying the authority from the public side, so refusing a connection
for a certificate that could not be issued refused the LAN side too, which
never depended on that certificate.

Give each side its own entry, and let only the public one carry an
authority. The two are told apart by the source address: IPv4 hands a
forwarded WAN dial and a local one the same arrival gateway, so a target
that claims a connection as one of our own private addresses is preferred
over one that claims it on the gateway alone. The local side is served the
server's own certificate, or the authority's where one has been issued —
the same certificate either way, as before.

That moves the decision to where the connection's identity is known, so the
vhost holds the two handlers itself rather than chaining them: an address
with an authority is served that authority's certificate or nothing, and one
without falls back to the local root CA as any LAN address does. The chained
handler and the reject action it needed are gone with it — declining is the
refusal now, since nothing is chained below.

A refused address explains itself: the first failure to obtain a certificate
for a name raises a notification naming it and the reason. Every retry while
that stands is silent, and the entry is dropped once a certificate lands, so
the next failure after a success speaks again.

Fixes part of #3717

* fix: never claim an authority for a certificate the service holds itself

An interface whose container serves its own TLS is passed through untouched:
StartOS never terminates it, so it can neither obtain a certificate from an
authority nor present one. A domain on such a host reported whichever
authority had been chosen for it all the same, and the choice was offered in
the first place — the same claim about the wrong certificate this release
removes elsewhere.

Report those addresses as self signed, from the binding rather than the
domain's config, and refuse an authority for a host with no binding StartOS
terminates. The refusal covers the CLI too; the form already hides the
selector where no binding on the host is ours to terminate.

* chore: cut the commentary back, and let a domain keep an authority it isn't using

An interface can move between terminating TLS and passing it through across
an update, and the ACME config a domain carries survives that either way, so
refusing to store one for a host with no binding we terminate asserted an
invariant that does not hold. The frontend keeps hiding the selector; that
is a UX choice, not a rule. The address's certificate column still reports
what is actually served.

* docs: state what makes an ACME challenge answerable, where it is relied on

fix(core): reap orphaned processes in the subcontainer init (#3754)

* fix(core): reap orphaned processes in the subcontainer init

`launch_init` is PID 1 of a subcontainer's PID namespace, and with an empty
command it blocked on TERM signals with SIGCHLD left at `SIG_DFL`. Daemons
`setns` into that namespace rather than creating their own, so every descendant
they orphan reparents to a PID 1 that never waits — and stays `<defunct>` for
the life of the container. It now catches SIGCHLD and drains `waitpid` on each
delivery, and once before the first, since the procfs mount that publishes
`/proc/1` is what lets a caller join the namespace in the first place.

`runAsInit` is unaffected: there the package's own command is PID 1 and reaping
belongs to the image's init. That is a trade-off now rather than a free choice,
so the packaging book, the `runAsInit` tsdoc and the SDK changelog say so — the
last of which also names `tini -s` rather than a bare `tini`, since a daemon
that leaves the option off joins the namespace rather than heading it, and only
the subreaper form ever collected anything there.

* docs(sdk): keep the runAsInit tsdoc timeless

Reverts the `runAsInit` doc comment to what it said before this branch. Naming
the init it displaces described the implementation rather than the option, and
would go stale the moment that init's responsibilities changed. What the option
does — run the command as PID 1 — is the part that stays true.

The reaping trade-off it was trying to convey is already in the packaging book
and the SDK changelog, where it can be dated.

fix(start-wrt): tell devices when IPv6 goes away — goodbye RAs on every teardown, verified device display, boot-time repair of diverged state (#3748)

* fix(start-wrt): only show IPv6 addresses devices still answer for

The Devices list took its IPv6 address straight from the neighbor table
with no liveness check. The kernel keeps a STALE entry indefinitely while
it sits below the GC threshold, so an address a device dropped hours ago
— when a prefix went away, say — kept displaying as current. Most
visibly: after disabling IPv6, devices carried on showing addresses.

Verify before displaying. Any GUA/ULA neighbor entry the kernel has not
just confirmed gets a unicast probe, and the neighbor table is re-read
afterwards; only addresses REACHABLE in either read survive to the UI.

The verdict comes from the NUD state rather than the ping's exit code
(how the IPv4 path judges): the probe's purpose is to force neighbor
discovery, and a device that still owns the address answers the
solicitation even when its firewall drops the echo — the Windows default
off a private network profile. Echo replies would produce false
negatives and hide addresses devices genuinely hold. This matches the
standard ipv6_tracker already applies, which cannot be reused directly
here because it records GUAs only and the field also shows ULAs.

Fails open: if the neighbor table cannot be re-read, every candidate is
kept, so a transient error blanks nobody's address. pick_ipv6 itself is
untouched, and candidate order is preserved, so its GUA-over-ULA
preference is unaffected.

* fix(start-wrt): withdraw IPv6 prefixes from clients before tearing them down

Disabling IPv6 left devices holding addresses that no longer worked, for
up to 90 minutes. SLAAC has no lease to expire, so the only way to revoke
a prefix is to advertise it once more with zero lifetimes (RFC 9096
§3.5). odhcpd emits that RA from router_setup_interface(iface, false),
reached when a config reload finds RA newly disabled — i.e. on SIGHUP,
which is what `/etc/init.d/odhcpd reload` sends.

Every caller used `restart` instead. odhcpd's exit path tears down the
process without touching its interfaces (its atexit handler only closes
/proc/net/ipv6_route, and uloop handles SIGTERM by leaving the event
loop), so the old process died silently and the new one started with RA
already off, having never told anyone. Clients then waited out the full
advertised valid lifetime, which odhcpd caps at 5400s.

Add deprecate_odhcpd_prefixes() and call it before the network is
reconfigured, on all three paths that can drop a prefix: the LAN IPv6
toggle, a profile edit that turns a VLAN's RA off, and a WAN IPv6 mode
change. profiles.rs bounced odhcpd only after the network action, by
which point the prefix was already gone and there was nothing left to
withdraw; that bounce stays, since it is what picks up new prefixes and
ra_default.

There is nothing to wait on — procd_send_signal returns as soon as the
signal is delivered, while the RA goes out later from odhcpd's event
loop — so the helper settles for a fixed 1s pause. Best-effort by
nature: odhcpd sends exactly one final RA (it deliberately does not rearm
the timer on the shutdown path), so a client that misses it, or is
asleep, still falls back to the lifetime timeout.

* fix(start-wrt): repair IPv6 state left diverged by the pre-1.0.2 admin-LAN bug

Before the !profile.owns_lan guard in rewrite_dhcp, any profile rewrite
re-derived dhcp.lan.ra from the *Admin* profile's outbound and could
write 'disabled' there while touching nothing else. That leaves a router
where dhcp.lan.ra says off — which is what is_ipv6_enabled, the LAN IPv6
page and the IPv6 published-port guard all read — while the profile VLANs
keep their ra='server' and ip6assign and carry on handing out addresses.
The UI asserts one thing, the network does another, and nothing converges
them: the guard prevents the divergence, it cannot undo one that already
happened. Shipping the guard alone strands every router upgrading from
<=1.0.1 in that state.

Add heal_ipv6_state, an idempotent boot-time repair alongside the other
self-healing steps in the daemon's normal-mode startup. It runs after
bootstrap_admin_profile, which must register the admin profile first.

Detection is deliberately narrow. On current code the state is
unreachable: lan::ipv6_set writes the LAN and every profile in one
transaction, and rewrite_dhcp derives each profile's ra from
is_ipv6_enabled, which reads dhcp.lan.ra. Firing only on the impossible
combination cannot clobber a legitimate configuration — covered by a test
asserting a healthy router is left untouched.

The repair reconciles down, toward off: the direction is_ipv6_enabled,
the UI and the published-port guard already believe, so it makes reality
match what the product is already telling the user, and it is fully
recoverable via the toggle. Reconciling up would be a guess at intent
that silently resumes advertising on VLANs the user was told are quiet.
It also clears the admin LAN's stranded ip6assign, which serves no client
with RA off but would return as a live prefix the moment RA came back.

The config half is split into a pure function so the tests exercise it
without spawning init scripts; the apply path withdraws the prefixes
(deprecate_odhcpd_prefixes) before reload_system_full does the network
restart netifd needs to drop an ip6assign.

If a per-profile IPv6 toggle ever lands, "LAN off, profile on" becomes
legitimate and this heal must be revisited — noted at the function.

* fix(start-wrt): withdraw IPv6 prefixes on profile create/delete reloads too

was missed when the goodbye RA was added to the other three. Send it
here too, before the network is touched, while the profile's clients
can still hear it.

feat(wrt): identify unnamed devices by OS/vendor and retry silent mDNS lookups (#3623)

* feat(wrt): label unnamed devices by MAC vendor instead of a placeholder

Some clients never advertise a hostname through any source devices.list
consults — ChromeOS deliberately sends no DHCP option 12 and answers no
reverse-mDNS query, and many stripped-down IoT DHCP clients behave the
same — so they surfaced as an opaque `device-3af2b1` placeholder.

Add a vendor-label rung to the name resolution chain, just above the
placeholder: look up the MAC's OUI in an embedded snapshot of the IEEE
registries (MA-L/MA-M/MA-S, longest-prefix match) and render e.g.
"Apple device (3af2b1)", keeping the stable MAC suffix so identical
unnamed devices stay distinguishable. Labels are derived, not learned:
recomputed each poll, never written to the name cache, so any real
hostname that later appears — or a user-assigned name — outranks them.

Randomized (locally-administered) MACs are skipped — they have no
registry entry by construction; on Ethernet, where MACs are burned in,
the lookup essentially always resolves. "IEEE Registration Authority"
parent rows and "Private" registrations are excluded at generation time
so an unassigned sub-block falls through to the placeholder rather than
yielding a meaningless label.

The snapshot (52,889 entries, ~490 KB gzipped) is generated by
build/gen-oui-table.sh; the registry is append-mostly, so the asset only
ever develops misses on brand-new vendors — refresh it opportunistically
by re-running the script. Version bumped to 1.1.0 (feature tier).

* feat(wrt): recognize unnamed devices' OS via DHCP fingerprinting

Layer an OS-recognition rung above the OUI vendor label: the order of a
client's DHCP option-55 parameter-request list and its option-60 vendor
class are characteristic of the OS's DHCP stack, ride the request
itself (so they survive MAC randomization, where OUI lookup is blind),
and cannot be withheld the way a hostname can. An unnamed Windows
laptop now shows "Windows device (3af2b1)" rather than falling to the
NIC vendor or the placeholder.

Capture: a hook script sourced by dnsmasq's dhcp-script wrapper appends
"MAC|options|vendor class" lines on every DHCP add/old event. The
wrapper sources the script inside the dnsmasq ujail, which dictates the
design: no `exit` (it would abort the wrapper's ubus hotplug notify),
shell builtins only (the jail mounts no coreutils), and the output
lands in /var/run/dnsmasq/ — the jail's only writable directory (/tmp
is silently unwritable there). The daemon parses the file defensively
(it is the validation layer for client-controlled bytes) and compacts
it when it outgrows 64 KiB.

Wiring: the daemon provisions the hook at every boot — writes the
script, points every `config dnsmasq` section's `dhcpscript` at it via
a minimal partial TypedSection (preserving all other options), and
reloads dnsmasq only on change — so OTA-updated routers converge
without a reflash; profile creation sets `dhcpscript` on new instances
directly.

Persistence: fingerprints are cached per-MAC in device_names.json
(hostname becomes optional there — a Chromebook has a fingerprint but
no name; legacy files load unchanged), so OS labels survive reboots
even though the capture file is tmpfs. Labels themselves stay derived:
recomputed each poll from fingerprint-else-OUI, never cached as names.

The rule table is seeded from widely-documented signatures (MSFT/
android-dhcp/dhcpcd/udhcp vendor classes; Apple and Windows option-55
sequences) and is deliberately conservative — a miss falls through to
the OUI rung. Live bench validation, documented in device_ident.rs:
capture /var/run/dnsmasq/dhcp.fingerprints for Windows, macOS, iOS,
Android, Debian, and above all ChromeOS (the client this feature exists
for), whose vendor-class behavior is undocumented and decides whether
it earns a dedicated rule or lands on "Linux"/the OUI rung.

* fix(wrt): retry silent mDNS name lookups on a backoff schedule

Reverse-mDNS name recovery attempted each device exactly once per
daemon run: a silent device went into MDNS_ATTEMPTED and was never
queried again until restart — potentially months. That single attempt
is a bad sampler: it usually fires the moment the device first appears
(before its mDNS responder is up) or in the reassociation chaos right
after a router reboot, and sleeping phones/laptops don't answer at all,
so devices that do have Bonjour names got stuck on the generic label.

Replace the attempted-set with a per-MAC attempt history and retry
still-unnamed devices on a bounded backoff schedule: 6 attempts total,
gated at 1 min -> 10 min -> 1 h -> 6 h -> 24 h after the previous try,
then done until restart (the old behavior becomes the end state instead
of the first). The shape follows RFC 6762 §5.2, mDNS's own doubling
retry for unanswered queries; unlike a standing query we cap attempts,
since many devices genuinely have no responder and each attempt spawns
avahi-resolve. The early rungs catch responder-startup lag and boot
chaos (avahi-daemon also caches answers that arrive after our 1.5 s
timeout kills the CLI, so a quick retry often hits the cache); the late
rungs catch sleepers. A permanently silent device now costs 6 spawns
per daemon run instead of 1 — still nothing.

Backoff runs on Instant, not wall time: routers boot with a wrong clock
and NTP-jump minutes later, which would garble a wall-clock schedule.
Retries ride the existing devices.list polls, so nothing fires while no
client is viewing the device list, and success still persists to the
name cache, which gates any further attempts. devices.forget now also
drops the attempt history, so a forgotten device that reconnects starts
a fresh schedule (matching the "appears as a new entry" docs contract).

* feat(wrt): recognize NetworkManager's DHCP fingerprint as Linux

Bench capture 2026-08-03 (Ubuntu, NetworkManager internal client): option-55
list 1,2,6,12,15,26,28,121,3,33,40,41,42,119,249,252,17 with no vendor class —
the default DHCP client on Ubuntu/Fedora desktops. Exact-match rule in the
table's conservative style; a drifted list in a future NM version just falls
through to the OUI rung as before.

* chore(wrt): move additions clear of master's edits so the PR automerges

Master now inserts its own boot step and changelog entries at the exact

feat(start-wrt): provision the eMMC boot partitions (boot0/boot1) in flash and sysupgrade (#3607)

* feat(start-wrt): provision the eMMC boot partitions in flash and sysupgrade

The K1 BootROM boots eMMC from the hardware boot partitions (an 80-byte
bootinfo header at boot0 offset 0 pointing at the FSBL/u-boot SPL, with a
mirror in boot1) — regions only vendor factory tooling (Titan/fastboot)
ever wrote. The wizard's raw copy covers just the user area, so a DIY
BananaPi BPI-F3 whose factory left boot0 empty or carrying an incompatible
bootloader vintage completed setup but couldn't boot once the microSD was
removed. Boards that worked did so on unversioned factory FSBLs that every
sysupgrade re-pairs with new OpenSBI/u-boot — an untested combination.

Converge boot0/boot1 to the release's own bootinfo + FSBL (built from the
pinned spacemit-com/uboot-2022.10 source; the FSBL is read from the image's
fsbl partition — the binary that booted the running system) in both write
paths:

- flash wizard/CLI: backend/ctrl/src/boot0.rs, called from run_flash_core
  after the user-area copy (progress stays within the existing flash step)
- sysupgrade: /lib/upgrade/spacemit_boot0.sh (target-level base-files,
  auto-sourced), called from both subtargets' platform_do_upgrade; logs
  but never aborts the upgrade

Idempotent (byte-compared, skipped when already current), read-back
verified (O_DIRECT / iflag=direct where supported), commit-safe write
order (boot1 mirror, boot0 FSBL, single-sector bootinfo header last).
EXT_CSD boot-enable bits are deliberately untouched — the vendor factory
flasher never sets them either. bootinfo_emmc.bin now ships in the bootfs
FAT partition (previously only packed into the Titan archive) as the
runtime source for both paths, and uboot-spacemit gains a real
PKG_MIRROR_HASH in place of skip.

* fix(start-wrt): make sysupgrade boot0 provisioning actually run in stage2

Two bugs found by the corrupted-boot1 OTA smoke test (boot1 came back
unrepaired, hash-identified as untouched):

- The bootinfo magic was validated against the wrong decimal (2953778416 =
  0xb00f14f0, a mistranslation of 0xb00714f0 = 2953254128), so the helper
  rejected every valid bootinfo_emmc.bin and bailed before writing anything.
  The Rust path was unaffected (it compares in hex, golden-tested).
- Region comparison used cmp, which is not in the fixed binary list stage2's
  switch_to_ramfs copies into the upgrade ramfs — the gate and the read-back
  verify would both fail there. Compare via md5sum instead, which is on the
  upstream list.

* feat(start-wrt): ship MT7915 wifi firmware so MT7915-based DIY cards initialize

The image carries the kmod-mt7915e driver (it covers MT7915 and MT7916)
but only the MT7916 firmware files, so an MT7915-based card (e.g. AsiaRF
AW7915-NP1) probes, fails the mt7915_rom_patch.bin load with -2, and
never registers a PHY. Add kmod-mt7915-firmware; the two firmware
packages coexist and the driver requests the set matching the detected
chip. Band-selectable MT7915 cards still run one band at a time: radio0
(2.4 GHz, bare PCIe path) resolves to the single PHY, radio1 (+1 path
suffix) only exists on DBDC cards. Document the DIY wifi-card support
matrix.

* docs(start-wrt): move eMMC boot-provisioning changelog entry under 1.0.2

The entry was written under 1.0.0 while that version was still prospective,
but 1.0.0 and 1.0.1 have since been released from master without this
branch — the feature actually ships in 1.0.2.

* chore(start-wrt): bump the prospective version to 1.1.0

New-hardware support (MT7915 Wi-Fi firmware) is a minor per semver, not a
patch, so the unreleased 1.0.2 heading — never tagged, never shipped —
becomes 1.1.0 in place, with the manifest bumped to match.

* feat(start-wrt): converge eMMC boot firmware on every boot

sysupgrade stage2 runs the OLD system's upgrade scripts, so the release
that introduces boot0 provisioning (or a future FSBL change) cannot
converge a box during its own installation — only the upgrade after it
could. Add a preinit hook (registered after 79_move_config on the same
preinit_mount_root stage) that runs the existing spacemit_provision_boot0
helper on every boot: provisioning takes effect on the first boot after
installing this release, and damaged or interrupted boot-firmware writes
self-heal thereafter. A converged board performs three region reads and
writes nothing. Output lands in /tmp/spacemit_boot0.log — syslog is not
up during preinit.

The stage2 hook stays: only upgrade-time provisioning can move the whole
boot chain within a single power cycle when a future release changes the
FSBL.
