fix(start-wrt): stop stale cached UIs after firmware updates — cache headers, live detection, and an auto-reload/prompt flow (#3756)

* fix(start-wrt): stop browsers from serving a stale cached UI after updates

The embedded web UI was served with no cache headers at all, leaving cache
behavior to per-browser heuristics: after a firmware update, Firefox/Safari
could silently keep running the previous UI bundle against the new backend
(observed as the "fixed" outbound-VPN dialog still failing on beta.4 until a
hard refresh).

Serve the UI with explicit caching now:

- Stable-named files (index.html, assets/) get `Cache-Control: no-cache` plus
  a per-build ETag (the baked-in STARTWRT_GIT_HASH), so every load revalidates
  and costs a 304 until the firmware actually changes.
- Angular's content-hashed bundles (main-*.js, chunk-*.js, styles-*.css) get
  `public, max-age=31536000, immutable` — their names change with content, so
  caching forever is safe and speeds up loads.
- The SPA fallback now only serves index.html for extensionless (route-like)
  paths; asset-like requests, e.g. a hashed chunk from an older build, 404
  instead of receiving a mis-typed HTML body that can break module loading.

Follows start-os's static_server.rs (ETag + 304 + immutable) but diverges on
index.html: start-os caches it immutable and compensates with a "Refresh
Needed" dialog; revalidating it instead removes the stale-UI state entirely.

Unit tests exercise the handler against the real embedded dist (skipped when
the dist placeholder is empty, e.g. plain `cargo test` in CI).

* feat(start-wrt): detect a stale UI after firmware updates and reload it

The cache-header fix guarantees any page load picks up a new firmware's UI,
but a tab that is already open never refetches index.html — in-app navigation
is client-side routing, so a running bundle stays stale until the user
reloads. Close that gap by detecting the mismatch and reloading (or prompting):

- Unify the build stamp. build-rust.sh and ctrl's build.rs fallback now emit
  the same stamp as build/env/check-git-hash.sh (full git hash, "-modified"
  suffix on a dirty tree) instead of a separate short-hash "-dirty" format, so
  the binary's UI ETag / system.info / `startwrt verify` output and the web
  bundle's baked-in config.json gitHash are the identical string.
- Expose the stamp over RPC: system.info (no_auth) now returns gitHash, so
  detection works even when an update reboot wiped the session store.
- Detect divergence in StaleUiService (dirty-marker-insensitive compare,
  skipping dev "@branch"/"unknown" stamps) fed from every system.info
  consumer: SystemService init/refresh and the connection-recovery probe —
  the exact path a tab lands on after the daemon restarts under it.
- An update initiated from this tab reloads automatically once the router is
  back (the session is gone either way; the "Updated to vX" confirmation
  rides sessionStorage across the reload and shows after login). An update
  applied any other way (CLI deploy, another device) shows a "Refresh Needed"
  dialog with a Reload button instead — never reloading out from under
  unsaved work. A plain reload suffices because index.html revalidates its
  ETag on every load.

Strings are translated in all five locales.

* fix(start-wrt): translate the post-update confirmation and document the update UX

Audit follow-ups on this branch: the "Updated to vX" toast was the one
untranslated user-facing string in the new update flow (i18n id 533, all
five locales), and docs/src/updating.md now describes the automatic
post-update reload, the post-login confirmation, and the "Refresh
Needed" dialog shown to pages open elsewhere during an update.

* fix(start-wrt): detect a stale UI on every RPC response, not just connection loss

Stale-UI detection only ran when the tab fetched system.info — app boot,
the in-tab update flow, or the reconnect probe after a request failed. A
CLI deploy (make start-wrt-update) restarts the daemon faster than the
5s background poll cadence, so no request ever failed and an open tab
never noticed the new firmware; a tab backgrounded through a whole OTA
reboot could miss it the same way (throttled timers resume against the
new daemon successfully).

The daemon now stamps x-startwrt-git-hash (the same build stamp as
system.info's gitHash, exposed through CORS for the dev serve) on every
/rpc/v1 response, and HttpService feeds it to StaleUiService — so any
request an open tab makes, including the periodic form polls, detects a
deploy within seconds. The reconnect-probe check remains as a fallback
for disruptive updates with a wiped session.

* fix(start-wrt): re-check for a stale UI every 30s on idle pages

Stale-UI detection rides the x-startwrt-git-hash header on RPC
responses, but non-FormService pages (e.g. Settings General, which
renders from the info signal loaded at boot) make no requests while
idle — a firmware deploy went unnoticed there until navigating to a
polling page. SystemService now runs a 30s system.info heartbeat as a
detection floor (and keeps the displayed system date fresh), skipped
while the tab is hidden, while the in-tab update flow owns polling, or
while the reconnect loop is already probing.

* fix(start-wrt): stop periodic info refreshes from reverting unsaved theme/language previews

The 30s stale-UI heartbeat refreshes system.info, and the app-level effect
re-applied the saved theme and language on every info object. Key the effect
on the values instead, so a refresh that changes neither no longer stomps a
live preview on Settings -> General.

* fix(start-wrt): re-arm a dismissed stale-UI prompt when the firmware updates again

Latch the newer build's base hash instead of a boolean and silence dismissal
per build, matching start-os's refresh alert, which re-prompts on the next
version change after a dismissal.

feat(start-wrt): automatic port forwarding (PCP + UPnP IGD server) (#3634)

* feat(start-wrt): automatic port forwarding (PCP + UPnP IGD server)

Implement the server half of gateway autoconfiguration (start-os #3306)
for StartWRT, using the shared start-core protocol cores: a PCP server
(UDP 5351), a UPnP IGD server (SSDP responder + HTTP control on 49001),
and a lease-expiry sweep, all driven by a new GatewayBackend impl that
maps device-requested forwards onto auto-tagged UCI redirects (_apf_*).

Authorization is per-device and off by default: a new "Allow automatic
port forwarding" toggle on the device detail page (devices.set-auto-forward)
sets an _allow_pcp flag on the DHCP host entry, and only flagged devices
can create forwards — and only to themselves. Forwards are keyed by
external port (apf_<mac>_<extport>, UPnP's mapping identity), persist
across reboots, renew on in-memory leases honoring the lifetime granted
to the client (no flash writes on renewal), and expire via a per-minute
sweep serialized against renewals. The Published Ports page gains a
read-only "Automatic" section (published-ports.auto-list).

Two rules keep an automatic forward from outliving the user's intent,
neither of which the shared cores can enforce for us:

- A request for a *permanent* mapping (UPnP NewLeaseDuration = 0, which
  reaches the backend as `lifetime: None`) is granted MAX_LEASE — a week
  — not held forever. An unattended router must never carry a WAN port
  with nothing scheduled to close it; a client that still wants the port
  renews long before then.
- Turning a device's toggle back off removes that device's forwards
  immediately, rather than leaving them open until their leases lapse.
  The toggle is the only control a user has over an automatic forward
  (the Automatic table is read-only), so it has to actually close them.

Conflicts are enforced both ways: a device request overlapping any
enabled WAN DNAT redirect is refused (718), and publishing a manual port
over an auto-held external port removes the auto forward — manual wins.

Shared start-core changes (also affect StartTunnel):
- GatewayBackend::sni() now returns Option<&Arc<SniDemux>>, replacing
  supports_hostname(): a gateway without an SNI dataplane (StartWRT)
  cannot advertise the Start9 HOSTNAME capability by accident, and
  HOSTNAME-bound MAPs are refused instead of registering into a dead
  demux. Both PCP ANNOUNCE paths (v4 and v6) report it truthfully.
- The IGD layer parses NewLeaseDuration and passes it to add_forward,
  so a lease-tracking backend expires mappings on the schedule reported
  to the client. A lease of 0 stays permanent (None), leaving StartTunnel
  — whose forwards are DB-persisted, not leased — unchanged.
- GetExternalIPAddress requires is_known_client, matching AddPortMapping,
  so unauthorized/guest-VLAN hosts can no longer read the WAN IP through
  the well-known control path.

Also consolidates crate-internal duplication the feature would have
deepened: one DHCP-host upsert (devices + auto-forward toggle) and one
device-zone resolver (manual + auto forwards).

* fix(start-wrt): close the gaps an audit found in automatic port forwarding

Follow-up to 2a56b79b3, from a full audit of the feature.

Security and lifecycle:

- Refuse an automatic forward for a port the router answers on itself from
  the WAN. Remote Access (80/443/22) and a VPN server's listen port are
  input-chain ACCEPT rules, invisible to the DNAT conflict scan, and a
  prerouting DNAT wins over an input ACCEPT — so a device could divert the
  router's own web UI, SSH, or inbound VPN to itself. The reservation is read
  from the live rules rather than a hardcoded list, so a port frees up when
  its feature is turned off and any future WAN-exposed service is covered.
  This is the automatic half of the collision in #3451; the manual half, which
  asks for a warning rather than a refusal, is untouched.

- Close a device's forwards when it is forgotten, not just when its toggle is
  turned off. Forgetting drops the `_allow_pcp` flag with the DHCP host entry,
  so the device can no longer create forwards — but the ones it held stayed
  open for up to a week, with no way to close them.

- Bind a forward to the address assignment behind it. A renewing client
  re-resolves its own address, but a client that asked for a permanent mapping
  never renews, so its forward kept pointing at an address DHCP is free to
  reissue. The sweep now drops a forward whose owner no longer holds the
  address it points at (RFC 6887 §15, RFC 6970 §5.10). A static reservation
  pins it regardless, and with no lease files readable the check is skipped
  rather than guessed.

- Don't strand auto forwards on a profile move, and don't silently revoke the
  permission. `remove_ports_for_macs` matched only `_pp_*` sections, leaving an
  auto forward with a stale `dest_ip` and zone; it also deletes unnamed DHCP
  hosts, and a host created solely to carry `_allow_pcp` is unnamed.

- Supervise the four port-control servers independently. Sharing one
  `tokio::join!` meant a panic in any of them could take the lease sweep down,
  leaving every forward open with nothing scheduled to close it.

Smaller fixes:

- `auto_list` honored `/etc/config` instead of the context's UCI root.
- `set_auto_forward` validates the MAC before writing it into a new host
  section, and reloads dnsmasq like `devices.update` does.
- The device page's auto-forward switch is a `linkedSignal` that resets when
  the write is rejected. It was bound one-way to the stored value, which
  cannot re-sync: the value never changes, so Angular writes nothing and the
  switch keeps the position the click left it.
- One Spanish string referenced a page title that didn't match its own
  dictionary.

* docs(start-tunnel): file the UPnP changelog entries under the unreleased version

The `GetExternalIPAddress` authorization entry added in 2a56b79b3 landed inside
`## [1.1.1]` — a released version, tagged on origin — where it also created a
second `### Fixed` heading in that section. Users of 1.1.1 never received it.
Moved under the unreleased 1.2.2, as `### Security`, and reworded: the gate is
a device with Auto-publish enabled, which is narrower than "a known device".

Also documents the other user-visible change from that commit, which had no
entry at all: a UPnP mapping requested with an explicit lease now expires when
the lease runs out instead of being kept as though it were permanent. This is
what the docs already claimed automatic ports do. Clients asking for a
permanent mapping, which is what StartOS does, are unaffected.

* fix(start-wrt): fold the auto-forward permission into the device settings form

The Permissions toggle sat outside the settings form, so it auto-saved on
change and overlapped the Cancel/Save buttons — `.g-footer` is
`position: absolute; inset: 100% 0 auto`, pinned to the form's bottom edge and
out of normal flow, so anything rendered after the form lands on top of it.

It is now a control in the same form: Save applies it, Cancel discards it, and
the footer sits below it. The permission is a separate endpoint, so it rides
along inside the existing update action and only when it actually changed —
one Save raises one loader and one toast, and revocation (which closes the
device's existing forwards) never fires from merely renaming a device.

This also removes the optimistic-switch machinery added in 70c8b8f9c, which
existed only to undo an auto-save the user never asked for.

* fix(start-core): serve a UPnP IGD that third-party clients will actually use

Discovered on hardware: `upnpc` refused the router outright —

    UPnP device found. Is it an IGD ? : http://192.168.0.1:49001/ctl/IPConn
    No valid UPNP Internet Gateway Device found.

Three gaps, all in the shared IGD server, so StartTunnel had every one of them
too. The four actions we implemented were exactly the set StartOS needs, and
StartOS is the only client that had ever talked to either gateway, so nothing
had exercised the rest of the surface.

- **Not recognized as an IGD.** A client identifies one by finding the
  `WANCommonInterfaceConfig` service in the device description; ours declared
  only `WANIPConnection`, so miniupnpc classified us `UPNP_UNKNOWN_DEVICE` and
  its main loop — which proceeds only on `UPNP_CONNECTED_IGD` or
  `UPNP_PRIVATEIP_IGD` — gave up before sending a single request. Declared on
  the `WANDevice`, with its own SCPD at `/WANCfg.xml`. Both services share the
  one control endpoint; actions dispatch by name.

- **No connection status.** Validation then calls `GetStatusInfo` and treats
  anything but `Connected` as a disconnected IGD. Added, along with
  `GetConnectionTypeInfo`, `GetNATRSIPStatus` and `GetCommonLinkProperties` —
  all static.

- **Mappings could not be read back.** Clients confirm a mapping by reading it
  back, so `AddPortMapping` succeeded and was then reported as failed on the
  `GetSpecificPortMappingEntry` fault. Added that and
  `GetGenericPortMappingEntry` over a new `GatewayBackend::list_forwards`,
  scoped to the requesting peer's own automatic forwards — a device can neither
  enumerate another's nor see operator-created ones. StartWRT reads them from
  the tagged UCI sections; StartTunnel from PatchDb, reporting `lease_seconds`
  as 0 ("permanent" in IGD terms) since expiry lives in the lease map rather
  than on the forward.

Additive throughout: no existing action's behavior changes, and the new ones
previously returned fault 401. StartOS is unaffected — its client requires none
of them and reads `WANIPConnection` from an untouched part of the description.

* fix(start-wrt): reload the firewall instead of restarting it, and name the gateway correctly

Two loose ends from the port-forwarding audit.

**Apply firewall changes atomically.** `/etc/init.d/firewall restart` runs
`fw4 restart`, which is `stop` — `nft delete table inet fw4` — followed by
`start`, as two separate invocations. In between, the router has no firewall
and no NAT, and traffic arriving in that window is unfiltered. `reload` renders
the ruleset into a single `nft -f` transaction (`table` / `flush table` /
`table {…}`), so there is no gap, and a ruleset that fails to build aborts and
leaves the running one in place instead of leaving nothing. Renamed the
function to match what it now does.

Every other firewall call site in the backend already used `reload`; this path
did not, so both manual and automatic published-port changes opened the window.
`profiles.rs` still restarts on profile create/delete — zones are added and
removed there and it wasn't audited here, so it's left alone deliberately.

The reload falls back to a restart when reload fails, which is the one case
`restart` handled and `reload` doesn't: `fw4 reload` refuses to run when the
firewall isn't loaded at all. Note `run_quiet_async` reports a non-zero exit as
`Ok(status)` rather than an error, so the status is checked explicitly —
otherwise a failed reload would look like success and the fallback would never
fire.

**Identify the gateway as the product serving it.** `root_desc.xml` hardcoded
"StartTunnel" in `friendlyName`, `modelName` and `modelDescription`, so a
StartWRT router advertised itself to every UPnP client as StartTunnel. It went
unnoticed because until the preceding commit no third-party client got far
enough to display a name. `render_root_desc` now takes the product name, with a
test asserting no other product's name can leak back into the description.

* fix(start-wrt): keep pages fully visible on small screens; align the device form with house patterns

Four fixes, one per mechanism:

- The help aside gave the shell's 1fr grid row a content-height
  minimum: grid items default to min-height auto, and the aside had no
  height constraint (its tui-scrollbar never resolved a height), so on
  routes with long help content the shell grew past the viewport —
  clipping the nav's Collapse button and the bottom of the page (a
  form's Cancel/Save could not be scrolled into view), even with help
  closed, since [inert] only collapses the aside's column, not its row.
  Fix: min-block-size: 0 on the aside host + block-size: 100% on its
  scrollbar — the constraints start-tunnel's aside carries (not
  overflow: hidden, which would clip the ::before corner decoration).

- Below Taiga's mobile breakpoint the shell pins page content to the
  collapsed-rail width, but the nav-open state was initialized once
  from the user agent and never reacted: a desktop window dragged below
  768px kept its expanded in-flow sidebar while the content laid out
  for the rail, pushing the right side of the page (the right-aligned
  Save/Cancel first) under main's overflow clip with nothing to scroll.
  The nav-open state is now a linkedSignal on TUI_BREAKPOINT — the very
  signal that flips tui-root._mobile — so the rail collapses in step
  with the pinning (and re-collapses after navigating on a phone),
  mirroring start-tunnel's outlet.

- The mobile pin itself moved from the scrollport (tui-scrollbar) onto
  the page content. A pinned scrollport wider than the visible column
  is itself clipped by main, and since its content fits it exactly, no
  horizontal scrollbar can ever appear — the hole left when the old
  viewport fix (min-width: 100%) got a mobile carve-out that
  reintroduced the fixed width at the scrollport level. With the
  content pinned instead (100vw - 6rem: the old pin minus the content's
  side margins, so the collapsed-rail layout is pixel-identical), a
  hand-expanded sidebar produces real overflow: the nav still slides
  over the content rather than squishing it, and everything stays
  reachable by horizontal scroll.

- The device page's new Permissions group used a header nested inside
  the form card — the app's only one; titled groups in a [tuiForm] card
  are fieldset/legend (as settings/general). And its switch explained
  itself via a tuiHint that could never display: hints inside checkbox
  labels are revealed only for disabled controls, and this control is
  never disabled. The explanation is now visible secondary copy under
  the switch, reusing the page's note idiom and the exact i18n string,
  so all five dictionaries are untouched.

Verified headless at 743px CSS: fresh load starts collapsed with
nothing clipped; expanding by hand yields a working horizontal
scrollbar with Save reachable at full scroll; 1200px desktop still
starts expanded with no overflow. check:wrt, build:wrt, check:i18n
green.

* feat(start-wrt): confirm before publishing a port the router answers on itself

Publishing an IPv4 forward on a port the router serves from the WAN —
Remote Access to its web interface or SSH (80/443/22, including the
behind-NAT mode whenever the WAN address is private) or an inbound
VPN's listen port — silently cut that service off from outside the
network: nftables applies prerouting DNAT before the routing decision,
so the forward captures the router's own traffic (the manual-forward
half of issue #3451; the automatic PCP/UPnP half already refuses).

`published-ports.set` now checks each enabled IPv4 forward against the
live WAN-input ACCEPT rules — the same scan the auto path uses, made
transport-aware (Remote Access is TCP, WireGuard is UDP, so a UDP-only
forward on 443 collides with nothing). On an unconfirmed collision it
applies nothing and returns the colliding rules and port specs; the UI
raises a confirmation dialog and re-saves with
`override_router_ports` on the named rules. The confirmation persists
on the redirect (`_pp_router_override`) and round-trips through
`list`, so you are asked once per rule — toggling or deleting other
rules never re-prompts — while editing a rule rebuilds it without the
flag and asks again. The UI re-save recurses through the same
collision handling, so a collision that appears while the dialog sits
open gets its own prompt rather than a silently unapplied save.

Configs-only mode skips the check (the CLI editor confirms implicitly,
like ethernet.set/wifi.set); the automatic path still refuses outright
— a protocol client can't be asked.

cargo tests (492), check:wrt, and check:i18n:wrt green.

* chore: minor fixes

* fix(start-wrt): reject cross-segment source-spoofed PCP requests

PCP rides on unauthenticated UDP, so the automatic-forwarding server
trusted the *claimed* source address of a MAP: any LAN host could send a
datagram spoofing an authorized device's IP and open — or, with
lifetime 0, tear down — that device's WAN forwards. UPnP is unaffected;
it is TCP, so the handshake proves the source.

Close the cross-segment case: enable IP_PKTINFO on the PCP socket and
require that a request arrived on the same interface the neighbor table
places its claimed source on. A datagram received on br-lan can no
longer act as a device the neighbor table locates on br-lan.101. The
check gates is_known_client, so a mismatch falls through the shared
core's handler as NOT_AUTHORIZED and never reaches add/remove_forward,
covering both MAP and lifetime-0 delete. UPnP stays Unchecked.

Fail closed: a request whose arrival interface can't be resolved is
rejected rather than waved through.

The same-segment case (attacker and victim on one bridge) is unchanged
and unsolvable without L2 source guard, which the K1's single wired
bridge can't provide; the honest boundary there is a separate security
profile, now documented on the Published Ports page. Folded into the
still-unreleased 1.1.0 auto-forwarding changelog entry rather than a
separate fix line, since to the user the feature simply ships correct.

* refactor(start-wrt): inline the router-port confirm dialog into its only caller

Review feedback on #3634: confirmRouterPortOverride had a single call site
and PublishedPortsService.save() already funnels every UI path through it,
so it lives in the service now — dialogs/i18n come from the service's own
injections instead of parameters.

* chore(start-wrt): taplo-format ctrl Cargo.toml

* fix(start-core): stop web pages from driving the UPnP IGD endpoints

The IGD endpoints are plain HTTP on a private interface, which puts
them in reach of a victim's browser. A malicious page can rebind its
own domain to the gateway's IP and read responses as same-origin — the
classic UPnP deanonymization oracle (`GetExternalIPAddress`), plus the
device description's product name and stable UUID. Or it can skip
rebinding and fire a "simple" no-preflight POST at a guessed gateway
IP: blind, but enough to open the visiting device's own ports if that
device is authorized.

Two gates in the shared server:

- **`Host` must be an IP literal** — on the control endpoint and the
  static description/SCPD documents alike. Rebinding forces the
  attacker's *domain* into `Host` (that name is what makes the
  response read same-origin), while every real client requests the
  IP-literal URL that SSDP advertised. StartOS's igd-next client rides
  hyper 0.14, which fills `Host` from the request URI — the gateway's
  SocketAddr — and miniupnpc-class clients resolve the control URL
  against LOCATION the same way. A missing `Host` is rejected too:
  UPnP mandates HTTP/1.1, where it is required.

- **Mutations must name themselves in the `SOAPAction` header**
  (`AddPortMapping`/`AddAnyPortMapping`/`DeletePortMapping`). A
  browser can put a SOAP body on a no-preflight POST but can never
  attach that header cross-origin. The spec mandates it and every real
  client sends it; the body-parse fallback for the action name now
  serves only the reads, whose responses a page can't see without the
  rebinding the first gate blocks.

On StartWRT both vectors are live: browsers are everywhere on a LAN,
and any device the user toggles auto-forwarding on is a target. On
StartTunnel the permission gate already covered them — browsers live
on Client-kind peers, which never hold allow_auto_port_forward — so
there these gates are inherited defense-in-depth, except the device
description, which had no gate at all: any peer's browser could be
rebound to read "StartTunnel" plus a stable UUID derived from the wg
key, a cross-site identifier for the tunnel's users. That read is the
tunnel's live fix here.

Functionally free for legitimate clients: both gates key on what every
compliant client already sends, and the only real client reads state
only after AddPortMapping has already passed the same authorization
(client.rs:962 runs inside the `if added` branch). Covered by unit
tests for the Host classifier and end-to-end dispatch tests (rebound
Host and headerless mutation refused, headered mutation and headerless
read answered, static docs gated).

Changelog: StartTunnel gets a Security entry led by the description
fingerprint, since UPnP shipped released there; folded into StartWRT's
still-unreleased 1.1.0 auto-forwarding entry, since to the user the
feature simply ships correct.

* fix(start-core): answer the UPnP external-IP read without authorization

`GetExternalIPAddress` required the same authorization a mapping does.
The read is not what closes the deanonymization oracle it was meant to
close: the `Host` gate rejects a rebound request before dispatch, so a
malicious page — the attack that needs nothing installed on the device
— is refused whether or not that device is allowed to forward ports.
What authorization adds on top reaches only a caller that addresses
the control URL by IP for real, which is software already installed
there, and on the dual-stack LAN StartWRT configures by default such
software reads the subscriber's delegated IPv6 prefix off its own
interface without asking the router anything.

So the check bought a partial, ISP-contingent mitigation in exchange
for refusing an action the standard says answers, at the point in
discovery where clients read it. Drop it on both gateways; the test
now pins the read as answered for a peer the gateway would not map
for, so it is not silently re-gated.

Restores StartTunnel's released behavior, so its changelog entry goes
with it; the device-description fingerprint stays as that version's
Security entry.

fix(ci): run pull-request checks when a draft is marked ready (#3769)

The jobs in these workflows skip a draft PR (`if: github.event.pull_request.draft != true`),
and `pull_request` defaults to the activity types opened, synchronize and reopened. Marking a
draft ready is `ready_for_review`, which none of them listen for — so the checks stayed skipped
for the life of the PR unless somebody pushed another commit to it.

Measured on a scratch repo carrying the same trigger shape: a draft PR produced one run with
the job skipped, and marking it ready produced no run at all; with `ready_for_review` added,
marking it ready produced a fresh run whose job executed.

fix(start-sdk): i18n throws on numeric params, and exec never closes stdin (#3770)

* fix(start-sdk): resolve a locale Intl accepts before formatting i18n params

setupI18n derives its Intl locale from $LANG, and a StartOS service container
runs with LANG=C.UTF-8. That reduces to the POSIX locale C, which Intl rejects
with "RangeError: Incorrect locale information provided" — so interpolating a
number or a Date into a translated string threw at runtime for every package,
on the server only, having worked wherever $LANG names a real locale.

Settle once on a locale Intl will construct with, falling back through the
package's own defaultLang to the runtime default. Where the environment names a
real locale nothing changes, so locale-aware grouping is preserved.

Found by an action whose result message interpolated a count; it failed on a
0.4.0 server and passed everywhere it was developed.

* fix(start-sdk): close subcontainer stdin even when exec has no input

The stdin write and the stdin.end() that followed it shared one
`if (options.input)` guard, and cp.spawn is given no stdio override — so the
child always gets a pipe, and with nothing to write that pipe stayed open for
the life of the process. Any command reading stdin to EOF blocked until the
exec timeout elapsed and SIGKILLed it, thirty seconds later, surfacing as a
bare signal with nothing to connect it to stdin.

An omitted input and an empty-string input both mean the command gets nothing,
not that it gets a stdin which never ends. Close the pipe on every path, and
tolerate a caller that inherited stdio and has no pipe to close.

launch() and spawn() are untouched: both pass stdio: 'inherit'.

* docs(start-sdk): changelog entries for the i18n locale and exec stdin fixes

* docs(start-sdk): tighten the unreleased 2.0.10 changelog entries

The section had drifted to a median entry of 111 words against 16 across the
released history, and carried a duplicate `### Changed` heading. Cut the
mechanism, the rationale and the rejected alternatives — which belong to the
commits that made each change — and kept what a package developer acts on:
migration syntax for the breaking change, the docs links for the new APIs, and
the symptom that each fix removes.

Safe to edit because 2.0.10 has no origin tag: nobody has received these.

* docs: say what a changelog entry carries, and what the commit carries instead

The existing guidance covered where an entry goes — which heading, released
versus unreleased, checking origin tags — and nothing about what belongs in
one. So entries drift toward explaining the change to whoever reviewed it
rather than to whoever is upgrading, which is how the SDK's unreleased section
came to hold multi-paragraph entries for fixes no package author could observe.

No length target: entries should run as long as the change needs, and a figure
would only invite writing to it.

docs(packaging): fix what you find; file only what needs deciding (#3795)

"Bugs and feature requests are GitHub issues on the package repo — filed as
you find them" reads, to an agent already holding the package open, as an
instruction to write up a defect it could simply fix. Helix did exactly that
on its update sweep: lightning-terminal issue #65 and PR #66 five seconds
apart, the issue restated in full in the PR body under "Found while reviewing,
not fixed here". Two records of one finding, immediately free to disagree.

So order the two. A defect you spot with the package open is a fix in the
branch you are on, related to your task or not — you have the context to be
sure and the next person won't. An issue is for the call that isn't yours:
cause unpinned, two defensible fixes, or too large to ride on the work in
hand. Never both.

The tracker in the other direction needed saying too, because nothing said it:
an open issue is somebody's report, not a queue an agent may pick from. Taking
one on wants an invitation — being asked, or the `Approved` label the package
repos already carry.

The TODO.md prohibition survives all of this, reworded. Every package has
since dropped the file, so "there is no TODO.md" now records a past state
rather than preventing a future mistake; what earns its place is "don't create
one".

Four copies to keep in step: workflow.md holds it, agent-context.md digests
it, package-template/AGENTS.md ships it into every new package, and
new-package-checklist.md links the section — retitled, so that link moves too.

feat(ci): prune superseded StartOS images from S3 after each deploy (#3773)

No code path has ever removed an object from s3://startos-images — not this
workflow, not manage-release.sh, and not the registry crate, whose
`os version remove` touches only the PatchDB index. Image basenames embed the
commit hash, so every master push writes a fresh set of keys, and the alpha
deploy un-indexes the previous build while leaving its bytes behind.

The deploy job now reclaims them, keyed on what the registries still
reference. An object is deleted only when its version is still published, no
registry references its commit any more, and it is at least 14 days old.
Versions no registry knows about are never touched — those are the ones where
a release-notes link or a registry we don't consult could be the only
reference, and they want a human looking at an inventory rather than a rule.
The step prints what it kept, by reason and size, so that pile is visible.

The direction is the safety property. The registries supply the candidates
for deletion, never the exemptions: deleting "everything unreferenced" turns
a registry that is unreachable, errors, or answers in a shape we no longer
parse into an instruction to delete the images it serves, and all three of
those return an empty list rather than a failure. Read the other way round,
every one of them is a no-op.

Reclaiming has no deadline, so the step separates the two ways it can decline.
Anything that stops it reading a trustworthy keep set — a registry timing out,
a JSON-RPC error, a registry with no versions yet, an index shape it doesn't
recognise — warns and skips, because by then the images are uploaded and
indexed, and painting that red would cost a re-run the upload step's
`force-overwrite: false` will refuse anyway. It still fails hard on the three
conditions that mean this step is itself wrong: images this run just indexed
not coming back out of the registries, a delete set that intersects what they
reference, or objects surviving a delete.

Matching is on asset name alone, so an object stays protected when its URL is
served from a mirror, a path-style host, or a future CNAME.

fix(start-core): allow digits and hyphens in a domain's final label (#3804)

The FQDN pattern required the final label to be alphabetic-only, which
rejected non-delegated private TLDs (nextcloud.lan2), the hyphenated
example in the private-domains documentation (nextcloud.fake-tld), and
every IDN A-label TLD (example.xn--p1ai). The same pattern accepted
malformed input the RFCs forbid: empty labels, leading and trailing
hyphens, and labels over 63 characters.

RFC 1123 § 2.1 requires only that a name not be mistakable for a
dotted-decimal IPv4 literal. Requiring the final label to start with a
letter satisfies that while admitting the rest.

The private-domain form shares this validator with the public one, and its
own help text says the domain "can be any domain you want".

fix(start-os): keep the decoded block backup-fs just read (#3779)

backup-fs splits file contents into 1 MiB blocks, each independently
sealed (zstd -> SHA-256 tag -> ChaCha20 -> Reed-Solomon 10+2), and
`read_block` decodes a whole one however few bytes were asked for.
Nothing kept the result, and a handle from `open` is served
`FOPEN_DIRECT_IO`, so the kernel supplies neither a page cache nor
readahead: one FUSE read cost one whole-block fetch and decode.

The s9pk unpack that dominates a restore reads in 8 KiB units — the
`tokio::io::copy` default — which is the worst point on that curve.
Measured over a local NVMe, 64 MiB file, backing-store bytes from
`read_bytes` in /proc/self/io:

    read size   before          after
    8 KiB       5.5 MiB/s 154x   505 MiB/s 1.2x
    64 KiB       45 MiB/s  19x   639 MiB/s 1.2x
    128 KiB      89 MiB/s  10x   651 MiB/s 1.2x
    1 MiB       344 MiB/s 2.4x   658 MiB/s 1.2x

1.2x is the floor: one sealed block (1 MiB plaintext plus tag and ECC)
per block of file. Scaled to the report in #3708, a 480 MiB package
pulled ~72 GiB across an SMB share, which at an ordinary ~29 MiB/s is
the 42 minutes observed.

`Contents` is per inode and every op on one inode runs on a single pool
shard, so the block sits behind a lock it already holds. A block is
never both dirty and cached, which is what keeps a write-out from
leaving a stale copy: `load_block` caches only what the dirty map does
not hold, `write_blocks_at` takes the cached copy as it dirties a block,
and the flush drops a cached block the trailing prune is about to
unlink.

Dropping the pad `load_block` used to apply also fixes a panic it was
hiding. The pad ran after the dirty-map early return, so a block still
holding a short pending write reached `&block[within..within + copy]`
unpadded, and a read landing past those bytes panicked the worker. The
pool catches that unwind, so the damage looks confined — the read gets
EIO and other files still serve — until the program closes the file:
`release` runs on the dispatch thread holding the `Handler` lock, hits
the poisoned `Contents` mutex, and poisons the `Handler` mutex too, at
which point the session stops answering and the mount hangs. Reachable
from an ordinary sparse write-then-read.

Each guard has a test, and each test fails on its own mutation:
reverting the file fails the cache and panic tests, and dropping either
`take_if` or the dirty-map guard fails exactly the test that covers it.

fix(core): raise the install/uninstall failure notification before the rollback (#3786)

* fix(core): raise the install/uninstall failure notification before the rollback

`ServiceRefReloadInfo::reload` awaited `services.load(.., Undo)` before writing
the failure notification. That rollback shuts the service down and re-enters
`Service::load`, which rebuilds the persistent container and — for a `Removing`
entry — re-runs the uninstall from scratch. Several minutes pass, and the user
is told nothing about the failure until they are over.

Swap the two, and drop the notification's `?`: a failed notification write must
not skip the rollback, and the crate already treats one as `log_err` material
(`report_failed_rollback`, `backup::target`). Notifying first also closes a
narrower hole — a rollback that failed before `ServiceMap::load` could swallow
the error, on a failed shutdown or a failed db write, short-circuited on `?` and
the notification was never written at all.

`reload` serves every operation the reload guard wraps, so this covers install,
update and restore failures as well as uninstall.

Also log the reload result on the `Drop` path, which discarded it while the
`handle` path already logs its own. A rollback that fails there
strands the package mid-`Installing` with nothing in the journal naming why.

Closes #2937

* docs(start-os): drop the overstated recovery-failure clause from the changelog entry

A failed volume rollback never suppressed the notification on master:
`report_failed_rollback` returns `Err`, but `ServiceMap::load` absorbs
`Service::load`'s error into `status_info.error` and returns `Ok`, so the old
`load(.., Undo).await?` did not short-circuit. The notification was already
written — twice over, alongside the rollback-failed one.

The reorder does still close a hole, but only where `ServiceMap::load` itself
returns `Err` — a failed shutdown or a failed db write. That is too narrow and
too internal to be worth a user's attention, and the timing fix is the whole of
what they will notice.

* docs(start-os): describe the recovery direction-neutrally in the changelog entry

The entry said the notification waited on StartOS "putting the service back the
way it was". That inverts the case the issue is named for: `Service::load`
handles `Removing` alongside `Restoring`, rebuilding the container and re-running
`service.uninstall(..)`, and on success returns `Ok(None)` — the service is gone,
not restored. Only if that retry also fails does `err_state` put it back.

So a user whose uninstall failed would read that StartOS was restoring the
service, then watch it disappear. "Cleaning up after the attempt" holds for all
four arms: the old version coming back, the entry being removed, or the removal
completing on the retry.

fix(start-cli): stop scaffolding a host that breaks every command (#3752)

* fix(start-cli): stop scaffolding a host that breaks every command

`s9pk init-workspace` wrote `host.default: https://dev-vm.local` as a
placeholder for the packager to replace. That is not inert.

`CliContext::init` pins a `.local` host eagerly, before the command runs:
musl's getaddrinfo cannot do mDNS, so start-core shells out to getent, and
the lookup's failure propagates and aborts context construction. Since
`dev-vm.local` resolves on nobody's network, every command in a fresh
workspace died on DNS — including `s9pk pack` and `s9pk list-ingredients`,
neither of which opens a socket. Those two are what `s9pk.mk` calls, so
`make` could not run at all until the file was edited.

Environment Setup has the packager set `host.default` in the *Install to
StartOS* step, after Quick Start has them run `make x86`. So the documented
order walks into it, and the error names neither the placeholder nor the
file it came from.

The `host` block now ships commented out, with a line saying what to do with
it. An unset host falls back to `http://localhost`, which is not `.local` and
so is never resolved. Repointing the placeholder at an address would work
equally well for the DNS failure but would assert a default that is wrong for
everyone; there is no address that is right.

The scaffold test asserted a non-empty host map. It now asserts the opposite
— no host at all — so a future placeholder cannot come back unnoticed.

Existing workspaces are untouched: `write_if_absent` never rewrites a config
that exists, so a packager on 1.1.0 picks this up by commenting out or
repointing `host.default` themselves.

feat(ci): fail a pull request that carries conflict markers (#3794)

* feat(ci): fail a pull request that carries conflict markers

The live-docs backport keeps a conflict's markers on purpose so a
maintainer settles it in the PR it opens, but nothing holds that branch
back. GitHub reports it as mergeable, and the only red check is prettier,
which wants to rewrite `>>>>>>> <sha>` as nested blockquotes — a
formatting nit, nowhere near what is wrong. #3729 shipped three such
files and read exactly that way. A file prettier does not format, or a
path in `.prettierignore`, has no check at all.

This greps the files a pull request changes for an opening marker, a
closing marker, the diff3 base marker, or the divider a half-resolved
conflict leaves behind, annotates every line it finds, and fails. A file
that cannot be scanned fails it too, since a gate that goes green when it
did not run is worse than no gate. It runs on drafts, so a branch says so
from its first push.

Neither the check nor the docs claim more than it delivers. A file git
cannot merge line by line comes through as one side with no marker, so
green is not the same as a clean backport, and both `CONTRIBUTING.md` and
`AGENTS.md` say to compare a backport PR against `live-docs`.

A pull request against `live-docs` is not covered: a workflow has to
exist on the refs the pull request merges, and `live-docs` carries its
own `.github/workflows` tree. Carrying this file there is a follow-up PR
against that branch, after this one lands.

* docs(agents): cut the backport bullet to the rule an agent needs

The bullet packed three ideas into a branch-policy section: that markers
do not block a merge, that a check now catches them, and that a green
check still is not a clean backport. Only the last is a rule an agent has
to know and cannot learn from the check itself, so keep that one.

fix(core): refuse an impossible migration before the service is stopped (#3813)

Downgrading Nextcloud 33.0.8:3 to 33.0.7:0 failed with "uninit target
range `!` is unsatisfiable — no version can satisfy it (host contract
violation)", after the package had downloaded and the running service
had been quiesced and snapshotted.

33.0.8:3 declares `down: IMPOSSIBLE`, so it ships `canMigrateTo =
"=33.0.8:3"`; 33.0.7:0 ships `canMigrateFrom = ">=32.0.11:0 &&
<=33.0.7:0"`. `install()` picks the uninit target through three
branches, and the third had no guard: neither of the first two matched,
so it fell through to `and(canMigrateTo, canMigrateFrom)` — an empty
range. `RpcListener` normalizes that to `!`, and `VersionGraph` threw
its internal assertion.

Extract the branches into `uninit_target` and add the fourth case: two
ranges that do not intersect leave no data version the outgoing package
can produce and the incoming one can consume. It returns
`VersionIncompatible` worded for whoever pressed Downgrade. `install()`
calls it up front — before the download, before the service is touched
— and again at the original site, where the data version is re-read
after the container comes down.

This narrows what reaches the container: a pair whose ranges do not
intersect but that ships a hand-written uninit ignoring the target used
to get further before failing. Since `setupManifest` derives both
ranges from the `VersionGraph`, an empty intersection is the packager's
own declaration that there is no path.

The SDK's two messages now say what happened rather than name the range
algebra; the `uninit` guard stays as a backstop for an older host.

Co-authored-by: Matt Hill <9935159+MattDHill@users.noreply.github.com>
Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(registry): publish canMigrateFrom as a version's sourceVersion (#3807)

* fix(registry): publish canMigrateFrom as a version's sourceVersion

PackageVersionInfo::from_s9pk left source_version at None, so every
indexed package version advertised "anything can migrate into me". Two
mechanisms that already exist were dead as a result:

- get_matching_models filters candidates on
  caller_version.satisfies(candidate.source_version), and picks best from
  what survives. With the field null it unwrap_or's to any() and every
  version passes.
- updates-refinement.service.ts detects that best excludes the installed
  version, refetches with sourceVersion=<local>, and swaps in the highest
  reachable version. findUnreachable reads pkg.sourceVersion || '*', so it
  never found anything.

Together those are what should stop the Updates tab offering a version
the version graph cannot migrate into. Nextcloud is the live example: an
install on 32.0.11:0 is offered the Nextcloud 34 package, which then
refuses the two-major jump during init and rolls back. With this in
place the registry answers that query with the 33 release instead.

sideload.utils.ts already maps manifest.canMigrateFrom onto sourceVersion
for a sideloaded s9pk, so this only makes the registry path agree with
the path beside it.

source_version needs no handling in merge_with: that only folds in a
second asset for a version already indexed, and it errors unless the
metadata matches exactly — git_hash included — so both sides are the same
build and carry the same range.

fix(ui): say so when a value is too long for any QR code (#3824)

#3656 raised the ceiling from correction level M to L, which carries a
version-40 code's full capacity — but a payload past that still throws inside
ng-qrcode, which calls qrcode.toCanvas with no catch. The rejection is
unhandled, the canvas stays blank, and the dialog opens empty with only a
console error, exactly the symptom that PR set out to remove. An lndconnect
gRPC URI reached 3815 bytes against level L's 2953, so this was reachable in
production until Start9Labs/lnd-startos#189 shrank it.

Decide the level from version-40 capacity per encoding mode rather than a
byte count, and render a message when neither level holds the payload. Mode
matters: a byte-length test alone would refuse an uppercase alphanumeric
payload up to 4296 characters, which is exactly what a hardware wallet's
uppercase BC-UR code is, and those encode fine.

Checked against qrcode 1.5.4, the encoder ng-qrcode wraps, over 4172 payloads
spanning numeric, alphanumeric, mixed-case byte and multi-byte UTF-8 content
at lengths 1 through 7300: the rule never claims a payload the encoder throws
on and never refuses one it can draw.

Renders it through `app-placeholder`, the empty state the rest of the UI uses
for an absent thing, rather than a sentence: at body weight it read as a
second message competing with the action's own. The component moves beside
that placeholder under `routes/portal/components/`, where all three of its
call sites already live — nothing outside `routes/` imports from it.

Adds two mocks reaching the branch, both built on one oversized query string:
a 'gRPC Connect' interface on bitcoind, which is the path a user actually
takes, and a 'Show Unencodable QR' action for the result-modal path.

fix(start-os): check the port a certificate authority validates on (#3768)

* fix(start-os): check the port a certificate authority validates on

A Let's Encrypt domain on an interface served somewhere other than 443 —
Electrum on 50002, clnrest on 3010, turns on 5349 — passed every check the
add-domain flow ran and then refused every connection. The two reachability
probes test the external port of the address being added, so on all-green
nothing opened and the user saw only a new row reading "Let's Encrypt",
while the one thing that decides whether the domain works — whether the
challenge reaches the box on 443 — went untested.

Probe 443 alongside the address's own port when the domain names an ACME
authority, the address is served elsewhere, and no certificate is on hand
to serve. That last condition uses `should_use_cert`, the predicate the
cert resolver itself applies, so the check comes back at the start of the
renewal window rather than on the last day of validity. The certificate
store is private and never reaches the browser, so the backend answers the
whole question: `net.acme.check-challenge` returns the probe or `None`,
and `add_public_domain` embeds the same answer in its response. The setup
modal gains a Certificate Authority section carrying it, and a failure
there opens the modal and holds Done exactly as a failed port forward does.

Make the challenge route uniform while it is in reach. The IPv4 SNI route
now maps 443 -> 443 rather than 443 -> the domain's own port: every
listener answers a challenge out of the same cache, so the box-side port
never had to be the interface's. IPv6 gets the matching pinhole, which it
was skipping. And port 443 now binds wherever an ACME domain is public,
derived per host-map owner from the vhost targets — port 443's own targets
cannot see a domain served on 50002, so its socket was held open only by
whatever else happened to be there, typically the admin UI's LAN address.

A client dialling https://<name>:443 for a domain published on another
port is refused rather than proxied. The name is only ever published on
its own port, so this is the more correct answer.

Closes #3760

* fix(start-os): withdraw a shared pinhole only when nobody wants it

Review of the challenge-port work found five defects in it, four of them
ways the fix could still leave a domain silently broken.

The IPv6 challenge pinhole is hostname-less, which made it the first
port-map key two owners can both ask for. `sync_port_maps` diffed each
owner against itself alone, so an Electrum domain going away called
`port_map.remove(GUA, 443)` and shut the pinhole a clnrest domain on the
same GUA was still using — its renewal would fail ~60 days later with
nothing on screen. Withdraw a key only once no owner wants it; the
per-owner bookkeeping already there is what decides.

The challenge probe failed open. An RPC error and "this domain does not
need 443" were both `null` on the client, so a probe that errored counted
as a pass and the setup modal never opened — the silent failure this
change exists to remove. `CheckChallengeRes` now carries each leg as an
option, so "outstanding but unmeasured" is representable end to end, and
it is what the client reports when a probe errors. That also stops a
`check_port(443)` error failing the whole `add-public-domain` call after
the domain has been committed.

The modal rendered its Certificate Authority row on one predicate and
gated Done on another, so a domain that already held a certificate could
show a red row beside an enabled Done. Both now read the one answer the
backend gives. The row's verdict drops the hairpinning requirement and
the warning that goes with it: a certificate authority dials from
outside, and whether the router loops back to itself says nothing.

Port Forwards listed the interface's own rule and not the `443` one, so
an operator who dismissed the modal and went to set their router up was
shown half of what they needed. `Host::port_forwards` now emits both.

Also: the v6 80->443 redirect no longer follows a challenge pinhole,
since TLS-ALPN-01 never uses port 80 and the redirect was opening a port
nothing serves; `sync_challenge_binds` takes its union under `servers`,
so a concurrent owner's reconcile cannot close 443 with a stale snapshot;
and `net acme check-challenge` is in the CLI reference.

* fix(start-os): show the certificate authority's requirement where it is asked for

Round 2 reviewed the commit that answered round 1 and found three of its
fixes closed their defect by opening another.

The Certificate Authority section was made to render on one predicate, and
the predicate chosen was "the backend says 443 is outstanding". That answer
is only computed on a path that probes, so the section vanished from the
Address Requirements view opened from an address's own menu — the one
screen named after requirements, and the one a user reaches after
dismissing the setup modal to go configure their router. The two-predicate
problem it was avoiding cannot arise there: that view renders no footer, so
there is no verdict for a red row to contradict. A view that reaches a
verdict shows what is outstanding; the manual view shows the requirement.

The Port Forwards rule keyed on `addr.ssl`, which is true for a TLS
passthrough binding. Every other expression of the same rule carries an
`add_ssl` term, because a service serving its own TLS is its own ACME
client and no challenge reaches the box for it — so a host with one
`addSsl` binding and one passthrough advertised a 443 rule against the
passthrough interface that nothing here would ever answer, with a Test that
stays red forever.

`take_ownership` made the bookkeeping atomic but still dispatched the
withdrawal after releasing the lock, so the interleaving it exists to
prevent survived in a narrower window: another owner could claim the key
and ensure the mapping between the decision and the send, and the remove
would land on top of it. Both calls hand the work to the port-mapper over a
channel, so the loop moves inside the lock.

Also: `showChallenge` read `isManualMode` from a field declared below it,
which a class initializer evaluates as undefined; and the comment rewrites
that answered round 1 shipped two false claims, one of them onto the
generated `CheckChallengeRes` binding — a null `port_v6` is the no-GUA case
as well as the errored one, and an address serves the certificate it holds
right through a renewal window rather than refusing every connection.

* fix(start-os): say which forwards your own devices dial

The hairpinning warning asks whether the router loops a connection from
your own network back to the box. That is worth knowing for an address
people on the LAN dial, and meaningless for the certificate authority's
port, which nothing here dials and which serves no address at all — so the
Certificate Authority rows in the setup modal already suppress it.

Port Forwards then grew a `443` row from the same requirement and kept the
warning, because the screen renders `port-check-warnings` with no `local`
and takes its default. Two screens, one forward, contradictory verdicts:
green check beside "This address will not work from your local network".

A flag on the widget could not fix it. Rows group by port pair, so a
challenge `443` and a genuinely served `443` coalesce, and `PortForward`
carried nothing to tell them apart — whether anything is dialled locally is
a property of the forwarding rule. It is one now, defaulting true so every
existing rule and every stored one keeps the warning, and a grouped row
takes it if any of its forwards does.

* chore(start-cli): regenerate the man pages for net acme check-challenge

The `Generated Artifacts` job regenerates them and fails on any drift, and
a new subcommand adds a page as well as a line to its parent's. Generated,
not written: `make manpages`.

* docs: say that a CLI subcommand needs its man pages regenerated

`start-core/AGENTS.md` tells you a `#[ts(export)]` change needs
`make start-core-ts-bindings`, and says nothing about the man pages —
so adding `net acme check-challenge` in that scope regenerated the
bindings and left the pages, and `Generated Artifacts` caught it. Both
artifacts come out of the same CI job; now both are named where someone
adding a subcommand is reading.

* refactor(start-os): let the caller decide it has already probed 443

Review: being served on 443 is not the backend's reason to answer
nothing. It is the caller saying it already has that probe — its own
port check *is* the challenge check — so it belongs where the request is
made. `check_challenge` now answers the question it was asked, and since
that port was the only thing `port` decided, the parameter goes with it:
the RPC takes an fqdn, a gateway and an authority. `add_public_domain`
reuses its own `check_port` result and the web client keeps the guard it
already had, so neither asks a question it can answer itself.

`PortForward::local` takes `const_true` rather than a fourth hand-rolled
spelling of it, and the two strings under the Certificate Authority
heading take the reviewer's wording — "regardless of which port" reads
plainly, and the IPv6 firewall allows connections to a port, not to an
address.

* refactor(start-os): require the authority check-challenge is asked about

Review: an optional `acme` made the command a no-op when it was left
out, which is a footgun and a wasted round trip — a caller with no ACME
authority has no question to ask, so it should not ask one. The
parameter is required, and the two callers skip the call instead:
`add_public_domain` alongside the check it already had for a domain
served on 443, and the web client with the guard it already had.

That leaves `check_challenge` with one reason to answer nothing — the
certificate on hand still has life in it — which is the only one it is
positioned to know.

* docs(core): tighten the PortForward.local doc to the reviewer's wording

Applied at the Rust `///` rather than the generated binding, so the
regeneration keeps it. The two places the frontend restates the same
field take the same wording, and `PortCheckTestComponent.local` loses its
comment: it is a passthrough, and the input it feeds carries the fact.

* docs: rewrite this branch's comments to the current code style

AGENTS.md's Code style section changed while this branch was open. The
comments here were written to the old one: paragraphs that argued the
reasoning, enumerated the cases behind a rule, and described what the
code does not do.

Held to the predicate rule instead, most of them had nothing left to
protect a reader from and are gone; the rest are one clause. About 120
comment lines become 47.

* docs: regardless of which port, not whatever port

Review, on both code comments. Applied to the two doc sentences that
carry the same phrase as well, so the branch reads one way.

docs: backport live-docs 32c74be6e to master

Backports the following from live-docs:

- 32c74be6e docs(sdk): say where the start-cli installer puts the binary (#3843)

fix(start-os): reflect the upstream's ALPN across an add_ssl rewrap (#3777)

* fix(start-os): reflect the upstream's ALPN across an add_ssl rewrap

`ProxyTarget::preprocess` read the backend's negotiated ALPN from
`TlsConnector::connect_with`'s closure, which rustls runs before any
handshake byte moves — so it read `None` on every connection and the
client-facing config was left with an empty ALPN list.

The client therefore settled on no protocol while the backend, offered
the client's own list, was free to select `h2`; `run_http_proxy` keys
both legs off the client's negotiation, so it wrote HTTP/1 framing onto
a connection the backend was reading as HTTP/2. Read the protocol off
the connected stream instead, which the client's handshake still
follows.

Closes #3739

* fix(start-os): assign the reflected ALPN rather than appending it

rustls selects the client-facing protocol by the server list's order, so a
base config that already carried a protocol the client offered would be
chosen over the one the backend actually selected — reinstating exactly the
mismatch this fixes. No config on this path carries one today, so assigning
changes nothing now and makes the invariant local rather than inherited.

Also correct the packaging guide: `addSsl.alpn` takes an `AlpnInfo`, not a
string, and setting it dials the container over plain TCP — which the new
paragraph on rewrap ALPN would otherwise send a reader straight into.

* fix(start-os): set the client-facing ALPN in every branch, not just the rewrap

rustls picks the client-facing protocol by the server list's order, so an
entry inherited from the base config outranks whatever the branch chose.
The rewrap branch guarded against that; `Reflect` and `Specified` still
appended, and between them they cover more bindings than the rewrap does —
every `http` and `ws` binding resolves to `Specified`. All three now assign,
so the invariant holds wherever the list is set. No config on this path
carries an entry today, so this is a guard rather than a behavior change.

Name the container address when the upstream handshake fails: a bare
`log_err` reported `received fatal alert: NoApplicationProtocol` with no
address, service or SNI, while the client saw an `unrecognized_name` alert —
a mismatch whose whole diagnostic trail pointed at certificates.

Tests: cover the refusal the packaging guide describes, drop an assertion
that compared the two ends of one TLS session against each other, and stop
writing an HTTP/1 request into the HTTP/2 leg, where it was an invalid
connection preface that the test survived only by reading bytes the upstream
handshake had already buffered.

* fix(start-os): vary the upstream ALPN through with_alpn, and cover both plaintext arms

`TlsConnector::with_alpn` threads the protocol list through the handshake, so
the rewrap no longer deep-clones the whole `ClientConfig` and builds a fresh
`Arc` for every accepted connection.

`Reflect` and `Specified` had no test at all, though `Reflect` is the default
and takes every plaintext container behind `add_ssl`. Both are covered now.

Fix a test helper that primed the upstream leg whenever the ALPN was absent,
when what decides the framing is whether it is `h2`: `upstream_framing` with
an explicit `http/1.1` proxied as HTTP/1, wrote nothing, and failed on a
timeout blaming the proxy. That case is the one the changelog is about, so it
is now asserted.

Rename the refused-upstream test for the guarantee it pins — the client is
declined rather than served over the plaintext stream — since the alert it
observes is the listener's generic decline and says nothing about ALPN.

Scope the changelog to the clients that were actually affected: a client
speaking only HTTP/1.1 negotiated HTTP/1.1 on both legs and was served
normally. Say what makes the extended-CONNECT warning true — StartOS
advertises it whether or not the container implements it — rather than
leaving a reader to refute it against RFC 8441, which makes it opt-in.

Drop the `addSsl.alpn` paragraph: it describes released behavior, so it ships
on live-docs (#3778) with the corrected type for that option.

* fix(start-os): make the plaintext-arm tests fail when the arms append

Both arm tests passed an empty base config, where appending to the list and
replacing it produce the same result — so they passed against the code they
were written to lock in. Each now starts from a base carrying the protocol
the other side prefers, which wins on server order under an append and loses
under a replace.

Say what the failure depended on in the changelog: a connection was lost
when the service chose HTTP/2 for it, not whenever a client asked for HTTP/2.
A service listing HTTP/1.1 first served a browser normally, and the previous
wording also claimed an HTTP/1.1-only client was always served, which is not
true of a service that speaks only HTTP/2 — the case this branch declines and
tests. Drop "serves its own TLS" from the heading too; the packaging guide
uses that phrase for passthrough, which this does not touch.

Restore the `addSsl.alpn` warning. Removing it left the section urging authors
to think about which protocols to advertise directly above an option that
looks like where to say so, and setting it drops the binding to a plaintext
dial into a TLS listener.

* test(start-os): pin that an ALPN-less client is offered to the backend as one

`with_alpn` falls back to the dialling config's own protocol list when it is
handed `None`, so offering it only for a non-empty list — which reads like an
obvious simplification — would put that config's protocols to the backend on
behalf of a client that asked for none. The backend would then choose one the
client never offered, and every ALPN-less client would stop being able to open
the binding. Nothing pinned it; the config the rewrap dials with carries no
protocols today, so the fallback is silent.

Also drop a claim that ALPN selection consults the client's preference, which
it does not: rustls takes the first of the server's list that the client also
offered, as the sibling test's own comment says. Say what the module covers now
that it holds plaintext-strategy tests too, and stop promising a TLS alert in a
doc whose test only observes that the handshake failed.

Drop the changelog's "where it chose HTTP/1.1" clause: it paired with the
failure case as though the two were exhaustive, when a service that advertises
nothing is the common case and a service sharing no protocol with the client is
refused outright, before and after.

* docs(start-os): name the call that performs the ALPN fallback, not the one that prevents it

`with_alpn` takes a plain list and always hands `connect_impl` a `Some`, so it
is the one call that cannot fall back to the dialling config. The fallback is
`connect_impl`'s own, reached by not going through `with_alpn` at all — which
is exactly the refactor the test exists to catch, so the comment naming
`with_alpn` as the culprit invited a reader to dismiss it as stale.

Drop that test's `assert_eq!`: a client offering no ALPN gets no extension
back whatever the config holds, so the comparison could not fail and only the
`expect` was ever doing the work.

* fix(start-os): stop addSsl.alpn deciding how the container is dialled

`connect_ssl` carried two unrelated decisions in one `Result`: `Ok` meant
"dial over TLS" and also "carry the ALPN the container negotiated", while
`Err` meant "dial plaintext" and also "apply this strategy". Setting `alpn`
could only be expressed as `Err`, so it silently moved the binding onto the
plaintext dial — a container serving its own TLS was handed cleartext on a
port expecting TLS, and `upstreamCertValidation` was dropped with it.

Split them: `connect_ssl` is now `Option<Arc<ClientConfig>>` and says only how
to dial, derived from `secure.ssl` alone; `alpn` says only what the client is
offered, and defaults to carrying the container's choice over a TLS leg or
reflecting the client's list without one. Every existing shape resolves to
what it did before — only `alpn` on a TLS-serving container changes, and that
one could not work.

`setting_alpn_does_not_stop_the_container_being_dialled_over_tls` observes the
container's own handshake completing, since the client-facing list alone
cannot tell the two dials apart.

* fix(start-os): let a pinned protocol reach the container, not just the client

Splitting the dial from the ALPN made `connect_ssl: Some` with `alpn: Some`
expressible for the first time, and in that state the two legs negotiated
separately: the container was dialled with the client's list and picked out of
that, while the client was handed the pinned list. One protocol frames both
legs, so a container that chose `h2` was then sent HTTP/1 requests — the
mismatch this branch exists to remove, reachable again through `alpn`.

The pin now narrows what the container is put through, and a dialled
container's own choice is what the client is offered. Every other shape is
unchanged: without a TLS leg the pin is still what the client sees, and an
unset `alpn` still puts the client's list forward.

`a_pinned_protocol_is_what_the_container_is_offered` reports the protocol the
container settled on, which is the only thing that separates the two designs —
the client is told `http/1.1` either way.

Also guard the `alpn` arm of `ProxyTarget`'s equality, which decides whether a
binding that changes only its protocols re-registers, and retire the
"dials plaintext" vocabulary the split made false.

* fix(start-os): put a pinned protocol to the container only if the client named it

Pinning `alpn` put the binding's whole list to the container regardless of what
the client asked for, and the container chooses by its own preference — so it
could settle on a protocol the client never named. The client was then offered
that one protocol alone, and rustls refused any client that could not speak it.
A client naming one of the pinned protocols was turned away.

The same gap reopened the mismatch this branch exists to close: a client that
names no protocol at all still had the pin put to the container, so the
container framed the connection `h2` while the client stayed on HTTP/1.1 —
rustls skips ALPN selection entirely when the ClientHello carries no extension,
so nothing on the client leg could correct it.

The container is now put through the pin intersected with the client's list.
Where the two share nothing the client is refused as it is without a TLS leg,
and where the client names nothing the container is named nothing either.

Also correct the packaging guide: a container that simply ignores ALPN leaves
the client without a protocol rather than refusing it, so the setting is inert
there, and a rewrap now hands the client whatever the container chose — which
is no longer a reason to reach for passthrough.

* test(start-os): guard the refusal a pin owes a client that cannot meet it

Deleting the arm that refuses a client sharing no protocol with the pin left
every test passing. Without it such a client is served with no protocol at all,
which makes `Specified` advisory rather than binding — the difference the arm
exists to draw, and the one thing about a pin a package author relies on.

* test(start-os): pin the rule that alpn does not decide the upstream transport

The derivation that sent plaintext to a container serving its own TLS had no
test: every ALPN test hand-builds a `ProxyTarget`, so restoring `alpn`'s old
precedence over `secure.ssl` broke nothing. Extract the predicate and table-test
it across the bindings that reach it.

Also correct the prose the intersection made wrong. `addSsl.alpn` is documented
for the rewrap alone, but every `http` and `ws` binding sets it with no
container TLS leg at all, where the list is simply what the client is offered.

* test(start-os): watch the leg the client is actually spliced onto

Every assertion here reads the client-facing handshake, so `preprocess` could
hand back the socket under the container's TLS session and nothing noticed —
which is the shape of the two faults this branch already fixed. Write a probe
through the returned stream and have the container read it back through its own
session.

Cover the refusal a plaintext binding owes a client that shares no protocol
with its pin. `addSsl.alpn` without a container TLS leg is the setting's
plainest deployment, and only the rewrap half was guarded.

* refactor(start-os): ask the binding whether it rewraps

`BindOptions` already answers `serves_own_tls`, so the complementary question
belongs beside it rather than in the controller, where it also had to test
`add_ssl` twice to reach the options it wanted. `AddSslOptions::alpn` is an
exported surface whose meaning this branch changes, so document it there — the
explanation reached the book and not the editor.

Correct the guidance the change makes wrong. Where StartOS terminates alone the
pinned list is the only thing holding a client to what the container speaks, so
"leave it unset" is advice for the rewrap only, and a client refused for sharing
no protocol is refused by the container, whose alert names the hostname.

* fix(start-os): repair the prose the last pass broke

Compressing the refusal comment left it claiming the socket was never dialled,
when only the TLS leg is skipped, and dropped the reason its guard tests both
lists for emptiness — rustls turns a client away only when both name something,
so the comment now argued for removing the two clauses that keep an ALPN-less
client off an unwrapped socket.

Taking the test backend's report slot after its handshake rather than on accept
kept the sender alive in a loop that never ends, so a container that fails its
handshake no longer closed the channel and the test waited out ten seconds to
blame a slow handshake instead. It bought nothing: each test opens one
connection.

The `addSsl.alpn` doc said the container is offered the pinned protocols, which
is what this branch stopped doing — it is offered the ones the client also
asked for. A pin that names nothing turns nobody away, so say that where the
book promises a refusal.

* docs(start-core): say what alpn does in one sentence

The field's doc walked a reader through both arrangements before telling them
what to set. Say what it is, and let the variants carry what `reflect` means.

* docs(start-core): call alpn a filter

It filters the client's list down to what the binding puts forward, so say
that instead of walking through where the result is sent.

* docs(start-sdk): drop "puts forward" for what the filter leaves

The phrase asked a reader to track a list being handed somewhere. Say what
survives the filter and who gets it, and let the two arrangements be two
sentences rather than one.

* feat(start-core)!: drop the reflect alpn value

Once setting `alpn` stopped deciding how the container is dialled, `reflect`
and leaving the option unset said the same thing. Keep the one that needs no
value, so the type offers a filter or nothing.

* feat(start-core)!: carry alpn as the list of protocols

A manifest wrote `{ specified: ['h2'] }` to name two things, one of which the
wrapper never said: a filter, and which kind of filter. With `reflect` gone
there is only the one kind, so write the list, and let no list at all be the
absence of a filter.

Bindings already on disk are converted on update, in both directions — a
`reflect` stored by an older server becomes no list, which is what it meant.

* docs(start-core): hold the comments to the rewritten style, and correct the option's type

The Code style section changed while this branch was open, and these comments
were written to the old one. Most of what went is the rejected alternative —
what the code would do if it appended rather than assigned, or offered the
container the client's list — which belongs here, not above the line it argues
about.

The reference table still gave `addSsl.alpn` as `string`, which the field has
never accepted. It takes the list of protocols or nothing, so say that where a
package author reads it. #3778 was going to carry this against the published
book; it is here instead.

* fix(start-os): write the UI mock's alpn as a list

The mock host still carried the wrapper object, so the UI build failed to
compile against the narrowed type. Every other writer moved with the format;
this one is behind the Angular build rather than a `tsc` the earlier sweep ran.

* docs(start-sdk): document alpn from the client's side, where the common case is

The option was written up inside the rewrap section, so it read as a filter
between the ClientHello and the container. The container is usually not
listening on TLS: StartOS terminates, forwards plain HTTP, and answers the
client's ALPN from this list alone, which makes the filter one between the
ClientHello and the response.

It now sits under TLS Termination and leads with that. The rewrap keeps the one
sentence it adds — that the container gets to choose from the list.

* refactor(start-core): make AlpnInfo the newtype it became

One variant carrying one list is a newtype wearing an enum's clothes, and
`untagged` was there to undo the wrapper the variant added. `transparent` says
the same thing without the indirection, and the wire format and the generated
binding are unchanged.

fix(sdk): drop the z.object loose-mode override (#3844)

* fix(sdk): drop the z.object loose-mode override

The SDK shadowed z.object so it produced loose objects, while the
declaration file typed it as plain zod. Every signal a developer sees
while writing a shape — hover, z.infer, excess-property checking — said
the schema stripped unknown keys, and only one paragraph of the
packaging book said otherwise. Package authors reasonably read
z.object as zod's z.object and did not know their file models were
preserving keys.

z is now plain zod, and every call site that relied on the override says
so: 110 z.object( calls across start-core and container-runtime become
z.looseObject(, which is byte-for-byte the same schema at runtime
(both build { type: 'object', shape, catchall: unknown() }).

z.deepLoose and z.deepPartial are untouched, and a new test fails if the
shadow comes back.

Packages must make the same substitution in their file models; the
changelog carries the migration note.
