fix(start-wrt): hairpin published ports for every profile with Internet or LAN access (#3888)

* fix(start-wrt): scope published-port NAT reflection to permitted zones

Published-port redirects never set `reflection_zone`, so fw4 defaulted it
to the redirect's `dest` zone and emitted hairpin rules matching only the
target device's own subnet. A client on a different Security Profile —
one already permitted to forward into the target's zone — hit the
router's INPUT chain instead of the DNAT when it used the router's WAN
address.

Set `reflection_zone` to the target's zone plus every zone a `config
forwarding` section already permits to forward into it. Not every zone:
each reflection zone becomes the reflection redirect's `src`, which sets
fw4's `dflags.dnat` and emits a blanket `ct status dnat accept` into that
zone's forward chain ahead of the zone policy, so a reflected flow cannot
be rejected afterwards.

Also set `reflection '0'` on any port carrying a source restriction.
fw4 builds the reflection redirect fresh and copies neither `src_ip` nor
`src_mac` (`fw4.uc` ~2898), taking its saddr from the reflection zone's
subnets — so a source-restricted forward was reachable by hairpin from
any client in the reflection zone, including the same-subnet case that
already worked before this change.

* refactor(start-wrt): type FirewallRedirect.reflection as Option<bool>

`FirewallZone.masq`/`masq6`/`mtu_fix` are `Option<bool>` and serialize
as '1'/'0'; `reflection` is the same kind of fw4 boolean in the same
struct family, so give it the same type instead of the older
`Option<String>` idiom. The bytes written are unchanged.

* fix(start-wrt): emit reflection zones only for existing, non-masq zones

`reflection_zones` copied `config forwarding` src names verbatim,
excluding only the literal "wan". fw4 parses each `reflection_zone`
entry as a zone reference: one name that is not a parsed zone fails the
whole option and drops the entire redirect — WAN-side DNAT included —
and a `src '*'` forwarding (legal fw4) would crash ruleset rendering
outright when fw4 dereferences the wildcard's subnets. Stock images
never write such forwardings, but an adopted config can carry them, and
a zone deleted after the list was written turns into exactly that
invalid name.

Filter the list against the `config zone` sections actually present,
and exclude WAN-like zones by property (`masq` set) rather than by the
name "wan"; the redirect's own src zone stays excluded as before. Also
write down why cross-zone hairpin is DNAT-only: the reflection SNAT
lands in the emitted zone's srcnat chain, which a hairpinned flow never
enters, so the server sees the client's real address and replies via
the router — intentional, not a missing rule.

* fix(start-wrt): resync reflection zones on profile changes and at boot

`reflection_zone` was written only by `published-ports set`, but it is
derived from the `config forwarding` set, which changes underneath it:

- Deleting a profile removed its zone but left the name in every list
  carrying it, and fw4 treats one unknown name as an invalid option —
  dropping the whole redirect, WAN-side DNAT included. Deleting a guest
  profile could silently kill an admin-LAN published port from the
  Internet until some unrelated re-save rewrote the pp_ sections.
- Revoking a profile's Access left it in the lists, so its clients kept
  reaching the port via the WAN address — the exact reflect-then-reject
  hole the scoped list exists to prevent, with no rule able to stop it.
- A profile granted Access later (or created with it) was missing from
  the lists, so its clients kept hitting the original bug.

Add `sync_reflection_zones`, one pass re-deriving the list on every
redirect tagged `_pp_id` or `_apf_label` (skipping `reflection '0'`),
and run it wherever the inputs or the redirects change: at the end of
`rewrite_firewall` and `delete_config` (both already restart the
firewall afterwards), in `published-ports set` (replacing the inline
computation), in `apply_forward` — automatic UPnP/PCP forwards now
get the same scoped hairpin instead of fw4's dest-zone default, closing
the canonical StartOS case of a phone on another profile reaching a
UPnP-opened port by the server's public hostname — and once at boot,
so routers already carrying stale lists heal (reloading the firewall
only when the pass changed something).

* fix(start-wrt): resolve a published device's zone by address, not guess

`dest_zone` came from the neighbor table alone and fell back to "lan"
whenever the device had no entry — and a device that is offline (or
whose entry aged out) still passes validation, because its IPv4
resolves from the static reservation `set` itself creates. Since every
save rewrites all rules, toggling any port while one target was
offline silently rewrote that target's rule with the guessed zone;
with scoped reflection the wrong guess also computes the wrong
permitted set, e.g. handing an IoT profile with Access to the admin
LAN a hairpin route to a server that actually lives in a guest zone.

Resolve the zone from the device's IPv4 against the interface subnets
of the non-masquerading firewall zones (every profile is a /24 at its
gateway; the static reservation covers an offline device, and
configs-only mode too), keeping the neighbor-table result as a logged
cross-check only. A device that still cannot be placed keeps
`dest 'lan'` — the WAN-side DNAT stays as it was — but gets
`reflection '0'`: never hairpin into a guessed zone, and never refuse
the save over one offline device. `set` now parses "network" alongside
"firewall"/"dhcp"; the file is round-tripped unchanged.

* docs(start-wrt): true up the hairpin section's wording and scope

- "every other profile that profile permits to reach it" read as
  though the target's profile grants the access; the Access setting
  lives on the *other* profile (see security-profiles.md), so say so.
- "answered by the router itself" becomes "the router answers instead
  of the device" — plainer.
- Reflection matches only addresses actually on the WAN interface:
  behind CGNAT or another upstream router the public IP a domain
  resolves to never hairpins, so one clause now says so before a
  support thread has to.
- Automatic (UPnP/PCP) forwards are scoped identically now, so the
  section says they are covered.

* fix(start-wrt): fall back to the neighbor table for a device's zone

Resolving the zone by address alone dropped the neighbor-table result
that the previous code relied on, so a device with no IPv4 at all —
an IPv6-only target, which has neither a lease nor a reservation to
place it — fell to the "lan" guess even while the neighbor table knew
its zone. The IPv6 forward rule's `dest` then named the wrong zone and
fw4 bound it to the wrong egress interfaces. The same applied to an
IPv4 outside every profile subnet.

Pull the resolution into `device_zone`: the address decides when it
resolves (an offline device with a reservation still places, and a
save while one target is offline no longer rewrites its rule around a
guess), and the neighbor table places what the address cannot. Only a
device neither can place keeps the "lan" guess, and only that one is
never hairpinned. Tests run non-effectful, so the helper is what makes
the fallback testable.

* fix(start-wrt): clear reflection zones on reflection-off redirects

`sync_reflection_zones` left `reflection '0'` redirects untouched on the
grounds that they carry no list. fw4 validates every `reflection_zone`
name before it reads `reflection` or `enabled`, so a stale name on such
a redirect still drops the whole section, WAN-side DNAT included. Our
writer never emits that combination, but a hand-edited config can, and
the boot heal exists precisely for configs we did not write.

Empty the list on those redirects instead of skipping them; a redirect
that is already clean still counts as unchanged.

* fix(start-wrt): hairpin published ports for every profile with Internet or LAN access

A published port is a public resource, so honoring profile isolation on the
router's public address only blocked the one path the operator had already
opened to the world (review on #3888). The hairpin now serves every zone that
qualifies on either ground: Internet access — a forwarding into a masquerading
zone with no unqualified REJECT toward it, which excludes WAN Access None,
Whitelist's catch-all, and an active blackout window — or Access to the
target's profile, which keeps the original fix for a permitted profile that
has no Internet.

Listing a zone in `reflection_zone` is not enough on its own: fw4 sets the
`dnat` flag that emits `ct status dnat accept` only on the redirect's src and
dest zones (fw4.uc:2748), never on the reflection zones, so a reflected flow
from an isolated zone reached that zone's forward chain and was rejected by
policy. The previous comment on `reflection_zones` claimed otherwise; the
bench never exercised it because every zone benched had a forwarding. The
daemon now installs one chain-pre include for fw4's top-level `forward`
chain — `ct status dnat accept` — at boot, so binary-updated routers converge
without a reflash. It matches only flows a DNAT rule rewrote, and the only
DNAT into the LAN is a published port or an automatic forward.

IPv6 has no DNAT, so each unrestricted `pp_*_v6` WAN rule is copied once per
hairpin zone with only `src` changed, tagged `_pp_hairpin`, and rebuilt
wholesale on every sync rather than tracked incrementally. `list` ignores the
copies (src != wan); `reconcile` retargets them and `remove_ports_for_macs`
drops them with the rule through `is_pp_v6_rule`.

The WAN-schedule crontab rewrites the firewall behind the daemon's back, so
both cron edges now run `startwrt-cli published-ports sync-hairpin` between
`uci commit` and the reload; `evaluate_and_apply_schedules` syncs in-process.

* fix(start-wrt): read WAN Whitelist and Blacklist entries against the published address

The Internet ground of the hairpin looked only at the shape of a profile's
rules toward its egress zone: an unqualified REJECT cancelled the forwarding,
anything else left it standing. That read a Whitelist as never having Internet
access and a Blacklist as always having it, whatever their entries named — so a
Whitelist holding the router's public address was denied the hairpin (closed
against the operator's intent) and a Blacklist blocking that address was
granted it (open against it).

`hairpin_zones` now walks the zone's rules toward the egress zone in config
order, as fw4 does ahead of the forwarding, and takes the first rule whose
destination covers one of the port's public addresses: ACCEPT grants, REJECT or
DROP cancels, no covering rule leaves the forwarding to decide. A rule
narrowed by anything but a destination address, or with a destination that
does not parse, covers nothing — the same strict reading unknown shapes had
before. The blackout and catch-all cases fall out of the same walk, so
`is_unqualified_reject` is gone.

An IPv4 redirect is public at the router's WAN IPv4 addresses, which are not in
the config: `sync_hairpin` takes them as an argument, callers obtain them
through the new `CtrlContext::wan_ipv4_addrs` (ubus, empty when not effectful
or unknown), and the two context-less daemon paths call `system::wan_ipv4_addrs`
directly. An unknown address degrades to the previous behavior. An IPv6 rule is
public at its own `dest_ip`, so its copies need no live input. Because the
lists now depend on the WAN address, the `wan` hotplug hook runs `sync-hairpin`
and a reload on ifup/ifupdate; the boot heal already covers restarts.

fix(start-wrt): keep a rule's WAN-port override across an edit

The confirmation for publishing a port already in use on the WAN is
persisted per rule, and the list round-trips it. The edit dialog built
its result from the form fields alone, so every edit — a label change
included — sent the rule with the flag cleared, the backend reported the
collision again, and the user was asked again.

Carry the flag over, but only while the rule still publishes what was
confirmed: the override is a blanket per-rule bypass, so repointing a
confirmed rule at a different external range or changing its protocol
must re-validate rather than inherit a confirmation the user never gave
for those ports.

fix(core): stop IPv6 stalls on a gateway with no IPv6 address of its own (#3911)

* fix(core): stop IPv6 stalls on a gateway with no IPv6 address of its own

Two fixes for one stall: an OS update from the registry sat at 0 bytes
for over four minutes on a box whose LAN router advertises an IPv6
default route with SLAAC off (A=0, M=1) and a DHCPv6 server that issues
no leases, so eno0 had only a link-local address while a StartTunnel
gateway held the box's only global one.

gateway.rs: `apply_policy_routing_v6` treated an interface as able to
carry v6 whenever NetworkManager reported an IPv6 gateway, so eno0 got a
real default route in its policy table and the kernel, finding no global
source on eno0, sent every IPv6 SYN out eno0 with the wg0 address, which
the LAN discards. The leak-guard blackhole now applies unless the
interface has a non-link-local address of its own (a global one where
there is no gateway), so such traffic fails at once and falls back to
IPv4 instead of hanging for the SYN timeout.

socks.rs: startd routes its outbound HTTP through its own SOCKS proxy,
whose CONNECT handler resolved a hostname with
`TcpStream::connect((domain, port))`. tokio tries the resolved addresses
one after another with no timeout, so every unreachable AAAA record
costs the kernel's full SYN timeout (about two minutes) before IPv4 is
tried. The proxy now resolves first and races the addresses RFC 8305
style: attempts start 250 ms apart, alternating address families, and
the first to connect wins while the rest are dropped. This covers a v6
path that is valid on the box but dead further along, which no local
guard can detect.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(core): replay multipath, lifetime and typed routes into gateway tables

apply_policy_routing and apply_policy_routing_v6 mirror the main table into
each gateway's policy table by feeding every line of `ip route show` back into
`ip route replace`, dropping only `linkdown` and `dead`. Show output is not
replace input: a multipath route prints as a header plus indented `nexthop …`
continuation lines, a lifetime prints as `expires 1786sec`, an unreachable or
prohibit route carries `error -113`, and offload flags print as words replace
rejects. The header of a multipath default is skipped and its continuation
lines are not, so `ip -6 route replace nexthop via … table N` runs on every
watch_ip pass for every gateway and iproute2 answers with its full usage text.
On a server whose LAN router advertises a two-next-hop IPv6 default that was
140 usage dumps in one 10,000-line log export — 40% of it.

The four loops now share one parser that folds continuation lines onto their
route, keeps the route type, drops the errno and display flags, and strips the
unit from a lifetime; `table` is emitted before the next hops because iproute2
rejects it after them. The destination is the token after an optional type, so
a `blackhole default` is skipped as a default in every loop rather than by a
special case in one of them.

Each transformed form was checked against iproute2 6.17. The parser's tests
were run standalone with rustc; the crate itself is left to CI.

* fix(core): cap SOCKS attempts, drop mirrored lifetimes, parse routes by position

Review follow-ups on the IPv6 stall fix.

socks.rs: at most two connection attempts are in flight per request.
Each address still starts 250 ms after the previous one, or as soon as
an earlier attempt fails, so a large non-answering RRset cannot hold a
socket per address until the kernel gives up. The connector is injected,
and the stagger tests run on paused Tokio time against a future that
never resolves, asserting exactly when each attempt starts.

gateway.rs: a mirrored route carries no `expires`. NetworkManager renews
a lifetime in `main` without a route-data change, and the policy tables
are otherwise reconciled only every 600 s, so a copy with a shorter
lifetime vanished from the selected table while `main` kept the route.
The copy now lives until reconciliation removes it. Token cleanup is
position-aware: a keyword that takes a value copies both, so an
interface named `trap`, `error` or `expires` after `dev` survives, and
`xresolve` is a recognised route type so stale cleanup deletes such a
route by destination.

The changelog entries for the two operational fixes move from Security
to Fixed, and the book's IPv6 section names the router-without-address
case and the dual-stack connection behaviour.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(core): stagger without a cap, replay nexthop ids, key mirrored routes by metric

socks.rs: the two-attempt cap is gone. With two dead addresses ahead of
a live one it held the live one back until a kernel timeout, which is
the stall this PR exists to remove. Attempts start on the 250 ms cadence
or on an earlier failure, and every pending socket is dropped the moment
one connects; the sockets held while nothing answers are bounded by the

gateway.rs: the IP6Config watcher subscribes to RouteData like the

table on the signal rather than at the 600 s tick. A `nhid` route is
replayed with its id alone: the kernel rejects a nexthop id alongside
the gateway and device that `show` prints as its expansion. Routes are
identified by prefix and metric, and a stale alias is deleted with its
metric, so a route that changed metric does not leave its predecessor
selected. Cleanup runs only when the `main` snapshot succeeded; a failed

* fix(core): keep a route's own tos behind a nexthop id's encap expansion

iproute2 prints a nexthop-id route as `nhid N`, the expanded encap
payload, the route's own `tos`, then `via`/`dev` (checked against

* fix(core): consult main for specific routes instead of mirroring it into gateway tables

The per-gateway tables copied main's non-default routes by feeding
`ip route show` back into `ip route replace`, and five review rounds
found five more ways that text fails to round-trip: lifetimes, errno,
display flags, nexthop-id expansions, encap payloads carrying their own
tos, multi-line option output, interface names that collide with
keywords. The kernel provides the mirror's semantics directly. A
`lookup main suppress_prefixlength 0` rule ahead of the table rules
consults main for every route except a default, which is exactly the
set the mirror copied. A table now holds only its default, or the v6
leak-guard blackhole.

Verified in a container with iproute2 6.9: on-link, container-subnet
and VPN-peer destinations, including an encap route the parser could
never replay, resolve from main; Internet destinations take the
selected table's default; global v6 hits the blackhole; a marked reply
to an on-link destination still takes main's route.

The rule sits at priority 50, behind the transparent divert at 49, and
the reply-mark rules move from 50 to 51 so a marked reply consults main
first; a reply-mark rule found at any other priority is deleted, so a
hot restart converges too. Two semantics differ from the mirror and are
accepted: a `throw` in main falls through to the outbound table's
default, and a reject-type default in main ends the lookup before it
can be suppressed. StartOS installs neither into main. Tables survive a
hot restart of startd but not the reboot every OS update performs, so
no cleanup of previously mirrored entries is carried.

The IPv6 RouteData subscription existed to reconcile the mirror and
goes with it.

* fix(web): skip zod's eval probe under the ui csp

The web UIs are served with `script-src 'self'`. Zod v4 probes
`new Function("")` when the first object schema is built, to decide whether

fix(start-wrt): write the eMMC partition table instead of trusting the card's (#3930)

The flash raw-copied sector 0 through the end of the squashfs from the
microSD card to the eMMC and then expected the copied primary GPT header
to parse. That holds only while the card still carries the image's own
header, which describes a ~580 MB disk. Any partition tool that "fixes" the
card (parted/gparted's Fix prompt, sgdisk -e, a write from fdisk) rewrites
the header's last usable LBA to the card's real size; copied onto a 16 GB
eMMC from a larger card, that header is rejected by libfdisk, the kernel
and U-Boot alike, and all three fall back to whatever backup GPT the eMMC
already held at its last sector. On a factory board that table has a
rootfs and no rootfs_data, so the flash died with `rootfs_data partition
not found on eMMC` and the board no longer booted from eMMC
(`GPT: last_usable_lba incorrect: 76F4FDE > 1d1f000`). The hardware
supplier hit this flashing v1.1.0 on 2026-09-11.

After the copy, dump the card's table with sfdisk, drop the two lines that
describe the card (`device`, `last-lba`) and the overlay's size, and write
the result to the eMMC with `sfdisk --force`. sfdisk derives the last
usable sector from the eMMC, writes both the primary and the backup copy,
and extends rootfs_data to the free space, which the existing expansion
step then pins to the last usable sector as before. Dropping the size
covers a card whose rootfs_data was also grown to fill it, which sfdisk
would otherwise refuse on the smaller eMMC.

Bench-verified on a BPI-F3 with a 32 GB card: the relocated-header case
reproduced the supplier's failure on 1.1.0 and flashed clean on this
build, as did a card with rootfs_data grown to 29.4 GB; the eMMC booted
after each. A pristine card is unaffected.

fix(scripts): resolve the personal signing key from the repo and overwrite partial signatures (#3904)

* fix(scripts): resolve the personal signing key from the repo and overwrite partial signatures

`cmd_sign` and `cmd_cosign` read `user.signingkey` after `enter_release_dir`
has moved into the release staging directory, so a repo-local key is never
seen and the global one is used. With a global SSH signing key that is a
`.pub` path, and gpg aborts with "No secret key" after the first Start9
signature. Read the key from `$REPO_ROOT`, and skip the personal signature
when that repo signs with SSH, which gpg cannot use.

Pass `--yes` to the detach-sign calls so re-running `sign` or `cosign` after a
partial failure overwrites the half-written `signatures/*.asc` instead of
stopping at gpg's overwrite prompt.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(scripts): keep the personal signature only for OpenPGP and use the configured program

`gpg.format` can also be `x509`, whose key the literal `gpg` calls cannot
use, so the personal signature is kept only when the format is unset or
`openpgp`. The sign and export calls for that key go through the repo's
`gpg.openpgp.program`, then `gpg.program`, then `gpg`, so a key that only
a configured program can reach still signs. The install guide no longer
promises the second signature unconditionally.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(scripts): sign the personal signature with gpg on PATH and drop stale copies on rerun

The release tooling's signing contract is GnuPG on PATH: the Start9 key, the
apt suite and pre-check all go through `gpg`, and the personal signature now
does too. Git's `gpg.program` is not consulted: Git guarantees only its own
`-bsau`/`--verify` interface for that program and resolves a relative path
from the worktree, neither of which holds for the `--detach-sign`/`--export`
calls made from the release directory.

A `sign` rerun removes the current signer's earlier `*.<user>.asc` and
`<user>.key.asc` before regenerating, so a signature that is skipped this time
cannot ride along stale. Other maintainers' cosignatures are left in place.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(scripts): preflight the personal key against gpg and rebuild the signature dir on every run

A configured `user.signingkey` proves nothing about the `gpg` on PATH, so the
personal key is kept only if `gpg --list-secret-keys` knows it; `sign` then
skips it with the existing warning and `cosign` fails before downloading.

`sign` rebuilds `signatures/` from empty, and `cosign` extracts the release's
current archive into an empty directory and drops the current user's entries
before regenerating them, so nothing left in the staging directory from an
earlier run can ride along against replaced artifacts.

fix(start-cli): say when the workspace's start-technologies checkout is off live-docs (#3910)

`s9pk init-package` scaffolds from the package template in whatever branch
the workspace's `start-technologies` checkout is on, and never looks at that
branch. A workspace scaffolded by start-cli 1.x cloned `master`, whose
template now pins an unpublished `@start9labs/start-sdk`, so `npm install`
fails with ETARGET and nothing names the cause. Re-running `init-workspace`
there has the same blind spot.

Both commands now print a one-line notice when the checkout is on a branch
other than `live-docs`, naming the checkout and its branch. A checkout the
workspace owns is to be moved out of the workspace and `init-workspace`
rerun, which clones fresh on `live-docs`; a symlinked one is left alone and
the link removed instead. No git operation is prescribed or performed: a
1.0.1 clone is single-branch, shallow and sparse, and no one command
sequence is right for every checkout state.

The branch is read from the checkout's own `.git/HEAD` (following a
`gitdir:` file), so an enclosing repository is never consulted and a
detached HEAD stays silent. The outdated-start-cli notice is gated on the
same check, since off `live-docs` the manifest names a version that has not
shipped. In `init-package` the notice fires right after workspace
discovery, so a scaffold left behind by a failed run cannot hide it.

Bumps start-cli to 2.0.1.

fix(sdk): add MariaDB 11 dump backup support (#3915)

* fix(sdk): make withMysqlDump work against MariaDB 11 images

MariaDB 11.x images ship only the mariadb-* binaries, so the mariadb path of
Backups.withMysqlDump could neither dump nor restore: it shelled out to mysqld,
mysqladmin, mysqldump, mysql and mysql_install_db. The server exec was also
fire-and-forget, so a missing binary or a crash surfaced only as the ready loop
timing out.

The mariadb engine now runs mariadbd directly on both sides, the same shape as
the mysql engine, so conventionally packaged MariaDB images work: the official
image, one built on it with its own entrypoint (romm), and Alpine's package
inside the app image (dojo). Backup dumps with mariadb-dump as `user`, gzips the
result and copies it to the backup target. Restore clears the data directory,
initializes it with mariadb-install-db, creates the database and `user`, gives
root `password`, and replays the dump. The server exit is checked around
readiness probes, and shutdown uses bounded SIGTERM and SIGKILL waits.

Both engines share the grant SQL and the import command. The SQL escapes every
literal and identifier and clears NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES first; the import binds
the database with `--database`; the dump clients get `--` before the database;
and dump/import client authentication uses MYSQL_PWD instead of `-p` arguments.
The mysql engine stops its server on every path. Regression coverage exercises
a leading-hyphen database through both restore command paths.

The `backup` package namespace now re-exports Backups and mountBackupTarget.

Closes #3766

A Local (private) IPv4 raw-port forward admitted only the gateway's
on-link subnet plus the container bridge, while the vhost path that
serves web interfaces admits any RFC 1918 source. A client on a second

source, the same set `is_private_ip` accepts on the vhost side. The
separate bridge rule goes: 10.0.3.0/24 is inside 10/8. IPv6 Local
forwards keep their on-link scope.

Closes #3912

fix(start-os): remove stale forward rules at startup (#3963)

The forward controller re-requests every forward from the database when
it starts, and each script call replaces only the rules carrying its own
tag, so a rule whose tuple no longer exists — after a crash, or a
restart across an address change — stayed in the kernel until the next
reboot.

The controller now deletes every rule tagged by forward-port or
forward-port6 before it serves its first request. Nothing else stamps
those shapes: the gateway, SNI and tunnel rules carry their own.

Both tags gain a family prefix and separator (`F4-` / `F6-` + digest) so
a prefix cannot read as part of the hex digest. Updating either product
reboots it, so no rule of the old shape reaches a run that sweeps.

StartTunnel shares the controller, so it gains the sweep and moves to
1.3.1.

fix(start-os): let UPnP port mappings expire on their own (#3964)

StartOS asked a UPnP router for a permanent mapping and relied on its
periodic re-assertion to keep it current, so a mapping outlived the
server: powered off or moved to another network, the router kept
forwarding the port indefinitely. PCP and NAT-PMP mappings, and the
hostname mappings on the same UPnP path, already carry a one-hour
lifetime.

Plain UPnP mappings now request the same hour, well past the 180 s
refresh that re-asserts them. A router that answers
OnlyPermanentLeasesSupported gets the permanent mapping it did before.

dir_copy_inner restored the mode and owner of every directory it created but
only chowned regular files, so each file was created through File::create
and kept the umask default of 0644 regardless of the source mode.

The setup wizard's Transfer copies the previous drive's main/ tree with

fix(start-core): refuse a dependency mount whose volume does not exist (#3961)

right for a package's own subpaths but wrong for a pointer mount: with the
dependency not installed, the effect created `volumes/<dep>/data/<vol>` on the

empty folder with only the dependency warning to say so. When the dependency

dependency's volume root does not exist, matching what a read-only mount

* feat(start-wrt): set the Wi-Fi regulatory country from the UI

Every router ran on the kernel's world regulatory domain because nothing ever
wrote `option country`: 2.4 GHz channels 1–11 and 5 GHz channels 36–48 at

get` to report the new domain so a follow-up read sees it. A new

AP may currently use per band, parsed from `iw phy` (skipping disabled and
no-IR frequencies).

The settings page gets a Country combobox at the top, named through
Intl.DisplayNames in the UI language, with a warning while unset; the channel
dropdowns list only what the current domain permits, and a country change
resets them to Auto since the old selection may no longer be legal.

* refactor(start-os): trim the disk identity plumbing

The install resolver returned the path it was handed, so it was a
validator in disguise; replace it with a listed-path check and look
the OS disk up once. The blkid wrapper existed only to inject a
failure in a test, and the fstab renderer wrapped one format! call;
fold both into fstab_source. Stop writing the root fstab entry:
from_fstab skips it and the initramfs finds root from the kernel
command line, so the third blkid call only added a failure mode.

The normalizer's root-on-partition-4 rows described the Raspberry
Pi layout, but every shipped Pi image already writes PARTUUID
entries and the Pi has no 0.3.5.1 migration, so drop them together
with the root rows. findmnt --target names the mount containing a
path, so an unmounted /boot/efi resolved to /boot's device and only
the later equality check caught it; --mountpoint states the intent.

The CLI still posted the legacy logicalname key and only worked
through the serde alias; send stablePath and drop the alias. The
changelog filed the new requirement under Fixed as if it were
additive, and the rejection error claimed the disk was gone; name
the rejected form in both. start-os-image-test ran a shell unit
suite and nothing about an image.

* fix(start-os): match the protected partition by device node

The disk list picks each disk's and each partition's stable path as
independent minimums over its by-path aliases, and Preserve only
found the protected partition when partition_for on the disk's
choice string-equalled the partition's choice. That holds for the
alias families udev emits today and nowhere else. Compare the
canonical device nodes instead, which is true for any alias.

* docs(start-os): list the scripts test target and the install-os change

Every place that enumerates the test targets now carries
start-os-scripts-test, and the 0.4.0.2 release notes tell script
authors that setup install-os takes stable paths, next to the two
other CLI changes they already list.

* refactor(start-os): normalize fstab from the live mounts only

The migration was the only consumer of the normalizer's --legacy
mode, and everything that mode required: the root-number layout
table, the partition lookup by number, and the special case for an
EFI mount the 0.3.5.1 chroot cannot see. It also ran the script on
the payload's bookworm userland, whose lsblk lacks the PARTN column
the table needed, so every 0.3.5.1 migration would have failed.

Stop normalizing during the migration. A migrated box keeps the
kernel-name fstab it has today and is normalized on its first 0.4
update, where the full mount table is visible. The ordinary path
then needs only what it can observe: the device mounted at each
boot path, that it shares a disk with the installed root, and its
PARTUUID resolving uniquely to that device.

* fix(start-os): quiesce the partitions sysfs reports

list_partitions had started returning partition_for on the disk
path, which for a by-path disk synthesizes a udev symlink name
rather than reporting the node sysfs lists. A partition whose
link udev had not created then dropped out of the quiesce set,
leaving its holders in place for partx to trip over. Push the
kernel node for each sysfs entry as before; nothing in quiesce
needs the by-path namespace.

* fix(start-os): derive -partN names under every /dev/disk directory

partition_for only produced udev's -partN form for by-path and
appended a kernel-style suffix to anything else, while the size
check in front of os install had started following symlinks. A
by-id disk therefore passed every pre-write check, had a fresh
table written, and failed at mkfs on a partition path that did not
exist. udev names partitions -partN under every /dev/disk
directory, so key on that directory instead.

* refactor(start-os): size block devices from sysfs

os install sized its target with a private sysfs reader while the
wizard sized the same disk for the same installer by forking
blockdev, and the private one had just grown a symlink prologue.
Keep one helper. The sysfs read wins: no process per device in the
disk list, a typed error on a path instead of parsed stderr, and a
stable kernel attribute. It lives under /sys/class/block, which
covers partitions and device-mapper nodes as well as whole disks.

* fix(start-os): let upgrade accept an image without the fstab normalizer

The dev deploy flows run the installed upgrade script against
whatever image they are handed, and -match made a missing
normalizer fatal, so a box on this build could no longer be rolled
back to an image built before it. The flag guarded nothing: an
installed upgrade that extracts the script also ships it, so the
next line runs the installed copy when the image has none.

* fix(start-os): keep updating when fstab cannot be normalized

A normalizer refusal aborted the whole update, so a server with a
cloned copy of its OS disk attached failed every update until the
clone was unplugged, for a step that only hardens the next boot.
Log the refusal, leave fstab as it is, and carry on as every
release before this one did.

* fix(start-os): resolve tagged fstab sources through their udev links

A PARTUUID= or UUID= source was resolved by forking blkid and
taking its whole output as one path, so two partitions carrying
the same id produced a path matching nothing and the real boot
partition was no longer recognised as the OS's own. systemd mounts
such an entry through /dev/disk/by-<tag>/<value>, so follow that
link: it names the device actually in use, duplicates included,
and costs a readlink instead of a process.

* fix(start-os): look up the pool target in pvscan by its device node

pvscan reports kernel names, and the target arrives as a by-path
handle, so the guard around pvremove never matched and the old
physical volume was only ever cleared by the zeroing that follows.
Canonicalize before the lookup so the teardown runs as intended.

Install the incoming updater in the CI deploy helper, matching the production update path so new pre-reboot migrations run on the first update. * fix(start-os): keep the running kernel until update-grub has replaced it

Removing every kernel the target image lacks took the running one
off /boot before the chroot regenerated grub.cfg, and the image
ships no grub.cfg of its own, so a grub failure at that point left
the old config naming a kernel that no longer existed. Only a
kernel newer than the target's can outrank it in update-grub, so
remove just those: an ordinary upgrade never touches its running
kernel and a rollback still sheds the one that would boot first.

* fix(start-os): pin each image's kernel as the default boot entry

update-grub made the highest-versioned kernel in /boot the default,
so an upgrade could only keep a rollback or a kernel downgrade
bootable by deleting the running kernel before grub.cfg had been
rewritten, and a grub failure at that point left nothing to boot.
Write GRUB_TOP_LEVEL for the image's own kernel at package install
instead: every update-grub run from that image now picks it whatever
else sits in /boot. The upgrade script extracts the boot files over
/boot again and removes nothing, and prune-boot keeps only the
running kernel, since a leftover no longer outranks anything.

fix(start-core): accept a manual passthrough on every gua of its gateway (#3994)

`add_passthrough` filled `ProxyTarget.public_v6` with a one-shot
`gua_ips(...)` of the interface watcher, and nothing recomputed it. IPv6 WAN
accept matches the exact arrival address, so a GUA missing from that snapshot
routed to no target and the client got TLS `unrecognized_name`, while IPv4
(keyed by gateway) kept working. The boot restore in `VHostController::new`
runs while the watcher is still filling in, so it captures whichever GUAs
exist at that instant.

A manual passthrough is public per gateway, not per address, so say that:
`public_v6_gateways` holds the gateways and `accepts` checks the arrival
gateway plus "is a GUA" against live listener metadata. Nothing is
snapshotted, so there is nothing to go stale.

Re-registering the target from a watcher task was the alternative. A changed
`ProxyTarget` is a new mapping entry whose predecessor's context is
cancelled, so every GUA change on the gateway would have cut the
passthrough's open connections, IPv4 ones included.

Bind requirements, port-map derivation and challenge binds honor the new
field wherever they honor `public_v6`.

* fix(start-tunnel): let a device repoint its own mapping, trim refresh handling

A device that asks for an external port it already holds, with a different
internal port or range size, now rewrites its own automatic mapping instead
of conflicting until the old lease lapses. The rule is the same for IPv4
DNAT and IPv6 pinholes: an entry's owner changes what it maps, and a device
never changes a manual entry or another device's. The pinhole half restores
what 1.3.0 allowed; the DNAT half is new.

The refresh paths read `enabled` directly rather than through DnatRefresh,
PinholeRefresh and RouteActions, which only renamed `enabled` and `auto`.
Lease stamping is unconditional again: every reap path re-checks `auto`, so
a lease on a manual entry costs one no-op wake. `sni.prepare()` is called
unconditionally again, since it is a once-only global init. Registering no
hostnames starts no SNI listener, which is what keeps a port whose routes
are all disabled off the dataplane.

* fix(start-core): let a device repoint its own sni routes and fallback

The SNI demux owned a hostname or fallback by its full target, so the device
that held one was refused when it asked for a different internal port, until
the old lease lapsed. Ownership is the device now: a binding is refused only
to a different address, and the holder's new port overwrites the old one. The
registration transaction already restores the previous binding on a failed
bind, so a repoint needs no unregister step.

The tunnel's stored routes follow the same rule as its DNAT forwards and
pinholes: an entry's owner repoints it within its own device, and a device
never changes a manual route. StartWRT keeps its routes in the demux alone and
takes the rule from there.

* docs(start-tunnel): state how manual and automatic entries share a port

The sentence about manual ports described the fixed bug rather than the rule,
and read as though a manual and an automatic entry could hold the same
external port. An external port holds one entry, and on an SNI port each
hostname does; a device's request against a manual entry is served by it or
refused.

fix(start-core): send a tunnel's ipv6 replies to same-lan clients back out the tunnel (#3996)

An IPv6 client on the server's own LAN could connect to a tunnel-delegated
GUA but never complete a TLS handshake. IPv6 has no NAT, so the server sees
the client's real address, which is on-link for the LAN interface. The
priority-50 `lookup main suppress_prefixlength 0` rule matches that /64
before the priority-51 CONNMARK rule or the priority-60 source rule is
consulted, so the reply left by the LAN with the tunnel GUA as its source.
The client accepted the SYN-ACK; the tunnel server never saw it, classed
the client's ACK and ClientHello as conntrack INVALID, and dropped them.

On a WireGuard interface that carries v6, install
`fwmark <T> to 2000::/3 lookup <T>` at priority 48, ahead of main.

The destination selector is load-bearing: restore-mark runs in prerouting
for both directions, so inbound packets DNAT'd to a container's ULA carry
the same mark and must still reach lxcbr0 through main. A source-keyed rule
was rejected because a reply forwarded from a container still has the
container's ULA as its source at routing time. The rule is WireGuard-only
because a LAN interface's table holds just a default via the router, which
would detour replies to on-link neighbours.

ensure_table_rules now recognises the rule, since its stray-rule sweep
deletes by fwmark/lookup/priority and `ip rule del` without `to` matches it.

* fix(start-core): route a service's ipv6 through its outbound gateway

The per-service outbound rule was `from <container v4>` only. Containers
also hold a ULA on lxcbr0 and reach the v6 internet through lxc-net's
NAT66, so a service with its own gateway kept sending IPv6 out the
system-wide default: the priority-75 catch-all when one is pinned,
main's v6 default on Auto. Dual-stack peers prefer v6, so most of such a
service's traffic could leave under the address the override was meant
to hide.

Install the same priority-70 rule in the v6 family, keyed on the
container's ULA. It points at the gateway's existing v6 table, which
already holds either a real default or the leak-guard blackhole, so a
service sent through a gateway without v6 has its v6 dropped.

`ip rule` rejects a v6 source without `-6`, so the five hand-rolled
invocations go through one helper that picks the family from the source.

fix(start-core): apply a service's outbound gateway when it starts (#4005)

* fix(start-core): apply a service's outbound gateway when it starts

The sync task purged a service's rules at startup and then waited: the
gateway watcher was marked seen and the database subscription carries no
initial event, so the rule was first installed by the next real gateway
change or write to `outboundGateway`. At boot the interface churn hid
it. A service restarted on a quiet network ran on the system-wide
default until something changed.

Reconcile once at startup, after both subscriptions are open so a change
that lands in between is still seen.

Every later event deleted the rule and added it back, including the
events that changed nothing. Forwarded traffic is routed per packet, so
in that window the service's established flows left by the system-wide
default, and a connection opened inside it was NATed to the wrong
address and stayed broken. Touch the rules only when the table changes,
and add the replacement before deleting the old rule: the kernel
evaluates equal-priority rules in insertion order, so the old one keeps
routing until it is removed. A failed add rolls back and leaves the old
rule in place for the next event to retry.

* refactor(start-core): name the policy-routing rule priorities

The rule ladder was spread across bare literals: `.arg("51")` on the way
in and `starts_with("51:")` on the way back out of `ip rule show`, with
only the two outbound priorities named. The ordering test compared those
two constants with each other while the wg-encap rule between them
stayed a literal, so moving either past it would have passed.

Name all eight priorities beside each other and assert at compile time
that they are in evaluation order. `rule_at_priority` reads the priority
column as a number, replacing the per-site string prefixes.

fix(sdk): hold rsync progress at its high-water mark (#4008)

Backup and restore progress polls rsync's --info=progress2 percentage,
and without --no-inc-recursive rsync's total grows as it walks the tree,
so the number a user sees drops every time rsync finds more data (50%
back to 43% on a Nextcloud backup). Keep the parsed percentage monotonic
instead; a pre-scan would make it exact but times out large backups.

fix(start-wrt): keep a device's generated label out of its DHCP reservation (#4007)

* fix(start-wrt): keep a device's generated label out of its DHCP reservation

Publishing a port to a device with no reserved address reserves one, and
the web app sent the device's resolved display name along as its name.
For a device that never shared a hostname that name is the derived label
("Android device (4c8f63)"), which `devices.update` wrote verbatim into
`dhcp.host_*.name`. dnsmasq refuses a dhcp-host name that is not a
hostname label and fails to start on its next reload or boot, so the LAN
lost DHCP. The device page had the same shape of problem: it pre-filled
the name field with the resolved name, so any save turned a learned
hostname into a static one, and a generated label blocked saving.

`devices.list` now reports the UCI static name as `custom_name`, which is
what the form edits and pre-fills; the resolved name is its placeholder.
`devices.update` takes `name` as optional: absent leaves it alone, empty
clears it, and anything else must be a hostname label (letters, digits,
hyphens, not at the ends, at most 63 bytes, the rule the form already
applied) or the request is rejected with InvalidRequest. The reserve
path no longer sends a name at all.

* fix(start-wrt): repair a DHCP reservation name dnsmasq refuses to serve

Preventing a bad name from being written leaves the routers that already
hold one broken, and an update did not help them: `sysupgrade` keeps the
overlay, so `/etc/config/dhcp` carries the name across and the new
firmware's dnsmasq dies on it too. The repair could only be done from the
UI, which needs an address from the DHCP server that is down — an
unexpired lease or a hand-configured static IPv4, and no DNS either way,
since dnsmasq serves both.

`heal_dhcp_host_names` runs at boot and clears any reservation name
`validate_device_name` rejects, next to the other converge steps in the
daemon. It precedes the fingerprint hook because both reload dnsmasq and
this one decides whether it can start at all; `reload_service` re-runs
`start_service`, so the reload starts a dnsmasq that is down. The name
was never in service — dnsmasq would not start on it, so it resolved for
nobody — and the cleared value is logged to Activity rather than
sanitized into a name the user did not choose.

`devices.update` now validates `mac` and `ipv4` as well. Every field it
takes lands in the config dnsmasq reads, and it refuses to start on any
of them malformed; `devices.set-auto-forward` already screened the same
`mac` for the same reason. Rejections are `InvalidValue` throughout,
matching that handler and the rest of the crate.

The activity entry for an update that leaves the name alone named the
device by MAC. It now falls back to the name already on the reservation,
which is the device's current name precisely because the request did not
touch it.

* docs(start-wrt): route the reservation-name repair through a reflash

A router whose DHCP server will not start is not one an update can be
started from: it serves DNS too, so reaching the UI takes an unexpired
lease or a hand-set static IPv4 and the literal address. Naming the
update as the way out describes a path most affected users cannot take.

Keep settings is the one that works, and not because it sidesteps the
bad name — `run_flash_core` formats rootfs_data clean and the wizard
restores conffiles over it, `/etc/config/dhcp` among them
(`dnsmasq.conffiles_static`), so the name comes back. It works because
what it lands on boots the heal.

* fix(start-core): move the divert table out of the gateway table range

Gateway tables are numbered 1000 + ifindex with no upper bound, and the
SNI divert table sat at 1344, inside that range. A gateway whose
interface landed on ifindex 344 would have replaced the divert table's
local-delivery default with its own. ifindex only grows, so a
long-running server gets there eventually.

StartWRT already used 5344 because it numbers its own tables by VLAN
tag, which makes 1344 a legal tag there. It is the same mechanism in all
three products, so the default moves to 5344 and StartWRT reads the
shared constant instead of repeating the number.

A process restarted without a reboot keeps the old rule and table beside
the new ones until the next boot. Both deliver locally, and every
product's update path reboots.

* fix(start-core): keep inbound connections alive under the outbound kill switch

The kill switch ends each gateway selection in an `unreachable` rule.
With the selected gateway down, that rule also caught two lookups that
are not outbound traffic, and every connection arriving from off-link
through another gateway died.

A local reply is routed before it is marked. The kernel routes a
SYN-ACK with mark 0 and only its source address, and mangle_output
restores the connection mark afterwards. IPv4 used to get through that
first lookup by falling into whatever default came later in the ladder.
The rejection took that away, so the SYN-ACK was never built. IPv6 hit
the same thing against the leak-guard blackhole in #3632 and got
source-address rules. Those rules now cover every routable address of a
gateway in both families.

The reverse-path filter routes too. StartOS runs rp_filter=2, and for a
packet forwarded to a container the reverse lookup is sourced from the
container's address, which both rejections match. The first packet of an
inbound connection now carries its mark, not only its conntrack entry,
and each gateway interface sets src_valid_mark, so the filter follows
the reply path. It is set per interface because on `all` it validates an
SNI-diverted reply against its local-delivery route and drops it.

A lookup is now installed before the rejection behind it and removed
after it, on both paths, so switching a selection never leaves the
rejection as the only match. A service lookup that fails to install
still gets its rejection. The per-service state is the set of installed
rules rather than a description of it.

policy-routing.md states the invariants the ladder has to hold, derives
the rule order from them, and records where each rule came from.
policy_routing_model.sh builds the ladder from the priority constants in
a throwaway network namespace and checks every invariant in every
selection state. The Auto rules at 1000 and 1100 join the ordering
assertion.

* fix(start-core): route the server's own connections by one dedicated mark

IPv6 retries a failed lookup: when a connection the server opens finds no
route, the kernel picks a source address anyway and looks up again, and
that second lookup matches the priority-60 source rule of whichever
gateway owns the address. With the selected gateway down or unable to
carry IPv6, the server's own IPv6 left through the ISP. IPv4 stops at the
first failure. The previous commit found this and closed it, by marking
new local connections with the selected gateway's table id, or with a
rejection mark matched by a new priority-52 rule.

The table id is the mark replies carry, and rule 48 sends that mark to any
global IPv6 destination ahead of `main`. Pinned to a tunnel that carries
IPv6, the server's traffic to an on-link global address on its own LAN
went into the tunnel.

New local connections now carry one dedicated mark, and nothing else
changes: source rules match unmarked lookups only, so the repeated lookup
passes them and ends in the selection's own lookup and rejection, which
already match any packet. Rule 52, the per-family choice of mark, and the
gateway capability check in the default-outbound path are gone. Only
`ct state new` packets are marked, so a flow opened before a selection
keeps its path.

`mangle_output` goes back to the coordinator, in one transaction with
prerouting. It had moved to the default-outbound path, which runs after a
fallible sync, so a failed pass left the chain without `restore-mark` and
replies to tunnel connections misrouted. The marking rule lives in a chain
of its own that `mangle_output` jumps to, so each chain keeps one writer.
It starts marking before a selection's rules are installed and stops after
they are removed.

The source-rule migration is dropped: no release carries the old shape and
every update reboots.

* fix(start-os): keep the install backup across a retried install

Reverts "restore install backup before retry" and "restore interrupted
migration snapshots".

InstallBackup::restore renames the backup into the live root, so
restoring ahead of the Installing retry consumed the only rollback
point. The retry calls Service::install directly, which takes no
snapshot, so a retry that failed left the volume as the failed init
wrote it and the fallthrough restore had nothing to put back. Retrying
with the backup intact keeps that fallthrough able to roll back.

The restore ahead of the migration's install was unreachable:
services.init loads every Installing package before post_init re-runs
post_up, and that load either consumes the backup or removes it. With
it gone the helper is a bare conversion again, so the volumes-path
variant that existed for its test goes too.

* test(start-os): assert the plain-directory snapshot by behavior

The snapshot test captured tracing output through a custom writer and
subscriber to match a substring of the warning. It now asserts what
the warning stands for: no backup is taken and the live tree is left
as it was.

Reword the changelog and release-notes entries to say what a user
keeps rather than how the snapshot is staged, and scope the recovery
comment to any data that predates the install, which includes a
soft-uninstalled volume as well as a migrated one.

* fix(start-os): remove a failed fresh install's volumes

Keeping volumes on every failed install stopped migrated data being
deleted, but left a failed fresh install's partial volume and logs on
disk, with no package entry to remove them through and every retry
initializing on top of them.

At recovery a fresh install and an install over data that could not be
snapshotted look the same on disk: a live root and no backup. The
original `keep_volumes = backup.exists()` guessed fresh and deleted
migrated data; it also deleted a soft-uninstalled package's data when
a reinstall was cancelled during the download, before any snapshot ran.

InstallBackup::begin now records which it is, as an `.install-fresh`
sibling, before the package entry is created. Every Installing entry
is therefore preceded by a begin() that either wrote the marker or
deleted it, so one left over from an earlier install is never read.

The marker authorizes deletion, so everything around it fails toward
keeping data: no marker keeps the volumes, a root that cannot be read
counts as present, begin() settles a pending restore before judging
the root (restore_old can hold the only copy while the root reads as
absent), and the boot sweep drops a stray marker but never the data
beside it.

fix(start-core): let watched callbacks finish (#4018)

* fix(start-core): let watched callbacks finish

Helix-Harness: pi
Helix-Model: openai-codex/gpt-5.6-sol

* fix(start-core): detach every self-removing callback watcher

A watcher task that removes its own map entry drops its own
NonDetachingJoinHandle, which aborts the running task at its next
Pending. The callback id has already been consumed from the container's
registered set by then, so a cancelled notify loses the callback and
nothing re-arms it.

It is intermittent because the notify usually never yields: an idle
pooled RPC connection and a socket with room complete synchronously. A
burst of changes drains the pool, the next notify has to connect, and
that Pending is where the task dies.

get_outbound_gateway had the identical `.map(|(_, handlers)| ..)` drop
and was still broken. get_ssl_certificate survived only because an
`if let` scrutinee keeps the handle alive to the end of the block. All
three now go through CallbackHandlers::detach_watcher.

Drop the watch-error logging: changed() fails only when the store is
dropped. Move the regression test to future.rs, where it tests detach
directly against a plain-drop control, and drop the init.md sentence,
which described internals the page already promised.

* refactor(start-core): detach a NonDetachingJoinHandle into its JoinHandle

detach() returns the inner JoinHandle instead of flipping an
abort-on-drop flag, so the type goes back to a tuple struct and carries
no state for a case only one caller has. A PinnedDrop type cannot give
up a field by move, so it reads the handle out of a ManuallyDrop.

* docs(start-core): say why a detached callback watcher cannot leak

Once a watcher removes its own entry, the handle it detaches was the
last one, so detaching gives up no cancellation anyone else had. What
remains is CallbackHandlers::call: Callback is a notification
(Response = Never), so each handler is one line written to the
container's unix socket with no reply awaited, retried at most
MAX_TRIES times. The write resolves once the kernel buffers it and
errors when the container closes the socket, so the task ends no later
than the container does.

fix(start-core): wait for the network to settle before starting services (#4031)

* fix(start-core): keep last-known addresses until an interface reports

The interface watcher seeded every known gateway as disconnected, and the
sync task wrote that snapshot into every host's address table before
NetworkManager reported, wiping the `.local` and IP rows. Each device
then reported on its own, so the table was also rebuilt from partial
snapshots: the always-on container bridge publishes first, and a host
recomputed at that moment still lacked its LAN rows. Services initialize
with no wait for any of it, so an init hook reading its own addresses at
boot could see a table without them. The same pass rewrote timesyncd's
`NTP=` to nothing and restarted it.

The seed now keeps each gateway's last-known state, so the first sync and
every partial one leave a not-yet-reported interface's rows in place. A
device NetworkManager reports unmanaged or without an active connection
now clears its own entry, which the watcher never did, so a disconnected
interface drops its rows at boot and on a link loss alike, and absent
devices are cleared by the enumeration as before.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(start-core): wait for the network to settle before starting services

Keeping each gateway's last-known ip_info in the seed handed last boot's
addresses, ifindexes and WAN IP to every consumer of the interface watch
as live state, and left an interface connected forever when its watcher
never got to report. The seed marks every gateway disconnected again.

Services wait for a complete address table instead. settle() waits for
NetworkManager's Startup property to clear, lists the devices it
activated, and returns once the sync task has written a snapshot with
every one of them connected. Startup is read when services are about to
start rather than tracked from watcher start: init restarts
NetworkManager after binding the persistent connection profiles, and the
first instance finishes startup holding none of them. A 30 second
timeout keeps a link that never activates from holding services.

fix(start-core): match sni hostnames in any case (#4039)

* fix(start-tunnel): match sni hostnames in any case

The demux lowercases the name it reads from a ClientHello and then looks
it up in its hostname map by exact string. PCP and UPnP both lowercase a
hostname when they parse it, but `port-forward add --sni` stores what the
operator typed, so a manual route entered as `Cloud.Example.com` could
never match: the database listed it as enabled, the listener was bound,
and every connection was closed after the ClientHello with nothing logged.

Lowercase on the way into the demux, in `register_transaction` and
`unregister`, rather than at the one input that lacked it. The database
keeps the name as typed, so removing, toggling and relabelling a route by
its stored key still work, and a route already saved with capitals is
repaired when the daemon next restores it instead of staying dead until
someone re-adds it.

StartOS and StartWRT only ever reach the demux through PCP and UPnP, so
their behaviour does not change.

* fix(start-os): match a tls passthrough hostname in any case

The same gap as the tunnel's SNI demux, in StartOS's own handler. rustls
lowercases the server name it reports from a ClientHello, and the vhost
map is keyed by that name. Public and private domains are lowercased
where they are added, but `net vhost add-passthrough --hostname` used the
name as typed for the map key, so a passthrough entered with a capital
letter was listed and never matched.

`VHostController::add_passthrough` and `remove_passthrough` lowercase the
name, which also covers the restore at startup, so a passthrough already
saved with capitals starts working on the next boot. The RPC handlers
store the lowercased name and compare saved rows without regard to case,
so an older row can still be replaced or removed whichever way it is
typed.

it left `available` whenever the network was down: at the boot seed, and,
since the network-settle change, on link loss too. Packages comparing a stored

other interface. The row goes once the gateway leaves the table. The SDK
prunes `.local` only when LAN IP rows exist on its gateways and every one of
them is disabled, rather than whenever none is enabled.

A private IP's state becomes an override against its `.local` row: explicit

it follows `.local`. That makes `.local`'s setting the default for an address
the server is assigned later with nothing written at discovery, which matters
because the boot seed makes every address look newly discovered. `enabled`
could not hold the explicit-on record: `set_gua_wan` and `resolve_nonssl_gua`

its switch says; `.local` reads as on there while any IP it resolves to is on.
The non-SSL LAN group reads and writes through the same effective state, and
a `.local` toggle re-asserts a linked gateway's group at its private domain's
state so the linked IPv4 keeps following the domain.

The UI shows the backend's state through a shared `isAddressEnabled` in place
of its own copy, and the `.local` switch is interactive, locked only while an
IP holds it on.

does, and every other LAN IP it resolves to loses its explicit-on override and
follows `.local` off. Re-enabling `.local` brings the followers back.

A public GUA no longer holds `.local` on. A `.local` switch must not
un-publish a WAN address, and nothing else may leave the switch stuck.

inputs, so the Interfaces tab and a package could disagree about the same
address. It was also wrong where it fired: a forward is built per gateway and
a `.local` vhost answers on every subnet IP of its gateways, so the name was

fix(sdk): retry lazy subcontainer materialization (#4040)

* fix(sdk): retry lazy subcontainer materialization

Clear failed materialization promises so the daemon restart loop can create a fresh subcontainer after transient mount failures. Keep daemon holds pending across failed attempts so recovery preserves shared-container teardown semantics.

Helix-Model: openai-codex/gpt-5.6-sol

* fix(sdk): treat a failed lazy materialization as not materialized

Reset the cached attempt when `_of` itself rejects, and only then. A
throw from the pending destroy that follows a successful `_of` used to
clear the cache too, so the next call built a second subcontainer while
the first still existed.

destroy(), detach() and onDrop() now see a failed in-flight attempt as
nothing to tear down instead of rejecting with the mount error, while a
real post-materialization failure still propagates.

Log each failed attempt once at the point it fails, so the hold and
teardown paths that absorb the rejection cannot hide it. The daemon
restart loop logs through logErrorOnce so an attempt is not reported
twice.

* fix(sdk): track subcontainer teardown apart from materialization

A lazy handle's cached materialization awaited the pending destroy, so
it could reject after the subcontainer existed, and the teardown paths
needed a rethrow to tell that apart from a failed attempt. The destroy
is now requested once the subcontainer exists and is no part of that
promise, which rejects for a failed attempt alone.

That await was doing real work: destroy() called while materialization
was in flight resolved only once destroyFs had finished, and its
callers start replacements on that. SubContainerEager let a second
concurrent destroy() return while the first was still tearing down, so
moving the destroy out would have lost the ordering. Teardown is now
one shared promise that every caller joins.

The teardown error needs no tracking of its own. Every caller only
logs it, and destroyFs forgets the guid before it unmounts, so a retry
finds nothing to do.

* refactor(sdk): name the subcontainer destroy and detach flags for what they record

`destroyPending` sat on both SubContainerEager and SubContainerLazy and
recorded the same fact on each, that destroy() had been called, while
the word left open what it was pending on: holds on one, materialization
on the other. On the lazy handle it read as a destroy already queued.
Both are now `destroyRequested`, and the lazy handle's `detachPending`
is `detachRequested`.

fix(start-os): carry a pre-RDTS 0.3.5.1 Knots over as #knotsprerdts (#4042)

The 0.3.5.1 migration tags any `bitcoind` titled "…Knots…" with the `#knots`
flavor. That was the 0.4 Knots lineage when the rule was written; since the
BIP-110 (RDTS) split it names the package a third-party registry publishes
for the hard-fork chain, while the Bitcoin-chain Knots continues as
`#knotsprerdts` on the Community Registry. A migrated Knots therefore lands
as `#knots:29.3.0:0` with `canMigrateTo` none: no Bitcoin package accepts
it, and a server with that registry added is offered the fork chain as an
ordinary update.

Tag a Knots at or below 29.3.0 as `#knotsprerdts` instead. The Community
Registry's 0.3 index never served a later one — 29.3.0 is Knots
29.3.knots20260210, the last release before RDTS — and the package's own
`canMigrateFrom` already covers the result, so the update is offered
without a package change. 29.3.1 and later stay `#knots`: Retropex's 0.3
line published 29.3.knots20260507 and 20260508 under the same 29.3.1, and
the fork-chain builds follow.

The rewrite was duplicated between the s9pk conversion and the on-disk
`.version` write; both now call `migrated_version`, with unit tests.

feat(start-sdk,start-os): tell an action who is running it (#4045)

`access` decides whether another service may run an action, but the
action was never told which service that was: run_action used the
caller's id for the access check and then forwarded only the action id
and the input. Any identity an action needed had to come from its input,
where a service allowed to call it could name another package, so an
action could not be limited to the caller's own resources.

StartOS now forwards the caller. Service::run_action and
Service::get_action_input take it, the actor messages carry it into the
procedure's params, the container runtime passes it on, and the SDK hands
it to the run handler, the prefill function and a function-valued input
spec as `caller`: a package id, or null for the user and for StartOS
reading a form to evaluate a task. It comes from the effect context the
call arrived on, so a package cannot set it.

SDK 3.0.0 already requires StartOS 0.4.0.2, which is where this lands.

feat(start-sdk): add setupPrimaryUrl (#4030)

* feat(start-sdk): add setupPrimaryUrl and the configured address view

The "Set Primary URL" watcher every package hand-rolls raises a critical
task whenever the stored URL is missing from the interface's reachable
addresses. That list loses `.local` while the address table is rebuilt
and whenever the LAN IP is down, so a server that initializes services
without its LAN address, or loses the link, stops the service and asks the
user to pick the URL they already had.

`sdk.setupPrimaryUrl()` owns the pattern: the action, the init hook and a
reactive reader over the package's own store field. The hook judges the
choice against the interface's configured addresses, follows the hostname
through a port or scheme change, and clears the task once the hostname is
back. A `.local` choice is judged only while some LAN interface is up, the
always-on container bridge not counting. An IP choice is judged only while
the interface it came from is up; the hook records that interface when the
URL is stored, in a file beside the store named after it and the action
id, so no caller model or second helper instance can claim it, and a
damaged record reads as none. An IP whose interface it never saw is left
alone, since another interface's address is no evidence about it. A
domain or Tor choice is judged at once, as those rows never come and go
with the link.

A choice judged gone is replaced by `defaultUrl`'s pick, the `.local`
address unless the package says otherwise, which is what the services
that already handle this do. A package whose users must be told rather
than moved passes `onRemoved: 'task'`, raised at `important` unless told
otherwise; the task is also raised when nothing is left to fall back to.

`addressInfo.configured` exposes the unpruned enabled rows for it, and for
any package that needs "one of my addresses" rather than "reachable now".

* fix(start-sdk): isolate each dependency init watcher

Helix-Harness: pi

* fix(start-sdk,start-os): scope dependency reactivity and clear disabled dependency tasks

Each dependency now watches `enabled`, its narrowing, and each init in
separate effects contexts. `enabled` was read inside the requirement and
every init, so any change to a value it watched reran the narrowing and all
of the dependency's inits even when the result was unchanged. Now an
unchanged `enabled` result stops there; a change republishes the
requirements, and only a false-to-true change restarts the narrowing and the
inits (with a null kind and a detached tracker). Stale watchers from an
earlier enablement no-op via a generation check, and an init that finishes
after its dependency is disabled forces a republish.

Initial init publishes the combined requirements before running any init
handler, so tasks created by an init target a dependency the OS already
lists.

`effects.setDependencies` now drops the caller's tasks on any other package
that is no longer among its current dependencies, so packages no longer
declare task replay IDs on `withInit` for the SDK to clear.

* fix(start-os,start-sdk): mute tasks on disabled dependencies instead of clearing them

Clearing tasks when setDependencies dropped a dependency raced with an init
still running on it: a task created after the disable was orphaned, and the
SDK had to force a redundant republish to clear it.

Tasks now persist regardless of dependency state. A task counts against its
owner only when its target is the owner itself or one of its current
dependencies: the start gate, recheck_tasks, install, run_action, and
create_task all go through `has_blocking_task` / `is_task_target`, and the
UI's task list, primary status, and action conflict check filter the same
way via `getLiveTasks`. setDependencies stops the service when a newly
listed dependency unmutes an active critical task. Re-enabling a dependency
brings its tasks back as they were, and its init reruns to refresh them.

fix(ssl): issue standards-conforming authority key identifiers on self-signed roots (#4099)

* fix(ssl): omit authority key identifier on self-signed certificates

RFC 5280 permits a self-signed root to omit AKI, but an included AKI must carry a key identifier. OpenSSL generated issuer/serial-only AKIs when there was no issuer certificate in the builder context. Keep intermediates and issued leaves keyed to their issuers; preserve stored roots across upgrades.

Helix-Harness: claude-code
Helix-Model: claude-opus-5-5

* fix(ssl): give self-signed certificates a key-ID-only authority key identifier

CA/B Forum BR 7.1.2.1.3 recommends an AKI on a root whose keyIdentifier
equals the subjectKeyIdentifier, with no issuer or serial. Appending the
SKI before building the AKI lets OpenSSL copy it from the certificate
being built.
